antarctica-protection-2026:
For more than two centuries, ships from my home state of Massachusetts sailed south into the Southern Ocean that encircles Antarctica. They returned carrying whale oil from a wilderness largely valued for what could be extracted from it.

Today, another vessel built in Britain works those same waters for a very different purpose. The RRS Sir David Attenborough carries scientists, like those from Woods Hole in Massachusetts, not to exploit the Southern Ocean, but to understand and protect it.

That transformation was built upon international cooperation. In 1959, the United States, Britain and 10 other countries agreed to put competing interests aside and work together to preserve Antarctica for peaceful purposes and science by forming the Antarctic Treaty System. The Southern Ocean became a place where countries could demonstrate that cooperation was possible even when their wider interests diverged.

In 2009 Britain helped establish the region’s first marine protected area (MPA) around the South Orkney Islands. And in 2016, when I was US secretary of state, I had the privilege of working with the UK foreign ministry to negotiate the Ross Sea Region Marine Protected Area. At about 1.55 million square km it was, at the time, the largest area of ocean ever set aside for conservation and science. It was not easy. China, Russia, the US, New Zealand and others had different interests. But ultimately we found common ground.

The Ross Sea agreement was meant to be a beginning, not an endpoint. Countries wanted the Antarctic continent encircled by protected areas. Yet a decade later, no new protections have been created, while pressure on the ecosystem has continued to grow.

When governments gather next week in Hobart, Australia, for the annual meeting of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), there is an opportunity for a breakthrough. At a moment when the international system is under strain, Antarctica offers a place where cooperation may yet still work.

A breakthrough, though, requires countries to agree on three things. The first is krill. They are the foundation of everything that lives in these waters—what brings the penguins, the seals, the whales. For decades, we have been fishing them at industrial scale. Conserving krill is the foundation of protecting this ocean. Governments should agree on a new, science-based approach to managing krill fishery. That means spreading catches out, across regions and seasons, rather than concentrating fishing pressure in sensitive areas and times of the year. The objective is not to eliminate fishing. It is to ensure that fishing and the wider ecosystem can coexist.

The second is marine protection. Even when the fishery is well managed, marine protected areas are needed to safeguard essential krill nursery habitats, protect vulnerable species, conserve sensitive sea floor ecosystems and allow scientists to measure the impacts of climate change in one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. Countries should start by agreeing, this year, the proposal from Chile and Argentina to create a protected area around the important krill predator feeding grounds of the Antarctic Peninsula or Domain 1 MPA.

Finally, countries should look beyond the D1 MPA and establish a firm timetable for completing their promise to encircle the Antarctic continent with protected areas, bringing forward a full representative network of Antarctic MPAs by 2030. Just agreeing to the proposals already on the table, combined with existing protections, would protect over a quarter of the Southern Ocean, giving it one of the highest levels of ocean protection anywhere in the world.

What makes this moment different is that the old divisions about the future of Antarctica are beginning to shift—including, crucially, within industry itself. Progress has not always come easily when fishing and conservation interests have met at the same table. That is changing.

Industry is now at the table in a new and constructive way, thanks in part to the engagement of His Majesty King Charles III, who has helped bring governments, scientists, industry and civil society together around shared objectives.

The urgency goes beyond Antarctica. In 2022, countries committed to protecting 30 per cent of the planet’s land and ocean by 2030. Today, just over 10 per cent of the ocean is protected, meaning coverage needs to triple in four years. Meeting that commitment is not possible without more protection in the Southern Ocean.

Meanwhile, the costs of delaying are becoming harder to ignore. Two years ago, governments allowed spatial controls on krill fishing to expire. That means industrial vessels can now concentrate their catch in the same feeding grounds that penguins, seals and whales depend on. Science should be setting those limits—how much can be caught, where, and when—based on what the ecosystem can sustain. Allowing those controls to lapse was a mistake that needs to be corrected in Hobart.

Hobart presents something rare. The governments meeting there do not have to resolve every geopolitical disagreement. They just need to agree on enough: a protected area, responsible fishery management and a credible route towards the wider MPA network on a defined timetable.

In 2016, we showed that this kind of diplomacy was possible. The institutions that produced the Ross Sea agreement still exist. The science is there. Industry is increasingly engaged. The proposals are on the table. What is needed now is political persistence, and the willingness to find common ground without compromising the underlying objective.

If governments can reach a deal in Hobart, the achievement will be measured not only in square kilometres of ocean protected. This will demonstrate that countries with competing interests can still sit down together, listen to science, negotiate patiently and leave the room having protected something that belongs to no single nation. That would be a victory for the Southern Ocean, but it would also be a meaningful victory for hope and for institutions.

Two centuries after Massachusetts and British ships first sailed south in search of what Antarctica could yield, our purpose has changed. In Hobart we will learn whether our diplomacy can change with it. Let’s give something back to the Southern Ocean which has already given us so much.

John Kerry is a former US secretary of state and served as a special presidential envoy for climate under former US President Joe Biden.
obama-foundation-salaries:
The Obama Foundation appears to have an income inequality problem, with the former president’s political allies enjoying six-figure salaries while low-paid workers are fighting for union representation.

That’s the conclusion of an exclusive report by Fox News Digital, which tracked the top salary of CEO Valerie Jarrett at $771,000, a number of others in the half-a-million-dollars-a-year range and nearly 200 more pulling in six-figure salaries.

According to Fox:

The workplace disparity comes to light just as Fox News Digital reported that the long-delayed Obama Presidential Center’s price tag hit $1 billion — nearly triple the original estimate for the Chicago facility. The Obama Foundation, former President Barack Obama’s private nonprofit, reported 172 employees receiving more than $100,000 in salary in its 2025 tax filing — roughly half its 342 reported employees.

Jarrett, one of former President Barack Obama’s closest advisors and a former senior White House official, “has led the Obama Foundation since 2021, overseeing the final years of construction of the Presidential Center on Chicago’s South Side.”

Jarrett is one of the non-profit’s highest-paid executives with “previous ties to the Obama White House or campaign,” according to the outlet.

Approximate reported top salaries in the 2025 tax filing include:

• Christina Tchen, former chief of staff to first lady Michelle Obama — $431,000.
• Michael Strautmanis, a former Obama campaign and White House aide — $404,000.
• Laura Lucas Magnuson, a former White House communications official — $396,000.
• Robbin Cohen, former real estate executive of Gov. JB Pritzker family — $666,000
• Ammar Rizki, former Cook County chief financial officer — $400,000.

“The Foundation pays our employees rates that are competitive with the market,” Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation’s vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. “We have more than 500 employees worldwide, roughly 300 of whom are based at the Center.”

However, Ohio State University accounting professor Brian Mittendorf, who specializes in nonprofit finances, told the news outlet that the percentage of employees earning more than $100,000 was striking compared to typical not-for-profit organizations.

“That’s clearly higher percentage than your average nonprofit,” Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. “But here we’re dealing with a nonprofit that’s probably very expertise heavy. It’s very heavy on like the think tank side. And as you look at a think tank, it would look very differently than say a local food bank.”

While the professor apparently offered a possible explanation for the higher salaries, the news outlet also reported the Obama foundation was an outlier compared to five other presidential nonprofits, starting with former presidents Jimmy Carter through George W. Bush, according to their tax filings.

The percentages of employees with $100,000 packages or more in those presidential centers were around 25 percent or below, with the exception of George W. Bush’s at 37 percent.

Fox also compared CEO salaries and found Jarrett’s comparable to the Reagan Foundation’s at $735,000, which includes overseeing the former president’s iconic library in Southern California, but well above other presidential foundation CEOs, which are more in the half-million range.

Meanwhile, “rank-and-file” employees are pushing to unionize, Fox reported. They allege rolled-back benefits and mounting workloads as well as “deteriorating conditions” that have driven experienced colleagues to leave, resulting in more work for those who remain, according to the outlet.

“Amidst increasing workloads we have seen our benefits rolled back and support from leadership to be minimal,” the workers wrote in a public letter, cited by Fox.

Not unexpectedly, some Republicans also took issue with the salaries.

Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan in the past criticized the foundation’s use of public parkland for a private enterprise. He is no less critical of the salary revelations.

“The Obama Center is another far-left political operation that acts as a non-profit while using taxpayer dollars to make Barack Obama’s inner circle rich,” Grogan told Fox News Digital.

The Obama Foundation, however, maintains its construction and operational costs are paid for by revenues and private donations, though infrastructure improvements surrounding the center’s large campus were paid for by taxpayers.

Former Michigan gubernatorial candidate Tudor Dixon discusses Vice President JD Vance's visit to Michigan, focusing on affordability and the crucial midterm elections. Dixon highlights the GOP's confidence in key races and criticizes Democrats for opposing DHS funding. The visit follows a West Bloomfield synagogue attack, raising concerns about terror links to Hezbollah within the state.

Vice President JD Vance faced questions from Michigan voters during a town hall in Flat Rock as the state emerges as a key battleground in the fight for Senate control in November's midterms.

The town hall hosted by CBS News came just weeks before the midterm elections as Republicans are fighting to keep their majorities in the House and Senate. Vying for the open Senate seat in Michigan is Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former member of the House of Representatives.

Here are the top moments from the town hall:

The first question Vance fielded Saturday came from a 43-year-old Detroit barber, who asked him why gas prices remain significantly higher than during Trump's first term.

Vance first pointed to Iran’s attacks on commercial shipping and the resulting disruption to global energy markets, but he also placed blame on the Biden administration.

"That's actually the biggest reason why gas prices are so high, because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline," Vance said.

Vance said the Trump administration was using the Defense Production Act to help restore domestic refining capacity, but cautioned that rebuilding that infrastructure would take time.

CBS News anchor Tony Dokoupil pushed back on Vance's attempts to blame Biden, noting that Trump and Vance have been in office for nearly two years while Americans continued to face high gas prices.

MORNING GLORY: PRESIDENT TRUMP AND THE AMERICAN MILITARY HAVE BEATEN IRAN

US Vice President JD Vance speaks at a MAGA Inc. super PAC event in Sterling Heights, Michigan, August 31, 2026. Saul Loeb/Pool via REUTERS

Dokoupil shifted the conversation to government corruption, citing a Fox News poll showing that 60% of voters were extremely concerned about the issue. He asked Vance whether anything he had witnessed inside the Trump White House made him feel "squeamish."

"You certainly see evidence of corruption in Washington, D.C. Do I see evidence of corruption from the president of the United States, from the administration? No, Tony, I just don’t," Vance said.

The exchange came days after Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations that she sought $100,000 from a donor seeking access to Trump administration officials. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.

Dokoupil pressed Vance on the allegations involving Guilfoyle, along with concerns about restrictions on IRS scrutiny of Trump's tax returns and the president's cryptocurrency earnings.

Vance said selling access to the White House would be "disgusting and despicable" and that anyone responsible should face consequences.

Dokoupil then asked whether Vance would comply with subpoenas investigating alleged corruption if Democrats took control of Congress in January.

"Of course, of course I will," Vance said. "Look, we follow the law. I follow the law."

KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE FACES POTENTIAL SENATE PROBE OVER BOMBSHELL $100K ALLEGATION

President Donald Trump hired U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after her engagement to his eldest son fell through and now, after Donald Trump Jr. has married, his administration might be forced to fire her. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Vance was confronted over his immigration rhetoric by a naturalized U.S. citizen who said she voted for the vice president but questioned why the administration was "scapegoating immigrants."

The voter, who immigrated to the United States 20 years ago, challenged Vance over his characterization of certain H-1B visa workers as "foreign indentured servants."

"To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said.

But Vance defended his remarks, arguing that his criticism was aimed at companies exploiting foreign workers rather than immigrants themselves. He said the H-1B visa system gives employers too much power over foreign workers whose ability to remain in the country depends on their employment, while also allowing companies to replace American workers with visa holders.

"That's not a criticism of the H-1B visa holder. That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker," Vance said.

Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether his rhetoric and that of the Trump administration dehumanized immigrants.

"My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant. And in fact, I love a number of immigrants," Vance said.

But Vance argued that allowing too many immigrants into the country too quickly could undermine social cohesion and fundamentally change American communities.

"I have neighbors, I have friends of mine who literally don't know a single person in their neighborhood who speaks the language they do," Vance said. "I don't think it's unreasonable for an American citizen to want to share their community with people they have something in common with."

Though the town hall was pre-recorded, Vance took to X shortly after it aired to share footage from showing a burning building in France amid mass riots. He said what's unfolding in France is a cautionary tale for the United States.

"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance posted on X.

"They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen. I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn," Vance continued.

A boat floats as commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP)

Dokoupil pressed Vance on why the war with Iran had dragged on longer than the Trump administration anticipated, asking the vice president, "Why haven't we won decisively?"

Vance argued that the U.S. had "in some ways" already won the war, claiming that American military strikes had successfully destroyed Iran's nuclear program, which he described as the central reason Trump launched the operation.

"Have we destroyed the Iranian nuclear program? The answer is yes," Vance said.

But Vance said the administration was still working to secure a "long-term" and "verifiable" commitment from Iran that it would not rebuild its nuclear capabilities, while also preventing Tehran from disrupting global energy supplies.

Vance said the Iranians responded by terrorizing commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global oil supplies and driving up gas prices.

He claimed gas prices would be "three times as high" if it weren't for the U.S. Navy protecting commercial shipping through the waterway.

VANCE TAKES AIM AT SOFT-ON-CRIME DEMS AS GOP FACES UPHILL MIDTERM BATTLE: ‘LOST THEIR MINDS’

Vance was also urged by a Michigan voter to condemn antisemitism within his own political base, including rhetoric from prominent conservative figures such as Tucker Carlson.

The question came from Eddie Rubin, a lifelong Democrat whose 5-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son survived the attack at Temple Israel, which occurred in March in Michigan.

The attacker, a Lebanese-born U.S. citizen, rammed his pickup truck through the synagogue's entrance before exchanging gunfire with security. The attacker was killed, but no children or synagogue staff members were injured.

"I condemn anti-Semitism. I condemn Jew hatred," Vance said.

But Vance also turned the conversation to Michigan's Senate race, criticizing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for his response to the synagogue attack. Vance pointed to El-Sayed's remark that "hurt people hurt people."

"He went around and said, 'hurt people, hurt people', showing empathy, not with you and your family, which is where I think that we got to show empathy. But showing empathy to a guy who nearly killed hundreds of innocent children," Vance said.

El-Sayed had condemned the attack and later apologized for his wording, saying he never intended to justify the violence.

(Photo by Luke Sharrett/Getty Images)

The Army is moving to field a new drone-killing laser — and one company is already showing how it could be powered in the field.

AeroVironment won a $464.8 million Army contract in September for its LOCUST X3 laser, and the company said in a Sept. 8 release that its LOCUST laser system “delivers engagements for less than $10 per shot.” Army officials said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington that the first LOCUST X3 could be ready to counter drones by early 2028, Military Times reported.

“We’re moving from science fiction to science reality,” John Garrity, AeroVironment’s vice president of directed energy systems, told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

“This first of its kind directed energy program will enable our formations to defeat unmanned systems and dominate from the outset,” Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army’s vice chief of staff, said in a Sept. 2 Army release that called the award the service’s first contract to produce a high-energy laser weapon.

The laser runs on electricity and has “a magazine that regenerates with the system’s power supply,” according to the release.

“Directed energy weapons have been considered S&T [science and technology] projects, and I’m proud that the Army is moving at speed and scale to deliver this first time capability,” Brent Ingraham, the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, said in the release.

Missiles that can cost $500,000 to $1 million are fired at drones that cost a few thousand dollars or less, and “even though we’re successful in taking those out, we’re still losing,” Garrity added. Lasers “really push that economic cost curve in the right direction for the first time reliably.”

Each laser shot costs “less than a cup of coffee” in energy, Garrity said, and the under-$10 figure is essentially the cost of that electricity. He said a laser’s upfront cost is about even with other counter-drone weapons, some of which need expensive radars, and that it comes out ahead after bringing down a single drone.

A hybrid truck built by Harbinger, a California maker of electric and hybrid truck chassis, powered a LOCUST X3 at American Rheinmetall’s booth during the meeting, Defence Blog reported. The LOCUST X3 is a 30-kilowatt laser, according to AeroVironment’s September contract release. (RELATED: Meet The Lasers That Eat Drones For Breakfast)

Harbinger’s battery system holds about 105 kilowatt-hours of energy, which “theoretically could support a continuous 30 kW load for approximately 3.5 hours,” John Harris, co-founder and CEO of Harbinger, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“However, counter-drone laser systems typically operate in short bursts rather than drawing power continuously, so actual operating time depends on the system’s power requirements and usage patterns,” Harris added.

Harbinger is part of an American Rheinmetall team building hybrid-powered uncrewed ground vehicles that carry supplies for the Army, according to a release on Harbinger’s website.

Leonardo DRS, which builds onboard power systems for military vehicles, has “proven across multiple vehicle platforms that our onboard power technology delivers the electrical power required for directed-energy missions,” Dennis Crumley, senior vice president and general manager of Leonardo DRS Land Electronics, said in a statement to the DCNF.

Drawing power from the vehicles a unit already drives can “reduce or eliminate separate generators and generator trailers, along with the equipment, spare parts, and maintenance associated with them,” Crumley said.

AeroVironment is due to deliver the first LOCUST X3 by the final quarter of fiscal 2027, and the Army plans to put it on its Joint Light Tactical Vehicle, Military Times reported.

Kirk Williams, chief engineer at the Army’s Directed Energy Project Office, told the outlet that the Army would like to keep the first unit for testing and training, but that every capable counter-drone system it builds “tends to get deployed somewhere.” The laser’s modular design will let soldiers handle field-level maintenance, Williams said, according to the outlet.

The Pentagon named three lasers, including one from AeroVironment, and Epirus’ Leonidas high-powered microwave on Oct. 5 for a counter-drone pilot at U.S. bases, Military Times reported. The Pentagon said the pilot will collect data on the weapons’ performance, cost and upkeep, according to the outlet.

“This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, who directs the joint task force running the pilot, said in the Pentagon’s release, according to Military Times.

“The more capabilities we put in the hands of soldiers, the easier they are to maintain, the more reliable they are, the better,” Col. Charles Kean, the 7th Infantry Division’s deputy commanding officer for support, told an audience at the meeting, according to Military Times. (RELATED: US Military Uses Laser At Border To Shoot Down Drug Cartel Drones)

“It’s not just the Army; it’s other allies, it’s other services throughout the Department of War that are all coming to us saying, ‘Hey, we need this capability. We need this capability now,’” Garrity told the DCNF.

AeroVironment is buying parts that take a long time to make, lining up second suppliers and expanding its manufacturing, and its directed energy business will have “well over 100 people in Albuquerque” working on the lasers, he said.

“Directed energy is here. It’s reliable. It is ready to get into the field at a fast rate,” Garrity said.

AeroVironment’s contract covers more than 26 laser weapons, Garrity told Military Times.

Ex-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia had nothing but kind words to say about President Trump hours after she left her post following just five days in the role.

“President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him,” she posted on X. “No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.”

The post included a photo of Zacharia smiling while standing next to Trump as he sat at the Resolute Desk inside the Oval Office during her brief tenure, with a map on the president’s desk that had its details blurred out.

It had 7.2 million views as of Saturday morning.

In a sign of the rapid disintegration of her tenure, the post “pinned” to the top of her account Oct. 9 had screen shots of Trump congratulating her on her appointment as press secretary.

She left her post Friday after a pair of shaky interviews on Fox News.

On Thursday, she appeared on Sean Hannity’s program where the host said her first and only White House press briefing had been “widely panned” and questioned her decision to label herself as an “attorney” despite failing to pass the California bar after graduating from law school.

During a Friday morning interview on “Fox & Friends,” she struggled to deliver talking points about the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home and wasn’t able to say when her next press briefing would occur.

Hours later, Trump publicly urged her to reconsider her role, telling the reporters before departing the White House for a rally, “I’ve watched her for years on television, but I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need this.’”

Zacharia isn’t out entirely: a source familiar with the situation said she would be transitioning to a new role, and she was to have dined Friday night with Vice President JD Vance.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia was sitting with the paper for a White House interview Friday when she was summoned away to learn that her assignment had ended.

She didn’t return to the interview.

Among those mentioned as possible successors is CNN commentator Scott Jennings, who is close to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Asked on air Friday if he was interested in the job, Jennings diverted, saying “I haven’t spoken to anybody about it tonight or today.”

(Aging Untold) — The FDA’s first-ever approval of a blood test to help diagnose Alzheimer’s disease marks a significant step forward in treating a condition that affects about 7 million Americans, with that number expected to nearly double by 2060, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.

The blood test, known as Lumipulse, was approved by the FDA in May 2025 as a “less invasive option” that “reduces reliance on PET scans and increases diagnosis accessibility.”

Rebecca Edelmayer, vice president of scientific engagement for the Alzheimer’s Association, said getting a diagnosis can be difficult and time-consuming.

“One of the things that we continue to see is that for some patients it could take years,” Edelmayer said. “And we know that having an early and accurate diagnosis is so critical — especially when there’s treatments that have been approved today, to really help slow down the disease process.”

Traditional diagnosis often involves referrals to specialists, expensive PET scans of the brain and lumbar punctures, also known as spinal taps.

“It’s a very, very exciting time in this field,” Edelmayer said.

The blood test detects amyloid plaques in the brain, which are considered key markers for Alzheimer’s disease.

Dr. Abhay Moghekar, an associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, helped study and evaluate the test for FDA approval.

“If this test is positive, there’s a greater than 90% chance that you have amyloid plaque in your brain,” Moghekar said.

Moghekar called it “absolutely a breakthrough in the field.”

“Getting a blood test is gonna be far easier, quicker and cheaper,” he said. “It’s going to allow early access to therapy, so it is going to revolutionize care of patients with dementia.”

The FDA has cleared the blood test for use only in patients 55 and older who are already experiencing memory problems. The agency cautions that this is not intended as a standalone diagnostic tool for Alzheimer’s. Results should be interpreted alongside a patient’s medical history and other assessments, such as cognitive testing.

Moghekar believes blood biomarker tests could eventually predict whether someone is at risk of developing Alzheimer’s before symptoms appear.

“I think we are moving towards a goal of preventing Alzheimer’s disease rather than treating it once you already have the disease,” he said.

Kathi Rigby was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2023 at the age of 68 after experiencing memory problems and difficulty finding words.

After her diagnosis, she entered a clinical trial for a drug that aims to slow cognitive decline by targeting and removing amyloid plaques. The treatment received FDA clearance in 2024.

“It was so wonderful because it did such a difference for me — night and day — it’s a blessing,” Rigby said.

Her husband, Brent, said doctors told them 95% of the plaque was removed.

“The longer you wait, the more damage is done,” Kathi Rigby said about the importance of early diagnosis.

Brad Cooper revealed Friday that America’s naval blockade and economic pressure campaign have inflicted “devastating costs” on Iran, denying the regime at least $25 billion in oil exports and leaving its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) unable to pay its own troops.

In a video update Friday, Cooper outlined how the United States has targeted three pillars of the Iranian regime’s financial survival — oil exports, digital financing, and security-force payroll — building on the devastation inflicted during the 38-day Operation Epic Fury military campaign earlier this year.

“The sum total of these actions has imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus and the IRGC specifically,” Cooper declared.

The blockade has prevented Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil, Cooper said, cutting off billions that Tehran could otherwise channel into its terrorist proxy networks, weapons production, and attacks against American forces and regional allies.

Beyond oil exports, CENTCOM has helped U.S. government agencies freeze nearly $350 million in cryptocurrency assets, further cutting off funds Iran could use to finance terrorism, replenish its weapons stockpiles, or rebuild military factories destroyed by American strikes.

The financial squeeze has now reached the regime’s own security apparatus, with Cooper reporting that Iran’s government is “withholding salaries, pensions, and benefits” across industries including oil, energy, manufacturing, construction, and the IRGC itself.

In a striking reversal of Tehran’s longstanding role as financier of its regional proxies, the money is now reportedly flowing in the opposite direction — back toward the IRGC itself.

“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said.

Cooper’s assessment underscores the mounting impact of President Donald Trump’s broader campaign to cripple Iran’s military capabilities and financial lifelines, combining the destruction inflicted during Operation Epic Fury with Operation Economic Outcast’s naval blockade and sweeping financial restrictions.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has spearheaded Operation Economic Outcast, described it as the greatest economic isolation operation in history and announced at the beginning of October that September marked the first month on record in which Iran loaded no crude oil for export.

Reimposed in July, the U.S. naval blockade has effectively shut down Iran’s seaborne crude exports while American forces keep the Strait of Hormuz open to commercial traffic, allowing Gulf oil shipments to continue flowing despite Tehran’s repeated attacks.

Cooper said humanitarian assistance was the only exception to the blockade, emphasizing that Iran has “no exports and no imports by sea.”

Despite continued Iranian attacks on commercial shipping, Cooper rejected Tehran’s claims of controlling the strategic waterway.

“Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran, and it remains open for business,” Cooper declared.

Over the past week alone, roughly 400 merchant ships passed through Hormuz, while U.S. forces helped regional partners move more than 100 million barrels of crude oil through the waterway, Cooper reported.

Those shipments add to more than 1.3 billion barrels of Gulf crude that American forces have helped regional partners move through Hormuz in recent months — even as the U.S. blockade continues to deny Tehran access to its own oil-export lifeline.

More than 50,000 American service members remain deployed across the Middle East, where U.S. forces continue clearing Iranian mines, enforcing the naval blockade, defending regional partners, and protecting commercial shipping.

“The Islamic regime is clearly feeling the economic pain, and the IRGC is increasingly showing signs of greater desperation as a result,” Cooper said.

The Revolutionary Guards have nevertheless continued attacking merchant vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, killing more than 20 civilian mariners since February, according to International Maritime Organization figures cited by Cooper.

(We can’t promise that nothing will ever slip through the cracks, but we’re vigilant!) Astonishingly, though, some editors have actually defended publishing the pieces even when writers have been caught. The Wall Street Journal published an op-ed from a hedge fund billionaire, Stan Druckenmiller, that turned out to have been AI-generated (probably because billionaires are inarticulate due to a lifetime of never having to craft arguments to persuade the yes-men around them), but the paper defended publishing the piece, since it reflected the billionaire’s genuine opinion.

The trends are dire. But it’s obvious why these publications are rushing to replace writers. They are for-profit corporations, whose ultimate loyalty is to shareholders, not workers. AI is great for them, because it can produce “content” at a fraction of the expense that a writer costs. In fact, on the Milton Friedman theory that the only responsibility a business has is to increase its profits, CEOs are obligated to replace writers with AI if doing so is better for the bottom line. It’s a simple calculation: if producing 100 posts with AI costs almost nothing and takes four minutes, but paying a writer to produce 20 posts costs $5,000, well, why would you pay the writer? The calculation might hold even if the quality drops substantially, errors are introduced, and audience loyalty plummets. Even if you lost 60 percent of your readership, you might still make a lot more per story, because you can pump them out in seconds.

Futurism reports that despite the common narrative that AI has not led to major job loss, creative industries are being “eviscerated” by AI, which is fueling “one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” with more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries being lost in four years. The situation is horrible for artists. Game studios are now designing their worlds and levels using “art assets generated with full AI workflows.” As Brian Merchant reported earlier this year:

Opportunities and pay rates declining as clients and employers embrace generative AI. Artists getting more touch-up jobs and fewer well-paying, sustainable gigs. Pessimism, anger, and even despair, growing common, if not universal, in the field.

This is especially galling given that all of the AI models that are being used to replace artists were trained through the mass theft of those very same artists’ work!

Now here at Current Affairs, we’ve decided to say: fuck that! Over 62 beautiful print issues, we have commissioned hundreds of original, handmade artworks from brilliant artists around the world. We’ve published meticulously researched and edited articles, which often take weeks or months to go from the draft stage to publication. We spend ages working on our page layouts, poring over photographs for the magazine, tweaking sketches, moving sentences around in articles. The labor that goes into this magazine has been extensive from the start, and most of it is hidden from view. We do it because we care about quality. If you pick up a copy of our magazine, you’ll see the result. I think it’s clear when you read it that we actually care about what we’re putting out. It’s not just Content designed to farm clicks.

Current Affairs has always been a bit of an anachronism. We started a print magazine in 2016. Nobody thought this was a good idea. (The editor in chief of Vanity Fair told me to my face that this was a wholly misguided project and certain to fail. I remain grateful to him for giving me the resolve to prove the prediction wrong.) Everyone else was pivoting to video. We pivoted to ink and paper, sent via the U.S. Postal Service. Ten years later, we are still here, while a lot of other places that began with a lot more money have folded (see, e.g., the Messenger, which burned through $50 million in a year and then died). The reason we’ve survived is that there are still many people who don’t like that all media is now just transient images on a social media feed. They experience a thrill when they get a cool thing in the mail that they can unwrap and hold. They know that seeing a beautiful illustration on the printed page is different, and better, from seeing it as a JPEG on your phone.

So we don’t really give a damn what the trends in the industry are. We located ourselves in New Orleans when everyone else is in New York. We defiantly publish on obscure topics that aren’t anywhere in the news cycle. (Have you read Alice Millar-Thompson’s article on eel smuggling?) And we’re going to keep paying human artists to create elaborate, gorgeous works of handmade art that take ages to make.

So our rule is simple: No AI generated articles or illustrations in the magazine! We are not going to feed you slop. And we think you should not give money to any publication that does feed you slop, because they’re both treating their audience with contempt, and avoiding paying workers so that their owners can get richer.

This doesn’t mean nobody doing work here can ever use any of the softwares that are broadly lumped together as AI. Much as we respect the Luddites around here, we’re not against technological innovation. Nothing in our rules prohibits writers from using a new tool to help them research something, or prevents an artist from using a tool to, say, add a texture or change a color, or make some kind of small element. But we need, first, to ensure that technologies are a tool used by workers to help them, rather than a tool used to replace workers. And, second, we need to make sure that readers aren’t being fed things that look like people’s genuine thoughts and creative expression but are in fact the product of disembodied mathematical formulas.

I’ll admit, I used to be excited by generative AI. I made goofy little images in DALL-E. I liked the dumb novelty songs. I thought it could be a cool tool for creative professionals to play around with. I forgot for a moment that we live under capitalism, where every new technology will be used by the ruling class to fuck over workers. As Garrison Lovely writes in his new book Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us—and How to Stop It, the developers of AI don’t see it as an asset for workers, but as a way to replace them. They’re trying to build a device whose success is literally measured by whether it successfully replaces people. It is not being designed to help the average person’s capacity to achieve their goals, but to help automate us all into obsolescence. That’s why it has to be fought aggressively.

We at Current Affairs are not capitalists. There are no profits to be made here. We’re a unionized 501c3 organization, which means that we have no incentive to try to replace our workers with machines. So we’re going to demonstrate that you don’t have to do this, that there’s another way, and that it results in better media that is more pleasurable to read and more informative. It’s not going to be easy, because competitor publications are going to be able to produce immense quantities of writing in the time we are painstakingly correcting and adjusting a single article.

But like John Henry, before we let that steam drill beat us, we will die with our hammer in our hand.

As anger builds online against comedian Shane Gillis’ description of women as “whores” during his “Saturday Night Live” monologue, one party is staying noticeably absent from the conversation: “SNL” itself.

The show and its network NBC haven’t commented publicly on the backlash, nor have they responded to requests for comment. It’s a familiar playbook for “SNL,” which has often chosen to stay mum and ride out the waves of controversy that have punctured its decades-long run.

The backlash over Gillis’ monologue was, perhaps, predictable. The Philadelphia-born comic was previously fired from his role as a cast member, just a few days after his hiring was announced, after clips emerged of him using an ethnic slur against Chinese people and a mock Asian accent on his podcast, as well as gay slurs. By way of explanation, he offered that he was a “comedian who pushes boundaries.”

Gillis’ return to the series as a guest host last weekend saw him in classic form, styling himself as a beer-swilling bro, an everyman who shirks political correctness. He hasn’t been to the gym in a while, he said during his “SNL” monologue, so he should be forgiven for being surprised by how women dress to work out now: “Like whores.”

“Look, I’m sorry. There’s no other way to describe it,” he said. They wear tight shorts, he said, with the color of “artificial bait.”

“SNL” and its longtime boss Lorne Michaels – have often stayed quiet after hosts or their comments attracted backlash, never commenting, for example, on the controversy over Dave Chappelle, who has hosted the show twice since being criticized for transphobic comments he made in 2021.

While “SNL” is staying quiet, others are speaking out — both in and outside 30 Rock.

For Jessie Leo, a graphic designer who works on the long-running sketch comedy show, Gillis’ comment wasn’t just offensive. It was also indicative of an unsafe workplace. “How am I ever supposed to feel comfortable going to NBC HR after knowing the company and people I work for gave the thumbs up for Shane’s whore joke during his monologue,” she wrote on Instagram late Tuesday. “In general, but especially at a time like this with rape culture and victim-blaming assailing women from all angles right now.”

Cecily Strong, who was the longest-tenured female cast member in “SNL” history, excoriated Gillis’ cruel characterization of women on her own Instagram story. “On my way to Pilates in my new slutty ass orange shoes and rainbow socks,” she wrote above a picture of her legs in workout gear. “Might sell sex on the way not sure.”

Former “SNL” cast member Ego Nwodim cast her own shade at Gillis, writing “whore reporting for duty” on a picture of herself dressed for the gym earlier this week. On TikTok, too, dozens of women have posted images of their gym outfits with references to Gillis’ comment.

Outside of “SNL”-world, “Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy made a minute-and-a-half video about the monologue, saying, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”

He called out other men, too. “More men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime,’” he said.

Like many of Gillis’ critics, Strong highlighted the timing of Gillis’ monologue. As Gillis was joking about women dressed like “whores” and working out at his friend Joe Rogan’s private gym, less than 200 miles north an investigation was unfolding into the alleged gang rape of a former undergraduate at Cornell University. The investigation into the 2024 incident, triggered after the former undergraduate filed a lawsuit, unleashed outrage and a flood of women to share similar stories of sexual violence and abuse.

Winter is arriving early across Montana and the Northern Rockies as heavy snow and rain blanket the region through Wednesday.

The winter weather comes as moisture from the remnants of former Tropical Storm Rachel moves across the region.

As Rachel’s remnants continue east toward New England, a deep dip in the jet stream is bringing colder air into the West, driving snowfall across the central and southern Rockies.

Meanwhile, cold air is pushing south, allowing snow to accumulate across higher elevations in Wyoming, Utah, and Colorado.

The heaviest snowfall is expected to affect high-elevation passes and mountain peaks across Utah’s Wasatch Range and the western and central slopes of Colorado.

Elevations above 8,000 feet could see an additional 8 to 12 inches of snow, with some mountain peaks receiving up to a foot.

The winter weather is expected to taper off by late Wednesday morning, leaving isolated mountain flurries as the trough weakens and moves east across the Plains.

The early-October snowfall could provide a welcome boost for ski resorts across the West, which are looking to rebound after a dismal, dry 2025-2026 winter season.

According to Travel Weekly, booking data through August from Inntopia DestiMetrics showed lodging occupancy rates were down 5.6% for November through February. The data covers 17 mountain destinations across Colorado, Utah, California, Nevada, Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho.

Last season, numerous ski resorts also closed early amid a lack of snow and periods of unseasonably warm weather.

Widespread snow drought conditions gripped much of the Intermountain West and Northern Rockies last winter, driven by persistent warm temperatures and a weakened northern storm track.

Many areas finished the season with snowfall totals among their 10 lowest on record, leaving snowpack levels well below what ski resorts typically hope to see.

A potentially strong Super El Niño could bring a different pattern this winter.

Because snowfall depends heavily on the overlap of moisture and freezing temperatures, El Niño can produce contrasting outcomes across the northern and southern U.S.

A more active Pacific jet stream can direct storms toward California and the Southwest, potentially boosting snowfall at higher elevations across the Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies.

Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports the latest on the ongoing conflict between Ukraine and Russia on ‘Special Report.’

Let’s get the preliminaries out of the way. Ukraine has corruption problems and political dysfunction of its own. But in this war, Ukraine is unequivocally the good guy. Russia’s invasion was unprovoked, unjustified and indefensible. Vladimir Putin is the aggressor. Volodymyr Zelensky is defending his country. Period.

Now let’s talk about geopolitical reality. Donald Trump is attempting something far more ambitious than ending the war in Ukraine. He is trying to rearrange the strategic chessboard for the next several decades. Understanding that objective is essential to understanding his seemingly contradictory decisions.

The United States has one truly consequential long-term strategic competitor: China. Russia is dangerous, nuclear-armed and capable of wreaking havoc on its neighbors. But Russia is also a declining power with an economy dependent on natural resources, deteriorating demographics and ambitions that, while unacceptable, are largely regional. China is something else entirely. Beijing seeks to challenge American economic, technological and military leadership globally. It has the industrial capacity, financial resources and strategic patience to pursue that ambition for generations. China’s challenge is in a different category altogether.

CHINA’S LONG-TERM FINANCES ARE ALL WET AS BILL TO MAINTAIN HUGE NAVY COMES DUE IN 2031

Here is Trump’s dilemma: Europe is not yet strong enough to contain Russia without substantial American support. Despite years of promises, too many NATO allies remain dependent on American military capabilities, intelligence, logistics and leadership. Until Europe can handle Russia largely on its own, the United States must continue devoting enormous resources to European security. Every additional weapons system, dollar and hour of strategic attention consumed by Moscow is a resource unavailable for deterring Beijing or addressing other threats around the world.

Trump is trying to change that equation. His apparent objective is to create conditions under which Russia can eventually become a more normal, economically engaged country rather than a permanent adversary requiring America’s undivided attention. Think of it as strategic triage. In the long run, we want a fully economically engaged Russia that has something meaningful to lose, but still needs a good kick in the ass from time to time to remind Putin and his successors to stay the hell out of Europe. That is a far better outcome than a permanently isolated, militarized Russia driven ever deeper into China’s embrace.

NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP

That doesn’t mean trusting Putin. It means understanding his incentives. Putin wants two things: money and real estate. He wants the economic benefits of international engagement and the territorial advantages of an empire. Trump is uniquely positioned to offer the former while making the latter prohibitively expensive. That is the needle Trump is trying to thread.

But he is threading it while balancing competing global equities: keeping energy prices manageable, maintaining pressure on Iran, deterring China, supporting Israel, reassuring allies and protecting the American economy. Europe’s continued military dependence makes every calculation harder. And until Europe is genuinely capable of assuming primary responsibility for its own defense, America cannot simply disengage from Russia, however much we might wish to concentrate our resources elsewhere.

Which brings us to Zelensky. I have enormous respect for his courage and determination. And when Ukraine strikes Russian oil refineries, the military logic is obvious. Petroleum revenues finance Putin’s war machine. Disrupting them is a legitimate strategic objective when conducted within the laws of war. Zelensky is right to hit Russia where it hurts. But being right is not always enough. An attack that makes perfect sense to Ukrainian military planners may complicate Trump’s larger negotiations, disrupt energy markets and create political problems at home.

Zelensky’s first responsibility is Ukraine’s survival. Trump’s first responsibility is America’s interests. Those interests overlap enormously, but they are not identical. Here is what Zelensky must understand: Trump is not simply Ukraine’s principal supplier of weapons, intelligence and money. He is a strategic partner managing a far larger set of global obligations. Zelensky needs to stop approaching Washington principally with a shopping list and start asking a different question: Mr. President, what can Ukraine do to help you accomplish your broader objectives while protecting our sovereignty?

TRUMP CALLS FOR UKRAINE TO REPLACE ZELENSKYY AFTER CLASH OVER RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL: 'GET A NEW PRESIDENT'

That is not capitulation. It is sophisticated diplomacy. It means coordinating major military and economic initiatives before they become surprises. It means understanding American energy concerns and domestic political pressures. It means offering Trump practical ways to demonstrate progress rather than simply demanding more assistance. And it means recognizing that Trump’s ability to sustain American support depends partly on convincing Americans that his policies are working.

There is another reality diplomats often prefer not to discuss: Donald Trump conducts foreign policy through personal relationships to an extraordinary degree. I worked for him. I know. The conventional diplomatic playbook emphasizes prepared meetings, formal communications and bureaucratic coordination. Trump places enormous weight on personal access and whether someone understands what he is trying to achieve. The late diplomat George Ball captured an enduring truth: "Nothing propinks like propinquity." In plain English, proximity matters.

TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

Zelensky needs to be talking to Trump constantly. Not once a month. Not only when he needs another weapons package. Almost every day. Sometimes to discuss the battlefield. Sometimes to share intelligence. Sometimes to float an idea. Sometimes just to tell him a joke or share some gossip. That may sound trivial when thousands are dying in Ukraine, but it isn’t. Personal familiarity creates trust. Trust creates access. Access creates influence.

Even Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with their almost hourly access to Trump, can occasionally be surprised by a decision. That is the nature of his unusually fluid, personalized decision-making process. Imagine the disadvantage of a foreign leader relying exclusively on traditional diplomatic channels. Zelensky cannot afford that disadvantage.

There is also the uncomfortable matter of American politics. Trump needs Republicans to retain control of the Senate in November. Zelensky needs Ukraine to survive the coming winter. To a neutral observer, those objectives are hardly equivalent. To each leader, however, they are critical. Should Zelensky intervene in an American election? Absolutely not. Should he understand Trump’s political pressures and help create conditions under which continued American support becomes easier to defend? Absolutely.

There is a world of difference between helping a political party and helping an American president demonstrate that his foreign policy is producing results. Zelensky should be looking for opportunities to do the latter every day. Understanding Trump’s political constraints is not the same as surrendering Ukraine’s interests. It is recognizing that the most effective way to secure American support is to make Ukraine’s success part of Trump’s success.

But this bargain must run both ways. Zelensky cannot be expected to restrain attacks on Russian energy infrastructure while Putin continues pounding Ukraine’s power plants, cities and civilian infrastructure. Ukraine has already demonstrated a willingness to consider reciprocal restraint. That willingness must be met by Russian action, not simply another American request for Ukrainian patience. If Trump wants Zelensky to accommodate his broader strategy, Trump must use America’s enormous economic leverage to make Putin accommodate it as well.

That means no unilateral rewards for aggression, no permanent sanctions relief in exchange for temporary gestures and no settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless while Russia rearms. A temporary diesel arrangement or sanctions reprieve is not normalization. It is a tactic. Real normalization requires verifiable Russian behavior and meaningful consequences for renewed aggression. Putin wants economic engagement. Trump controls much of what makes that engagement possible. That leverage should be used to secure lasting concessions, not exchanged for another fleeting promise.

Meanwhile, Europe must accelerate its military transformation. The United States cannot indefinitely remain Europe’s principal insurance policy while simultaneously preparing for the far greater strategic challenge posed by China. The ultimate prize is not a handshake with Putin or another White House announcement. It is a Europe capable of defending itself, a Russia with powerful incentives to stay within its borders and an America free to concentrate its strategic weight where the greatest long-term danger lies.

Until Europe reaches that point, Trump must balance competing military, economic and political demands that Zelensky cannot afford to ignore. And Trump must recognize that Ukraine’s survival is essential to making his larger strategy credible. Zelensky needs Trump’s leverage, weapons and economic power. Trump needs Zelensky’s cooperation to produce a sustainable settlement rather than a theatrical one. Putin must understand he cannot play them against each other indefinitely.

The message to Zelensky is simple: Help Trump succeed in his larger geopolitical mission, and insist that Ukraine’s survival be part of that success. The message to Trump is equally simple: Give Zelensky a reason to trust that helping you will not cost him his country. Neither man needs to abandon his interests. Both need to understand the other’s.

Two-thirds of Americans, including half of Republicans, say they want the government to spend more money to reduce health care costs — but they still like their health insurance and most are skeptical of Medicare for All, new polling data suggests.

When it comes to figuring out the specific policy to lower costs, only 43% want Medicare for All — which would create a single-payer health system operated by the US government, polling released on Tuesday by Axios-Ipsos shows.

In contrast, nearly a quarter (24%) oppose universal Medicare, while almost a third (32%) say they aren’t sure.

However, the move is popular with 62% of Democrats, many of whom want to see a similar system to the United Kingdom’s National Health Service, which is free at the point of access but paid for through taxes.

Nearly half (47%) of independents also said they supported the idea, polling showed.

“People are justifiably angry at the high and rising cost and inefficiency of health care in the US,” Mark Washawsky, Senior Fellow at the right-wing public policy think tank the American Enterprise Institute, told The Post.

“But, in these surveys, they are not aware of the extremely high taxes, restrictions on care, slowing of innovation, and political rent-seeking that will result if Medicare for all is adopted,” Washawsky said.

“A better way is to introduce effective competition into the sector, while making sure everyone is covered and supporting those most in financial need,” he added.

More than 70 million people are enrolled in Medicare, which insures Americans 65 and over and some people with disabilities.

It is the federal government’s third largest expense after Social Security and interest on the national debt — consuming 14% total spending. Medicare paid out $1.2 trillion last year — twice the figure a decade ago.

Opponents of Medicare for All said they fear a worse quality of care than private insurance, while others feared it would become too expensive for taxpayers or expand the size of the government too much.

Many respondents said they would be more likely to support a congressional candidate who favored expanding government subsidies of health care costs, reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in 2026, and expanding prescription drug discount platforms.

Republicans were particularly divided over expanding government subsidies for health care costs, with 31% more likely to back a candidate who supports the idea, 29% less likely, and 31% saying it would make no difference.

Insurance premiums are up 27% since 2020, according to Kaiser Family Foundation data.

The survey also showed plummeting support for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose level of trust is now at a record low of 25%.

Trust in both congressional Democrats (25%) and Republicans (20%) is also at record lows ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

And trust in President Trump for health-related information also fell to a record low of 20%, the survey shows.

Polling consistently shows that insurance costs are the biggest concerns for Americans when it comes to their health care.

Almost a third (29%) of Americans surveyed said that the cost of health care is the “most urgent health problem” facing the country, according to a Gallup study conducted in December 2025.

That represented a rise from 23% just a year earlier, and was the highest level recorded since 2004.

Health care cost now outpaces access and obesity—at 17% and 8% respectively—as what Americans consider the nation’s top health problem.

A federal appeals court on Tuesday ruled that a federal ban on gun possession by convicted felons cannot be constitutionally applied to some people whose prior offenses did not involve violence or threats indicating a risk of misusing firearms.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit issued two rulings clarifying when the federal prohibition on gun possession by convicted felons can be enforced under the Second Amendment.

The court, which includes several judges appointed by President Donald Trump, upheld the firearms restriction against a man with a conviction stemming from a carjacking but ruled that the ban could not be applied to another man based on his prior drunk-driving convictions.

One of the cases decided on Tuesday involved James Bost, who pleaded guilty to terroristic threats, criminal conspiracy, false imprisonment and simple assault in Pennsylvania state court following a 2002 carjacking.

MAJOR APPEALS COURT DECLARES NEW JERSEY AR-15 BAN UNCONSTITUTIONAL IN LANDMARK SECOND AMENDMENT RULING

A federal appeals court ruled that a federal law prohibiting felons from owning guns can only be constitutionally applied when a person's previous conviction involved violence or threats that indicate they could pose a risk of misusing firearms. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)

Bost was later indicted on federal firearms charges after authorities found him in possession of a gun despite his prior convictions. He sought to dismiss the charges, arguing that the federal ban violated his Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms.

U.S. Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas, writing for the majority in the decision against Bost, said people convicted of crimes demonstrating a risk of physical violence through the misuse of firearms may presumptively be disarmed based on those convictions alone.

"The right to keep and bear arms has limits, and this is one: Those who pose a risk of physical violence from misusing guns can be disarmed before that risk becomes a reality," wrote Bibas, an appointee of President Donald Trump.

In a separate case involving Edward Williams, the court ruled that the federal firearms restriction could not constitutionally be applied to him based on his prior convictions for driving under the influence of alcohol in the early 2000s. One of those convictions triggered the federal ban, which generally applies to offenses punishable by more than one year in prison.

Williams had been sentenced to a term of 90 days to two years, which he served under home confinement. After learning the conviction prevented him from owning guns, he sued to secure a declaration that the law was unconstitutional as applied to his offense.

The Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the primary federal law used to prevent felons from possessing guns does not violate the Second Amendment when a person's previous conviction involved violence or credible threats to others' safety. (Yasin Ozturk/Anadolu Agency)

Writing for the court, U.S. Circuit Judge Paul Matey, a Trump appointee, rejected the Justice Department's argument that historical restrictions on "habitual drunkards" justified applying the federal firearms ban to Williams.

Matey described Williams as "a peaceable ​citizen, capable of bearing arms consistent with the design of the Second Amendment."

"And with that rehabilitation comes restoration of the civic privileges guaranteed to citizens by the Constitution, and the freedom to again exercise the natural right of armed defense against threats and tyranny," the judge wrote.

U.S. Circuit Judge Arianna Freeman, writing separately in disagreement with the majority's reasoning, said she parted ways from the majority opinion "when it says a prior conviction is disarming on its face only if it involved violence or threats."

DOJ THREATENS TO SUE CALIFORNIA OVER 'GLOCK BAN,' ARGUING LAW VIOLATES SECOND AMENDMENT

The rulings come amid a series of cases evaluating whether modern gun restrictions are constitutional under a new legal standard established by the Supreme Court in 2022. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Freeman argued that the Second Amendment also permits restrictions on people whose criminal conduct demonstrates a credible threat to public safety, even when their offenses did not involve explicit violence or threats.

The judge argued that while convictions for crimes that involve violence or threats qualify, other offenses, such as drunk driving, should be covered as well because they show that a person "poses a credible threat to the physical safety of others."

Joshua Prince, a lawyer for Williams, praised the ruling, saying the decision made it clear that "there does not exist any historical tradition of stripping individuals with non-violent convictions of their Second Amendment rights and whom do not pose a threat to the public in possession of a firearm."

The rulings come amid a series of cases evaluating whether modern gun restrictions are constitutional under a new legal standard established by the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 Second Amendment decision.

In a 6-3 ruling in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, the high court held that modern gun restrictions must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at Cato’s Herbert A. Stiefel Center for Trade Policy Studies, discusses how tariffs and affordability could factor into the midterms.

Americans aren't just seeing the price tag increase for imported goods. Thanks to President Donald Trump's tariffs, they are now paying more for products made in the U.S.A., according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

In fact, the research finds that prices for many everyday goods would have fallen last year and into early 2026 without Trump's tariffs.

The findings offer new evidence of how the sweeping tariff policy, a centerpiece of the president's economic agenda during his second term, have affected Americans’ wallets — and it's only getting worse with just one month until the midterm elections.

TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK

Tariffs kept prices higher on many everyday consumer goods, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. (Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images)

Economists had long warned that tariffs would drive up consumer prices, but measuring their precise impact has been difficult as trade policies shifted and companies made decisions about whether to absorb higher costs or pass them along to shoppers.

Put simply, the New York Fed found that tariffs kept prices higher on many of the goods Americans buy every day. Without the tariffs, prices across the consumer goods examined for this study would have fallen by early 2026. Instead, they rose.

The researchers estimated that tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the goods they studied. And the impact, notably, was not limited to imported products facing the most fallout from tariffs. The New York Fed found that Trump's policies pushed up prices on American-made goods.

Researchers estimated that about two-thirds of the tariff-related price increase came from imports, while roughly one-third came from products made in the United States.

The White House pushed back, arguing that tariffs will ultimately benefit U.S. workers and be paid by foreign exporters.

"President Trump’s America First trade agenda is reshaping the international economic order to reduce our trade deficit, revitalize American manufacturing, and deliver lasting benefits to our workers, farmers and producers," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

The administration has maintained that foreign exporters reliant on access to the U.S. market will ultimately bear the cost of tariffs, Rogers added.

A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR

Trump has made tariffs a defining feature of his economic agenda, arguing they will strengthen American manufacturing and bring jobs and investment back to the United States. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, told Fox News Digital that consumers may not see significant relief as long as tariffs remain in place.

"What we know is that the tariffs have increased prices a bit," Lincicome said. "What we don't know is whether the prices will stay where they are or go up even a little bit more as companies finally cave and start passing on more of the tariff costs onto consumers."

"As long as the tariffs remain in place, it's unlikely we're going to see price declines," he added.

The research also found that tariff-related price increases can take up to a year to fully reach consumers, particularly when American manufacturers face higher costs for imported materials and components.

Although the researchers estimate that the inflationary impact of existing tariffs has largely peaked, they expect consumer goods prices to remain higher than they otherwise would have been.

5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS

Tariffs have played a central role in Trump’s second-term economic agenda as the administration seeks to bring more manufacturing and investment to the United States. (Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images)

The findings could carry political implications as Trump and Republicans face voters in November after campaigning on lowering the cost of living.

"When you campaign on lowering prices, and then you actually actively increase prices, it's probably gonna hurt when voters go back to the polls and are mad about prices still being too high," Lincicome said.

Meanwhile, higher energy costs are adding another layer of pressure on American households.

"It's really a double whammy for American consumers because first you had the tariffs which increased the prices of a lot of products. And then you had energy prices spike because of the Iran war," Lincicome said.

While gasoline prices have largely leveled off, diesel costs have surged to record highs, threatening to ripple through the broader economy. (Robyn Beck/AFP/Getty Images)

He warned that rising diesel costs could push prices higher beyond the gas pump, increasing transportation expenses for businesses that rely on trucks, trains and agricultural equipment.

"Those things are going to act as kind of another tariff because they're gonna increase the cost of getting that product to you," he said.
