eu-budget-cuts-joint-borrowing:
EUobserver

Opinion

Last Saturday, the Irish presidency of the EU proposed cutting nearly €160bn from the EU’s next seven-year budget against the European Commission’s proposal, a bid to bring the wealthiest, frugal member states on board. The deepest cuts fall on competitiveness (€75bn), external action (almost €38bn) and the EU’s administration costs (€10bn).

What the plan leaves alone is the borrowing.

The Irish text, known in Brussels as the negobox, keeps all three of the commission’s borrowing programmes that sit outside the budget’s normal limits: Catalyst Europe, a €150bn lending facility; a crisis mechanism of up to €395bn for major unforeseen shocks; and support for Ukraine of up to €100bn.

Add loans for defence and lending to other non-EU countries and, by our estimates, joint borrowing could still equal around 44 per cent of the new budget, about €800bn at current prices, up from 41 per cent under the Commission’s proposal. The budget shrinks, but the borrowing hardly changes.

Ireland’s proposed budget is too small for Europe’s mounting common challenges, and its borrowing approach is too ad hoc and risky.

Excluding the distorting effects of NextGenerationEU (NGEU), the Covid recovery fund, the Commission’s budget proposal is already far smaller than the headline figures suggest, and Ireland’s proposal would make it smaller still.

That matters because, as the Draghi report argued, Europe’s shared challenges such as Ukraine, rearmament and competitiveness require European public goods because no single member state captures their full benefits.

A budget worth just over one percent of the EU’s gross national income (GNI) is a poor match for that responsibility.

By comparison, total government expenditure across EU countries comes to close to half of their combined GNI. Keeping most fiscal capacity at national level, while expecting such a modest EU budget to finance increasingly vital continental priorities, is a bad use of public resources.

A stronger common budget needs more of its own revenue, at least what the Commission proposes in its Own Resources Decision, which Parliament broadly supports and which would raise nearly €60bn extra a year.

The Irish plan’s acceptance of five new resources is encouraging. But it has to survive the negotiations, and the details of the final reform will decide whether it means anything.

Read more

The Council’s approach to common borrowing remains haphazard, lacking a permanent framework and relying on crisis-driven compromises. Governments may not like it, but a more European approach is coming, and the €800bn is likely to grow.

Support for Kyiv, to be provided outside budget ceilings via the Ukraine Reserve and policy loans, is capped at €100bn for the whole period. This is already looking tight given the accelerating rate of disbursements to Ukraine seen in recent years.

And a successor to SAFE, the EU’s defence loan scheme, is widely expected, since €150bn has proved far from enough for Europe’s rearmament.

France has just shown what it costs to borrow alone. Its yields recently hit a 24-year high, and the state now pays more to borrow than some major French companies. Sharing the effort through the common budget, including prudent joint borrowing, would help spread that risk.

Read more

Yet Europe has no clear, sustainable plan for borrowing. To date, EU governments have reluctantly signed up to each new borrowing instrument and called it an exception.

European borrowing capacity has been assembled one crisis at a time, starting with the euro area crisis and accelerating since the pandemic.

NGEU was accepted by fiscally cautious states as a one-off decision to deal with the Covid-19 emergency. Then the war in Ukraine and the need to fund rearmament produced new exceptions.

This year, EU governments used enhanced cooperation, a procedure that lets a subset of member states go ahead without the rest, to approve the €90bn Ukraine Support Loan, the EU’s largest foreign loan ever.

For defence, they reached for Article 122, the treaties’ emergency clause, to set up SAFE. Parliament, which felt sidelined, decided to sue the Council before the European Court of Justice.

There is a catch though.

These exceptional programmes are guaranteed by the so-called budget headroom, the margin between the EU’s revenue ceiling and the spending limits in the seven-year budget, rather than by money set aside in advance.

In barely five years, headroom-backed exposure has climbed to €681bn (see Figure 1), 82 percent of all EU debt.

The European Court of Auditors has warned that if a Ukraine loan guaranteed this way goes bad, future EU budgets, and the national contributions that fund them, would have to cover the loss.

EU capitals remain divided over the new budget and over joint borrowing. Net contributors, sometimes referred to as the Frugal Six, want deep cuts in the commission’s proposal, argue that new common borrowing is not the solution and have misgivings about the creation of new own resources.

By contrast, a group of sixteen southern and eastern countries, that call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion”, are much more open to joint borrowing and back an approach closer to the Commission and Parliament on the budget and own resources.

Ireland’s plan largely reflects the influence of the frugal countries, yet one diplomat has already dismissed it as “not even close to a landing zone.”

Europe needs an ambitious budget, backed by at least the Commission’s proposed new own resources, so it relies less on national contributions based on GNI. Joint borrowing should become a permanent, predictable part of it, with safeguards.

First, it should fund loans, not grants, as the Commission suggests. Second, riskier exposures, especially to non-EU countries, should be at least partly backed by money set aside in advance, as the Court of Auditors recommends.

Where it makes sense, the headroom guarantee could be topped up with national guarantees in proportion to each country’s size, as under SURE, and like-minded partners outside the EU could sometimes take part.

Stronger capital at institutions such as the EIB, or at any future defence-financing vehicle, would also let Europe borrow more together without putting its creditworthiness at risk.

Governments should also consider deferring repayment of the NGEU bonds, as the Draghi report suggested, especially if the own-resources reform falls short. It would protect priority spending when it is needed most.

Sustained joint borrowing brings a bonus: more common safe assets in euros, which strengthens the euro’s international role. The demand is already there.

Last month Piotr Serafin, the EU's budget commissioner, flew to Seoul and Tokyo to meet investors. Asian buyers’ share of EU bond syndications has risen from 5 per cent to 9 per cent in the second half of 2025.

Wobbles in US bond markets, which partly reflect doubts about America’s fiscal health, its reliability as a partner and the dollar’s safe-haven status, give the euro an opening.

But it can only take it if EU governments put their own fiscal houses in order.

Ongoing tensions in the French bond market provide a clear warning. Putting France’s finances on a sustainable path would do more than reassure markets about the euro. It would restore French debt as a safe euro asset.

EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday in Brussels. Whatever they discuss (and later decide) on the budget, Europe should keep borrowing together, and in large amounts.

The task now is to give that borrowing a coherent plan: a permanent framework, money set aside in advance and safeguards that cautious capitals can accept.

Dora Meredith is the Director of ODI Europe, a Brussels-based global affairs think tank part of the ODI Global network.

Heliodoro Temprano Arroyo is a senior research Associate for ODI Europe and previously held managerial and advisory roles in the European Commission’s directorate-general for economic and financial affairs.

Topic:Cricket

Cummins and Maharaj produced magic while Smith pulled up lame on day four. (Getty Images, Fox Cricket)

Pat Cummins's explosive knock pushes Australia clear, Keshav Maharaj produces some magic in his follow-through and Steve Smith doesn't join his teammates in the field.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

Maddinson picked up where he left off. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Nic Maddinson hooked the first ball of the innings for four, so it was no surprise that he got a move on when day four began with Australia needing quick runs to set up a victory.

He hit two boundaries in his first three balls faced, but both were off the edge. Then, after watching opening partner Travis Head chip a tame shot to mid-on, Maddinson decided to force the issue.

Through cover, down to third man, back over the bowler … the controversially selected 34-year-old made a real statement as he raced to within one shot of a maiden half-century.

But it came to an end on 48 off 38 balls when Anrich Nortje uprooted his middle and leg stumps with a searing yorker.

A famous Test inning? Perhaps not, but a career high likely to earn him another chance to prolong his strange Test career.

Maharaj surprised himself with his bizarre juggling effort. (Fox Cricket)

With Matt Rensaw having pushed into the 80s and looking destined for a second century for the match, it felt like the South Africans were in need of something extraordinary to dismiss the Queenslander.

And although not quite a work of art, Keshav Maharaj's diving return catch was certainly out of the ordinary.

With Renshaw having chipped one back towards the bowler, the finger spinner did well to get down in his follow-through, before juggling the ball once, twice, taking his eye of the cherry, and ultimately securing it in his palm while lying on the turf.

He looked as surprised as anyone to have taken the catch, which was confirmed after a lengthy review by the TV umpire.

Pat Cummins made a quickfire cameo. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Australia was surprisingly circumspect during the middle session, with Matt Renshaw and Beau Webster doing little more than keeping the scoreboard ticking over.

Pat Cummins clearly had no plans to declare on Renshaw when he had a second ton for the match in the offing, but when Renshaw was caught out, the captain took it on himself to up the tempo.

He wasted little time attacking the spin of Simon Harmer, smacking his fourth ball for six over long-on and adding three more in his next four deliveries from the off-spinner before declaring on 6-314 having clattered 32 off 12 to take his team to a 420-run lead.

Steve Smith injured his finger as he took a catch on day three and copped a blow to the helmet on day four. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Steve Smith's slips catching changed the game on day three but soon after Cummins's declaration it became clear he would not have the same impact on day four.

Smith stayed in the pavilion when the Australian team took to the field for South Africa's run chase on account of a sharp blow he copped to the helmet from an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.

He carried on to 27 before holing out, but the after-effects of that head knock appeared to keep him sidelined.

He also hurt his finger taking the catch that ended South Africa's first innings, which could have caused issues in the slips.

Comfortably the top scorer in the match, Matt Renshaw added his maiden Test wicket late on day four. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Matt Renshaw couldn't have dreamt it better.

With shadows lengthening in Durban, and with South Africa's innings threatening to steady, Australia's freshly minted golden boy was thrown the ball.

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma had faced 18 balls for his one run and was set on seeing his team to stumps, but he was unable to contend with the drift and turn of Renshaw's part-time off spin, the Queenslander drawing the batter forward and having him caught at short leg by a diving Maddinson.

Renshaw was mobbed by his teammates as he celebrated his maiden Test wicket and Australia marched on to be six wickets from victory at stumps on day four.

That came after the southpaw had once again led Australia's efforts with the bat, peeling off 82 to add to the 190 he made in the first innings.

Remarkably, Renshaw remains the only player to pass 50 in the match.

replacing-columbus-day-indigenous-people:
The promotion of Indigenous Peoples’ Day has never been neutral or dispassionate. It is part of a broader ideological program to remake our great nation.

Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich and 14 of his Senate colleagues recently introduced a new resolution declaring their support for designating the second Monday of October, currently the federal holiday of Columbus Day, as “Indigenous Peoples’ Day.”

Although the sponsors of S. Res. 900 seem very purposefully to refrain from expressly condemning Columbus Day, this resolution is anything but politically neutral, explicitly describing Western contact in the New World as resulting in “suppression, forced assimilation, and genocide of Indigenous Peoples.” And with that, S. Res. 900 gives the game away as yet another Democrat attempt to erase American culture in favor of a new, woke, anti-West civilization. Rather than choose literally any other day of the year, its advocates selected Columbus Day as part of a broader campaign to redefine who and what we as Americans celebrate.

The resolution’s sponsors, including Democrat notables Elizabeth Warren, Tim Kaine, Adam Schiff, and Cory Booker, acknowledge that some cities and states still recognize the holiday, which has been celebrated in the United States since 1792 and officially became a federal holiday in 1971. They seek to justify their proposal by noting that Indigenous Peoples’ Day is widespread, with more than “200 municipalities, 17 states, and the District of Columbia” already observing or recognizing it. Left out of that comment is that in many of these locations, such as Maine, Vermont, New Mexico, and D.C., Columbus Day was replaced by Indigenous Peoples’ Day, with all mention of that “villain” Columbus excised from their calendars.

Moreover, the co-sponsors add, Columbus Day “does not currently provide an opportunity to reflect on the stories and perseverance of the Indigenous Peoples of the lands that are now part of the United States.” That’s a curious (if not disingenuous) assertion, given that Columbus Day wasn’t established to exclude anyone, but to honor a daring 15th- and 16th-century explorer who is singularly responsible for bringing the Old World and New World into contact with one another, thereby facilitating the circumstances that led to the establishment of the American colonies and the United States. To complain that Columbus Day doesn’t provide an opportunity to honor indigenous peoples is a bit like complaining that Independence Day doesn’t expressly honor the contributions of blacks who suffered slavery.

All of this makes it obvious that continued efforts to redefine the second Monday of October as Indigenous Peoples’ Day isn’t simply about honoring a certain group. Rather, the focus on Columbus Day is a classic example of damnatio memoriae, the ancient Roman practice of dishonoring disgraced rulers after their death by removing their names from inscriptions, destroying their portraits and statues, and posthumously stripping them of honors.

Now, some folks may ask: “So what?” Christopher Columbus, after all, was not an American, and he predates the founding of our country by centuries. He was not an outspoken advocate for such ideals as liberty, freedom of speech or religion, or representative government that we associate with the fundamentals of American identity. He was an Italian Catholic who hoped the riches he sought in the Far East would fund Catholic military efforts in the Old World to deter and even defeat encroaching Islamic powers such as the Ottomans.

Yet Columbus, from very early in American history, was identified as an integral component of our nation’s self-understanding. It was he who exhibited a remarkable creativity and courage in seeking to broaden the West’s horizons, and, though he did not seem to realize it even at his death, Columbus’ efforts dramatically reshaped world history. As early as 1791, what is now Washington, D.C., was being called the “Territory of Columbia,” in his honor.

Over the course of our nation’s history, Columbus took on additional meaning with waves of Italian immigrants who shared his ethnic heritage. President Benjamin Harrison in 1892 issued a proclamation for the 400th anniversary of Columbus “sailing the ocean blue,” which was in part intended as a conciliatory gesture to Italian Americans following anti-Italian violence in New Orleans. Italian immigrants embraced the holiday, as did many other Catholic immigrants, including Blessed Fr. Michael J. McGivney, who in 1882 founded the Knights of Columbus, a fraternal organization that today claims millions of members and is involved in literally millions of hours of volunteering and community service every year.

Today, many malign Columbus as a “genocidal” “colonizer.” Though his record of governance in the Caribbean is not an admirable one, these attacks represent presentist, chronological snobbery that applies anachronistic, absurd categories to historical figures. Indeed, the very fact that Columbus wanted natives to become baptized Christians like himself demonstrated that he could perceive, however inchoately, their inherent dignity as human beings.

Moreover, Democrats’ attacks on Columbus are emblematic of a broader, vicious program that aims to destroy America’s traditional heroes in favor of a new national narrative based on victimhood, entitlement, and “hyphenation” rather than heroic virtue possessed by men such as Columbus. As we all saw during the George Floyd riots in 2020, woke activists targeted for canceling not only Columbus but George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, George Mason, and Abraham Lincoln, among many others. It is not too much to interpret the aggressive, often violent attacks on statues and memorials of these great men as the foreshadowing of the more violent political activism we are witnessing today, with constant threats of violence against not only the president but other politicians, conservative members of the Supreme Court, and even the assassination of civilian Charlie Kirk.

There is nothing intrinsically wrong with honoring all those who contribute to our national identity, whatever their race or ethnicity. But the promotion of Indigenous Peoples’ Day has never been neutral or dispassionate. It is part of a broader ideological program in which “victimizers” like Columbus are out and “victims” of various minority hyphenated groups are in. To be complicit in this project is not merely a “nice thing to do” to show respect for American Indians. It is to participate in the woke remaking of our great nation.

Princess Diana used to leave Kensington Palace alone at night to hand out money to sex workers and check how 'the homeless were coping', former royal press secretary Dickie Arbiter has claimed.

Speaking to the Daily Mail's Palace Confidential, Arbiter said the princess felt the night-time trips were 'something she had to do', though they were also driven by loneliness and 'boredom'.

Arbiter, 86, sat down with host Luke Blackall to mark the release of his new book, On Duty with the Royals: The Inside Story of the Modern Monarchy, which draws on his 12 years as a royal press secretary.

He worked closely with King Charles, then Prince of Wales, and Princess Diana from 1988, through their separation and divorce, and was in charge of the media operation for her funeral in 1997.

Arbiter claimed that behind the gates of Kensington Palace the princess was 'very lonely', and she would give her protection officer the slip to set out on these secret mercy missions.

Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthi-run foreign ministry said on Sunday that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.

CCTV vision from King Khalid Airport showed hundreds of travellers caught in the blasts that tore through the travel hub.

Dr Bekier said the strikes in Saudi Arabia could still affect Australians travelling to Europe in the region, even if they connect through the UAE or Qatar.

The role of the gun industry in America’s gun violence epidemic.

Our team is examining a decade's worth of data from the Gun Violence Archive for insights into one of the most devastating public health crises in the United States.

The National Rifle Association is one of the most powerful special interest groups in America. We’re investigating how it spends its money.

A newsletter spotlighting the people, policies, and programs grappling with the gun violence crisis.

Our team, our mission, our partners, and more. Plus: How to contact us.

We report stories that would go untold. Generous readers sustain our work.

Sign up now to get our latest stories and eye-opening briefings.

Register for upcoming events and revisit past conversations.

Politics

The Trace reported in August when the CDC highlighted dubious figures on how often guns are used defensively on their website. This latest update also reflects the Trump administration’s staunch Second Amendment advocacy.

Share

The Trace reported last month that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had added a claim to its web page on firearm injury and death prevention stating that Americans use guns defensively an estimated 60,000 to 2.5 million times each year. On September 28, the CDC updated the defensive gun use estimate again, swapping out the lower number for a much higher one: 500,000.

The CDC did not state why they updated the number. They did not respond to The Trace’s request for comment.

Defensive gun use statistics are highly debated, and previous references to the range on the CDC’s website were removed during the Biden administration at the behest of researchers and gun safety advocates.

The changes reflect the Trump administration’s staunch Second Amendment advocacy, putting the president in lockstep with a gun lobby that’s long promoted the idea that “a good guy with a gun” is the only thing that can stop “a bad guy with a gun.”

Devin Hughes, who runs GVPedia, a nonprofit gun violence research outfit, had lobbied the CDC for the removal of the defensive gun use estimates in 2022. He told us in July that their reinsertion was “disappointing but unsurprising.” These latest changes, he told The Trace, are a major setback.

“Now search engines and AI chatbots will repeat the CDC’s false figure to Americans trying to make honest decisions about gun safety,” he said.

The September update was first reported by John Lott, an economist and gun researcher whose conclusions have been debunked by experts. Lott has been a strong proponent of expanding the figures on defensive gun use.

The 60,000 figure came from the National Crime Victimization Survey, a twice-yearly poll of crime victims conducted by the federal government. The 500,000 figure, as well as the 2.5 million figure, can be attributed to Florida State University professor Gary Kleck.

Kleck surveyed 5,000 adults by phone in 1993 and asked if they or their household members had used a gun for self-defense in the past five years, even if it wasn’t fired. Just over 1 percent of respondents said they had. Kleck extrapolated that figure to the entire adult population of 200 million, concluding that Americans use guns for self-defense as often as 2.1 million to 2.5 million times a year.

Researchers have found issues with Kleck’s estimates. While the adult population in the United States in 1993 was around 200 million people, not all of them owned guns — only about 42 percent did. So extrapolating the survey results to the entire adult population yields an overestimate.

Kleck has argued that respondents underreport defensive gun use because they fear the authorities. In some states, pointing a weapon at someone can lead to an arrest. Even if they’re eventually cleared, “you’ve lost thousands of dollars in legal fees, had your reputation ruined, maybe had your picture and name in the newspaper,” he told The Trace in 2022.

But Hughes said Kleck’s work extrapolated data from highly unusual circumstances. “Surveys of rare events reliably produce wildly inflated numbers, and defensive gun use is no different,” he said.

Jennifer Mascia is a senior news writer and founding staffer at The Trace. She previously reported on gun violence at The New York Times and was a contributor to CNN’s Guns in America team. In her dozen years on this beat she’s covered community gun violence, the intersection of domestic violence and guns, and the growing role of firearms in public life. She is a graduate of Columbia Journalism School and the author of Never Tell Our Business to Strangers, which details her investigation into her father’s criminal past.

Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin examines the history and use of firing squads in the United States and discusses the debate over plans to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan. She also looks at Vice President JD Vance’s concerns about live-streaming the execution on ‘Special Report.’

Pope Leo XIV condemned the death penalty as "inadmissible" as the Pentagon faces criticism over plans to livestream an execution later this year.

Leo, the first American pope, shared his opposition to capital punishment Saturday in a social media post marking World Day Against the Death Penalty.

Citing Catholic doctrine revised under his predecessor, Pope Francis, Leo emphasized that the death penalty violates human dignity.

"The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo wrote on X.

"#NoDeathPenalty," he added in the post.

VETERAN SHOT 7 TIMES IN FORT HOOD MASSACRE HAS A WARNING FOR AMERICANS PLANNING TO WATCH EXECUTION

Pope Leo XIV condemned the death penalty as "inadmissible" after the Pentagon announced unprecedented plans to livestream an execution later this year. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

In 2018, Francis revised the Catholic Church's official position on capital punishment, declaring the death penalty "inadmissible" in all circumstances.

"Consequently the church teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person," the revised Catechism states.

Before the change, Catholic teaching permitted the death penalty in cases where it was deemed the only effective means of protecting human life from a dangerous offender.

Earlier popes had maintained that exception, though Pope John Paul II increasingly advocated ending capital punishment, stressing that those convicted of crimes retain their human dignity.

Although Leo did not specifically mention the U.S. government's plans in his statement, his post comes after the Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had scheduled a firing squad execution for a man convicted of a mass shooting at a military base.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base. He is set to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, which would make him the first person to be executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base. (REUTERS/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)

President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not yet decided whether to allow the livestream plan, pushed by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, to move forward.

Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic, expressed skepticism about whether the Pentagon would proceed with a public execution. He said he would not watch the livestream if it were carried out.

Several lawmakers, including Republicans, have spoken out against plans to broadcast the execution.

CHRISTA PIKE DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, RETURNED TO PRISON AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION, ATTORNEYS SAY

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said on Thursday. "It should not be happening in America."

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, criticized the proposed broadcast, calling it "truly incomprehensible" and warning that it was "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."

"The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent," Parolin told reporters on Friday. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don’t know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."

President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had not yet decided whether to allow the livestream plan, pushed by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, to move forward. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)

He added that the death penalty "is incompatible with human dignity and does not serve as a deterrent."

The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" about the public execution plan and urged the U.S. to reconsider.

"In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement on Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

Leo's statement also did not mention the botched lethal injection of Christa Gail Pike in Tennessee. Pike survived the attempted execution despite two doses of pentobarbital being administered late last month.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

The parliament on Oct. 12 passed a bill reinforcing the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step that Hungary demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU talks to move forward.

The vote paves the way for the EU to formally open two more accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at a meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.

The bill passed with the support of 266 lawmakers, according to lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak. It still requires a presidential signature to become law.

The law would give Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking community and other EU-language national minorities more room to use their language in education. Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.

According to the new legislation, schools where more than 50% of pupils study in the relevant minority language may be granted special status, and the head or deputy head of such a school must be proficient in that language, among other measures outlined in the bill.

The bill "is the result of the bilateral agreement, which we negotiated with the Ukrainian side in May and June," Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban told journalists ahead of a foreign ministers' meeting in Luxembourg, calling the legislation a step toward advancing Kyiv's EU talks.

"I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone on both sides, Hungarian and Ukrainian experts and politicians, who made this possible," the minister said ahead of the parliament's vote.

The bill covers official EU languages but not Russian, reflecting Kyiv's ongoing push to remove Russian from official and public spaces and counter decades of Moscow-imposed Russification.

Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former Prime Minister Viktor Orban spent years blocking Ukraine's EU accession talks, claiming Kyiv failed to protect the rights of its Hungarian minority.

The victory of Peter Magyar's pro-European Tisza party in the Hungarian parliamentary elections in April provided new impetus to resolve the issue.

In early summer, Kyiv and Budapest announced an agreement on the educational, linguistic, and cultural rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority.

Hungary then lifted its veto on Kyiv's EU accession talks, allowing the launch of clusters one and six — lists of reforms focused on democratic institutions and the rule of law, and on external relations, respectively — in June and July.

The agreement also allowed Moldova's accession talks to move forward, as the EU has politically linked the membership bids of Kyiv and Chisinau.

But Budapest later blocked the launch of additional clusters until Kyiv begins implementing changes under the agreement, starting with educational rights.

Ukraine expects that the passage of the law will help unblock two more clusters, addressing internal market and competitiveness — a step that was preliminarily cleared by EU envoys on Oct. 7.

Kyiv aims to have all six accession clusters open by the end of the year.

Assistant Editor

Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia.  His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

Actors Anna Lambe and Zorga Qaunaq on learning about forgiveness and queerness through their award-winning show

Credit: Tobin Ng/Xtra

If you’ve ever wondered what it’s like to live in a town of just over 2,000 people in the Arctic, cuss out your toxic partner at a huge community event, scheme your way into hooking up with queer transients to make up for the small dating pool, and try to rebuild your life while navigating intergenerational trauma—you should probably watch the series North of North.

Actor Anna Lambe (The Grizzlies) plays Siaja, an Inuk woman who, along with her daughter Bun, moves in with her mother Neevee while looking for a job—and life—of her own. Produced by Inuit-led company Red Marrow Media and Canada’s Northwood Entertainment, the series follows Siaja as she learns about lost family members, burns through relationships and rekindles others.

But make no mistake, this is a comedy. North of North pulls laughter from audiences without trying to stifle the grief Siaja feels when she learns her sister was stolen from her mother, or conversations her mother has with an elder about her experiences in residential schools. The series helps viewers breathe through the pain.

After the inaugural season of the CBC, APTN and Netflix show hit nine million views in its first month, won nine Canadian Screen Awards and landed a spot in Netflix’s top 10 across 33 countries, North of North welcomes its second season. Its name is a nod to its setting in the fictional town of Ice Cove, which lies at the heart of the Arctic. In reality, it was filmed in Iqaluit—making it Netflix’s first original Canadian series. The second season premiered earlier this week on CBC Gem and APTN. It will be available to stream on Netflix this fall.

Get free Xtra newsletters

Xtra is being blocked on Facebook and Instagram for Canadians as part of Meta’s response to Bill C18. Stay connected, and tell a friend.

Xtra spoke with Lambe and Zorga Qaunaq, who plays Siaja’s friend Millie, about what viewers can expect from Season 2.

Siaja was determined to change her life when the show started, and by the time we get to Season 2, she’s in an entirely different phase. Whose character growth do you identify with?

Anna Lambe: There’s kind of this overarching question for [Siaja], which is, “What do I actually want and what does it mean to pursue it?” I had a bit of a breakdown because I don’t know the answer to that question for myself. Being able to play Siaja and go through that journey with her, I really do feel like I grew and changed so much. Siaja’s journey trying to pursue what she thinks she wants, doing so messily, hurting a lot of people in the process and then being told that she’s still lovable; that her determination sometimes hurts people, but it’s not for nothing—that made me really emotional and it was also quite cathartic.

Zorga Qaunaq: I also related a lot with [Siaja’s love interest] Kuuk’s arc this season, with him reconnecting with the community. He has a beautiful storyline that just feels so real to so many people I know, including myself, about finding your place in the community and finding your belonging even though you’ve never been there before or you’ve been away for decades. The [writers] told that story so beautifully this season.

Not knowing where you belong and trying to find yourself is very queer-coded. What advice would you give to a queer person who doesn’t feel like they’re in the right spot?

ZQ: I was thinking a lot about this in general. It relates to queerness, but just being your big, colourful self. The more yourself you are, the more you have to offer. I’m someone who just wants to give to my community and is so generous and helpful … I realized trying to give myself away all the time or making myself small or helping everyone else except me—that was not helping. Being myself as much as possible—that includes my queerness—is making space for all those people that feel like they can’t be themselves. And if we’re all ourselves, then we won’t fight over it.

AL: One of the takeaways that I really think a lot about is when you find your community, they allow you to make mistakes. They love you at every stage of who you are, whether that’s with a lot of warmth and celebration or with tough love. But they really hold space for you at all the points in your journey of you figuring out who you are.

There’s no extended family beyond Siaja, Neevee and Bun. They’ve really had to create a community around themselves and choose who they feel safe with, and who they go to when they feel vulnerable. That real chosen community is just as valid and just as important. The people that love you, love you because you’re you—not because of social structures or labels we give ourselves.

There’s so much forgiveness in that process too. How has playing these characters changed how you forgive and give grace?

AL: Forgiveness really is an art. It’s a skill that you have to build. It’s easy to be angry at someone for the rest of your life. It’s okay to protect yourself, if it’s what makes you feel safe. But there are also elements of forgiveness that we need to practise, and I’m really glad that the show gets to talk about this. It’s allowed me to think about the things that I’ve been angry about and ashamed about, and about how the act of grace, forgiveness and apology is a bit of a scary mountain. But I think it’s almost always worth looking and at least checking to see what the other side is like.

ZQ: That’s why it’s easier to be angry. There is no-one-size-fits-all to any relationship, to any identity, to any person’s growth. It is hard because you have to keep working at it. Having [North of North] show that by example; how people reconcile. You would think it should be just there for us to see all the time, but this is quite revolutionary for us Inuit—to see this healthy relationship building onscreen and to be able to talk about it. And I’ve seen with my own eyes and my own ears; I’ve witnessed people having healing conversations that I’m sure were inspired by seeing the relationship between Neevee and Siaja.

In the first season, Elder Elisapee shares their and Neevee’s late mother’s experience in residential school with Neevee, even though Elisapee makes it clear they don’t like Neevee. It was almost startling seeing them have such an emotional conversation.

ZQ: Yeah, I would say that’s Inuk culture. You’ll be talking with an elder, and they will—what people would call—“trauma dump.” They’ll just say some intense things. Most of the time, ideally, they wouldn’t just leave you with that. They would have some sort of story to help you through it. That’s amazing to see. Because everything can feel so fragmented when represented on TV. [Viewers may say], “It’s a comedy show, so you should only have comedy and no drama,” or “No, this is a drama. You should only talk about all the nitty-gritty stuff.” As a new actor to all this and a consumer of media, I love to see the mix between all the genres altogether because that’s what life is. It’s messy, and we Inuit live that and know that. We’ll be laughing one second, crying another, then mad one second. Our elders encourage us to move through our feelings as they come and go, so that’s shown really well in the show, for a comedy show with only, like, 20 minutes [per episode].

When Siaja is presenting on why Ice Cove should host a polar research station, she talks about how people come to the North ready to change the community, but she wants people to let the community change them. How has filming North of North and Iqaluit changed you, and how do you think it will change the entertainment industry’s approach to telling Arctic stories in the future?

AL: North of North has profoundly changed my life. I’m from Iqaluit, I grew up there, so there was a real comfort of being home while filming it, but being able to celebrate Nunavut and Inuit, and in many ways, each of us getting to celebrate this feat of television-making. It’s a miracle that we have a TV show now. It’s so difficult, and we had every challenge and everything kind of stacked against making a show like this happen.

So many people think that the North needs to be fixed because of what has happened with colonialism and the impacts on our community and how that continues to reverberate. I think it’s really interesting when people think that the answer is colonialism lite. You imposed yourselves on us once upon a time and continue to—but then you think if you impose yourself on us while saying you’re helping us that it’s different.

They don’t see Inuit as people with autonomy and people who are able to make decisions for themselves. But if they see the joy and the beauty, and not just the perseverance through colonialism; that our communities continue to thrive in many ways, even in struggle—I don’t want to say it’s like inspiring in like a trauma-porn way because that is what it can sound like, but I think it recontextualizes life for a lot of people.

ZQ: I’m spoiled to be able to shoot up there: having the community there, inspiration all around me because the people are there, and that’s what we’re making the show about, and that’s who I am. The community having the chance to see a real show being made and being able to participate in it. There’s going to be little kids who were born now who don’t know what it was like to not have North of North shooting every couple of years in the Arctic. So this is planting all the seeds.

In the episode when viewers find out Millie is queer, she’s waiting at the airport arrivals for new people for Siaja to hook up with, and finds a woman to flirt with as soon as she steps off her flight. What advice do you have for queer dating for people looking for love or hookups in small towns?

ZQ: Oh man, just go pan, bro. Just kidding. Travel, I guess. Get a private space and find spaces for your queer friends as well.

I realized through playing Millie that I’m pan[sexual]; it’d never really occurred to me. I’m representing a queer character. I’m gonna be facing people in the community who are mad or happy about it. Whether I want to or not, I’m representing this character, and I felt a lot more responsibility [to learn about] it.

I was like, “What is this? Oh my gosh, I think I’m pan. I don’t need to tell anybody.” But then I saw some homophobia in my own community online, and I was like, “Shit, my nephews and my family are there. It is nobody’s business, but if I am loud and proud about my queerness, it will make it safer for all those people in the community.”

During the airport scene, I was so proud of myself because I spoke my language [Inuktitut] with the lines, but I’m not fluent. I was hitting on a woman, and I haven’t talked to my dad about it yet. He’s probably proud of me, but also a little bit embarrassed. But he still loves me and accepts me, so I guess that’s a win.

What queer characters in the media have been significant for you in the way Millie’s may be significant for others?

ZQ: Orange Is the New Black. That was amazing. It just broke down the heteronormative stuff that I was used to all the time. I was talking to a friend of mine about how I want to see more queer representation and complicated relationships, because that’s what all human relationships are.

Your gender is so different from your sexuality, and colonialism tries to fragment everything. It’s so frustrating because when you do that, you’re always asking for an answer. [There’s an expectation that] you need an answer. You need some box to check.

We’re humans. We don’t even know. I don’t know shit. Just give me that time and space to figure out who I am whenever I want, and I can change whenever I want. And so can you.

As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power.

Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles.

Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight.

The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.”

Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.”

As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said.

Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department.

Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said.

“Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.”

The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said.

Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said.

Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. You can catch all the action this coming week in downtown San Francisco at Moscone West.

The Winnipeg Jets have plenty to be thankful for this holiday weekend, including a solid 3-1-1 start to the NHL campaign. Players and coaches are also counting their blessings at finally getting a breather after a busy stretch of five games in eight days.

“We don’t have another (break like this) until a week before Christmas. So we’re going to take advantage of it,” head coach Scott Arniel said following the club’s first regulation loss, a 5-1 stinker on Friday night against the visiting Anaheim Ducks.

JOHN WOODS / THE CANADIAN PRESS

Winnipeg Jets’ Kyle Connor (81), Dylan DeMelo (2), Mark Scheifele (55) and Cole Perfetti (91) celebrate Connor’s goal against the Colorado Avalanche during third period NHL hockey action in Winnipeg on Wednesday.

To borrow a funny old Thanksgiving-related phrase from former defenceman Nate Schmidt, the hockey club was “leaking gravy.” They looked like a group that could use a timeout — which they’ll get since they don’t play again until hosting the Minnesota Wild on Tuesday night.

“It’s nice for sure. We’ve been going pretty hard,” defenceman Dylan DeMelo told the Free Press on Saturday following an off-ice workout for his group.

The Jets will stay away from the rink entirely on Sunday, then will hold a full team practice on Monday. There will also be a lengthy video session to go over the highs and lows so far this season.

“We played a lot of good hockey in that five-game stretch. So a lot of things to build off. But also a lot of things to clean up and get ready for a huge stretch of games here against good opponents,” said DeMelo.

Divisional play is always a key area and teams will play their seven closest rivals four times each this year under the new 84-game schedule. Winnipeg’s most impressive outing so far was their only Central clash, a 3-2 triumph on Wednesday over Colorado.

Four of Winnipeg’s next five games are within the division, with Minnesota, Chicago, St. Louis and Dallas all on deck.

“Teams that we know, teams that we’ve had a lot of hard battles against. We’re going to be have to be really good, be at our best in this stretch,” said DeMelo.

One area of concern would be secondary scoring, or a lack of thereof. The Jets have 13 goals this season, with Kyle Connor (six) and Cole Perfetti (three) accounting for most of them. DeMelo, Mario Ferraro, Adam Lowry and Alex Iafallo have one each, with the other 15 skaters who have suited up combining for a grand total of zero.

In terms of defensive play, the Jets were quite porous against the Ducks, who used their speed to create chaos.

JOHN WOODS / FREE PRESS

Winnipeg Jets’ Cole Perfetti’s (91) shot goes high and wide against the Colorado Avalanche during third period NHL action in Winnipeg on Sept. 22. Perfetti has three goals in the Jets first five games, one of only two players with more than one goal.

“We hadn’t given up many rush goals against in the first four games, and then we got exploited (Friday) with it. That’s something to work on, some reminders for us,” said DeMelo.

“So it’s a good learning lesson, You’ve got to take the positives out of it because it is a long year. Things happens, we’re going to have games like that. We’re going to have better games, worse games. Take the positives and just continue to try and build that thing.”

There were plenty of question marks surrounding the Jets, especially with 10 different players in the opening night lineup compared to a year earlier, including plenty of inexperienced ones. Throw in the cloudy goaltending situation, with Connor Hellebuyck suspended for refusing to report to the team while he awaits a trade, and a 3-1-1 start is nothing to sneeze at.

“We would have taken that. If you can get off to a good start it’s important,” said DeMelo.

“That being said, it’s just a start. We still have a long way to go. But a very encouraging first five games, different contributions from everybody in the lineup. It’s been exciting. Definitely a good feeling in the room. Vibes have been really good. Just trying to keep that going. Keep working. We’ve got such a long way to go, and I think our game can continue to get better.”

The Jets are no strangers to strong starts. They won the first eight games of the 2024-25 season, and 14 of the first 15, to set an NHL record. There was no turning back that year, as the club went on to capture the Presidents’ Trophy.

Last year, Winnipeg got out of the gate by winning nine of the first 12 — but followed that up with a franchise-record 11 game winless streak which dug a hole they could never escape from.

Might either of those scenarios provide some valuable lessons this time around?

“We have a different group of guys. Some new blood in here, some new energy. Every year is different,” said DeMelo.

JOHN WOODS / THE CANADIAN PRESS

Winnipeg Jets’ Josh Morrissey (44) defends against Colorado Avalanche’s Zachary L’Heureux (68) during first period NHL hockey action in Winnipeg on Oct. 7. Morrissey missed Friday’s game against the Ducks due to injury and is listed as day-to-day.

“There’s things you can maybe look back on and try to rectify and maybe avoid. But even then, this group is so different than it was last year. Whichever way it goes, it’s not going to be indicative of years previous. This year I feel like we’ve laid down a better foundation. A lot of good things we can lean on.”

Thursdays

Keep up to date on sports with Mike McIntyre's weekly newsletter.

In addition to getting some potential help from whatever the eventual Hellebuyck trade brings — some additional offence should be high on the wish list — the Jets are also counting on the quick return of top defenceman Josh Morrissey, who missed Friday’s game with an upper-body injury he suffered against the Avalanche.

Morrissey is considered day-to-day, which is yet another thing the Jets are thankful for.

“Absolutely. He’s a huge, huge part of this team. One of our best players, one of the best defencemen in the league. He affects our game in so many ways, and in the room as well being the leader that he is,” said DeMelo.

“So any time he’s out we feel bad and we try to fill that void the best we can collectively as a group, because he’s such a crucial part of this team. So we hope he’s back soon and we’ll keep holding the fort down until he comes back.”

Commissioners eliminated paper-copy requirements and preserved the electronic filing deadline after objections, while postponing a request for easier public commenting.

By

Published on October 9, 2026 at 6:43 am CDT

The Alabama Public Service Commission has eliminated requirements for paper copies of electronic filings and retained its 11:59 p.m. electronic submission deadline after public interest organizations objected to a proposed earlier cutoff.

The changes eliminate paper-copy requirements for those participating in commission proceedings. However, the commission postponed a separate request to allow public comments without requiring users to obtain an electronic filing account, citing an upcoming software transition.

The commission began the rulemaking process September 2. Its proposal would have eliminated the requirement that electronic filings be followed by a paper copy and that physical filings include 10 additional copies. It also proposed moving the electronic filing deadline to 5 p.m.

Alabama Power, Energy Alabama, the Southern Environmental Law Center, Spire Alabama and Spire Gulf submitted comments. All supported eliminating the additional paper requirements.

Energy Alabama and the Southern Environmental Law Center challenged the proposed earlier deadline, arguing that it would create a new restriction without an apparent administrative benefit.

The organizations said a 5 p.m. cutoff would particularly affect members of the public and first-time filers who may be unable to submit documents during business hours. They also argued that submissions made shortly before closing and those made at 11:59 p.m. would both be processed the following morning.

The commission disputed part of that reasoning, explaining that its current software requires staff to manually process electronic filings. Under the previous procedure, processing also depended on receipt of the required paper copy.

Nevertheless, the commission concluded there was no adverse effect from keeping the existing deadline.

Under the amended rule, the commission considers a compliant electronic filing received on the day it arrives electronically, provided it is submitted by 11:59 p.m., prevailing Central time. An after-hours filing may not appear as received in the commission’s system until staff process it the following business day.

The commission also agreed with Alabama Power and the public interest organizations that references to “Central Standard Time” could create confusion during daylight saving time. The amended rules instead use “Prevailing Central Time.”

On public commenting, Energy Alabama and the Southern Environmental Law Center asked the commission to adopt a procedure that would not require commenters to obtain a filing system account.

The commission declined to make that change immediately, saying it is preparing to switch software systems in the coming months and intends to revisit the issue after evaluating the new system’s capabilities. The order does not establish a deadline for that review.

During the transition, the commission said it could authorize alternative commenting procedures in individual proceedings.

The order also removes a written 40-megabyte limit on electronic filings, although the commission said that limitation remains a feature of its current software. The commission instructs filers experiencing problems submitting documents larger than 40 megabytes to contact its secretary.

According to the order, the replacement system will not have that size restriction.

The amendments affect Rules 4, 8, 11 and 20 of the commission’s Rules of Practice.

seven_meteor_showers_october:
October will feature nothing less than 7 separate meteor showers, but in terms of activity, one above all others merits an entry on your calendar.

The Orionids will peak on the night of Wednesday, October 21st, promising a maximum rate of 15 shooting stars per hour.

The Orionids are not only one of the most active meteor showers of the year, but they are among those most easily found, as even children can spot the 3 recognizable stars which form Orion’s Belt. The shower was named after the constellation because it seems the shooting stars radiate out of this region of the sky.

Orion will be in the east, and the only shame is that the Moon will be three-quarters waxing, and may limit visibility.

If that’s a true buzz killer, Consider this Saturday, (Oct. 10th) when the New Moon will coincide with the peak of the Southern Taurid Meteor Shower. Despite its name, this stream of comet debris is easily seen in the Northern Hemisphere, and can produce up to one shooting star every 10 minutes.

That might not seem like much, but it’s double what can be seen watching the Camelopardalids, the Delta Aurigids, the ε-Geminids, and the Leonis Minorids—all of which peak this October.

zimbabwe-mps-extend-presidents-power:
Zimbabwe's lower house of parliament has passed a bill to extend presidential terms from five to seven years, which would allow President Emmerson Mnangagwa to remain in power until 2030.

More than 200 lawmakers voted in favour of the draft legislation on Thursday, surpassing the vote threshold required for a two-thirds majority to amend the constitution.

The bill also scraps direct presidential elections, with future presidents chosen by parliament.

Mnangagwa, 83, took power in 2017 after ousting long-time ruler Robert Mugabe with the backing of the military - and went on to win disputed elections in 2018 and 2023.

The bill now heads to the senate, where it is also expected to secure approval, before being enacted by the president.

This is the culmination of a campaign by the ruling Zanu-PF party - in power since independence in 1980 - to amend the constitution and extend presidential terms, a plan that received cabinet backing in February.

The president had previously described himself as a constitutionalist and pledged to respect term limits.

During Thursday's vote, Speaker of Parliament Jacob Mudenda announced that 216 lawmakers had backed the legislation, surpassing the 187 votes required to amend the constitution. Forty-two lawmakers voted against it.

The amendment contains several provisions:

Opposition parties, civil society groups and constitutional lawyers have argued that such fundamental changes should be put to a national referendum rather than being approved solely through parliament.

Initially hailed by supporters as a reformer who would restore economic growth and democratic governance, Mnangagwa's presidency has instead been marked by economic challenges, disputed elections and growing concerns over democratic backsliding.

The latest constitutional changes have intensified debate over Zimbabwe's political future, with opponents warning that the amendments could weaken democratic accountability, while supporters maintain they are necessary to ensure continuity and stability.

A new constitution adopted in 2013 restricted a president to serving a maximum of two terms, adding that any move to extend term limits would need to be endorsed by voters in a referendum and that a sitting president cannot benefit from any extension unless voters give their approval in a second referendum.

However, on Wednesday, the country's Constitutional Court dismissed a legal challenge seeking to block the bill.

washington-reenactors:
Jennifer Ludden

Reenactor John Koopman III, playing George Washington, waves to attendees at the Thomas Baird Homestead in Millstone Township, N.J., on May 30.  The event re-created a Revolutionary War encampment to celebrate America's 250th anniversary.
                
                    
                    Michelle Gustafson for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

MILLSTONE TOWNSHIP, N.J. — One recent day in central New Jersey, the grass field around a historic farmhouse was transformed into a Gen. George Washington Revolutionary War encampment, with tents, people in costume and families taking photos.

Suddenly, an unmistakable figure appeared on horseback, wearing a long navy wool coat and a black tricorn hat.

"March!" yelled a man, as a drum and fife (piccolo, actually) struck up a Revolutionary battle tune. Three people dressed as soldiers lined up for review by Washington, then fired shots from long muskets.

Scenes like these have played out across the country as America celebrates its 250th birthday and more people look for ways to take part.

"Anything that pops up, I try to go to," said Robin Fox, who's lived nearby for 21 years but never been to this site.

The semiquincentennial has meant a banner year for historical reenactors and interpreters, especially those who portray the ever-popular Founding Father. Some have driven hundreds of miles a week to meet the demand. And whether it's a hobby or a career, they believe George Washington's life holds important lessons for today, especially at a time of such divided politics.

John Koopman III looks straight out of a history book. It's not just his angular face and hair tied back with a ribbon, but his entire tall frame, as he learned from the tailor who made his military costume.

"Where my sleeves fall and my wrist, the size of my chest, where my breaches fall, is all identical to Washington," he explained. "That made my day."

We met under a shade tree as he stood next to his beloved horse, Bear. Koopman started this hobby nearly three decades ago, when his Connecticut town put on a reenactment to mark the 300th anniversary of its founding.

"Of course, now my wife regrets it, but she said, 'You know, John, you should join one of these units,'" he said. "And now she's sitting there, 'What was I thinking?'"

He liked the Revolutionary War time period and its sense of chivalry, so he stuck with it. The hobby inspired him to learn how to ride a horse. In 2006, a friend said he should try playing Washington because he looked so much like him.

Koopman used a small inheritance to pay for an appropriate saddle and the costume, which cost several thousand dollars each. For an authentic version of Washington's uniform, he commissioned a friend who'd been a tailor for the first president's historic home at Mount Vernon.

John Koopman III dons his replica of George Washington's military uniform before the event in New Jersey.  He said the tailor told him his dimensions are nearly the same as the general's, and "that made my day."
                
                    
                    Michelle Gustafson for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Koopman used a small inheritance to purchase a period-accurate saddle and specially tailored costume.
                
                    
                    Michelle Gustafson for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Since then, Koopman has performed in a film shown at Mount Vernon and multiple other documentaries. He even branched out to write a historical novel on the Revolutionary War.

He retired a year ago from his "regular job" at an alternative energy company and is reenacting full time these days, while the heightened interest lasts. He and his horse recently set a personal best with three separate events in one weekend.

"We had to get in the trailer and go to a different place," he said, adding that Bear "did very well."

Koopman concedes Washington was hardly perfect. He and his wife owned hundreds of slaves, freeing those he owned personally in his will. Still, he finds Washington's call for national unity more relevant than ever. Especially his warning that political parties would put their own needs before those of the people.

"And then you get the situation you have today," he said, where lawmakers oppose good legislation simply because it's proposed by the other party. "That's exactly what Washington predicted would happen."

Koopman's manager, Brad Fay, has had a lifelong fascination with Washington because a distant ancestor was an officer for him during the Revolutionary War. The family inherited a famous painting of the first president, "and it was literally over my shoulder, you know, for my entire teenage years," he said.

Fay believes the significance of America's birth, with its ideals of freedom and equality, has the power to unite.

"It's the one story we all subscribe to," he said, "and so I think it's more important than ever for us to feel a connection to our founding."

A surging hunger for that has kept him and his small team of reenactors busy: He booked 31 events from May through July 4. Beyond the battlefield, a popular experience is an evening dinner with Washington, which often includes the traditional 13 toasts for 13 colonies.

"They would usually be given to Washington, and then Washington would give a return toast," he said.

The central New Jersey encampment included a hospital tent, farm animals and a table where a woman demonstrated how laundry was done. Visitors also packed inside the farmhouse where Leslie Bramlett portrayed the enslaved cook Hannah Till, who traveled with Washington.

"She ends up being freed, and she still stays with George Washington, for seven years of the war," she explained to one family.

Bramlett is part of a broader push to tell the stories of those who made Washington's success possible but were long ignored.

Reenactor Leslie Bramlett, playing George Washington's enslaved cook Hannah Till, stands for a portrait after preparing a display that represents the women of color who played a pivotal role in Washington's army.
                
                    
                    Michelle Gustafson for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

"There were 850 women and children encamped with George Washington at Valley Forge, the beginning of the war, and then that number grows," she said. "So every time you see soldiers, you should remember that there are women and children following them."

Outside the farmhouse, Anthony Privetera said he brought his 7-year-old son to the day's event "because you always learn about history, because if not history repeats itself."

Down the hill, Lee Ann Folk said she became more focused on history in the past few years. Looking back in time helps her feel less worried about today's political divides.

"We've been through hard times," she said. "So it helps to calm the soul, to know that we've been there and we'll get through this."

A few hours south, at historic Mount Vernon, more fife and drum music heralded a recent ribbon-cutting for an updated exhibit. And another person portraying General Washington was on hand to work the crowd.

"Would you have changed anything in your life?" asked a middle school student on a class trip from Bettendorf, Iowa.

"I would not have stood for a second term," replied Doug Thomas, in full military uniform.

Thomas stayed in character as the students asked about his horses and his religion, and he explained how he made a point of attending different houses of worship to show that "bigotry had no place in America."

He also poked gentle fun at the shorts all the students wore, when he said at one point, "The thought is as absent as the rest of your trousers!"

And there was laughter when several middle schoolers from California tried to explain a "selfie" as they gathered around the Founding Father and mugged for the camera.

First-person interpreter Doug Thomas poses for a photo at Mount Vernon's education center on June 11. The students, from El Dorado Hills, Ca., had fun trying to explain a "selfie" while he stayed in character as George Washington.
                
                    
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU
                    
                
                hide caption

This is a career for Thomas, who is not a reenactor but a first-person interpreter. He's played more than 20 people in theater and at historic sites in Philadelphia and "aged into" Washington about seven years ago.

The 250th anniversary amped up his workload. In the past week, he'd driven hundreds of miles to various gigs, including one at a financial group in New York City. There, he talked about lessons from Washington the businessman, such as the importance of branding.

"Branding is literally because he used a branding iron to brand the barrels of flour that he sold at his mill," he explained. "They said 'G. Washington,' so you knew you were getting the finest quality flour that was out there."

Thomas said the nation has not always lived up to the ideals of Washington and its founding documents. But he sees his work as helping to pass them on to new generations, so they can keep building on what's come before.

"The fact that we have a government by the people, for the people, is really absolutely astounding," he said. "And we just need to make sure that we inform the populace that they are, in fact, in charge."

Doug Thomas poses for a portrait as Gen. George Washington in front of the Mount Vernon mansion in Virginia. He's made a career as a first-person interpreter and aims to pass along the ideals of America's founding to new generations.
                
                    
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU
                    
                
                hide caption

Also on hand for the ribbon cutting was Mount Vernon CEO Doug Bradburn, a scholar of early American history. He pointed out that Washington's government, too, had political division.

"Even in his own Cabinet, he had people that hated each other," Bradburn said, "and he constantly had to remind them, until we are governed by angels, we have to allow for differences of opinion."
