WASHINGTON — The 2026 primary elections officially wrapped on Tuesday, and after months of statewide battles, Democrats and Republicans have their lineup for the critical November battle for control of the House and Senate.

Democratic incumbents were rocked by a wave of upsets from far-left challengers as their primary voters indicated that “socialism” isn’t necessarily a dirty word for them. The real test of whether the far-left can win general election contests is still an open question heading into Nov. 3.

Meanwhile, on the Republican side, President Trump’s endorsement once again proved to be indomitable, with few exceptions.

But Trump’s continued dominance has raised questions about what the party will look like when he’s out of office, especially as it deals with fighting between MAGA populists and traditionalists.

Here is what we learned from the 2026 primaries:

Democratic primary voters were angry, not just at Trump, but also at their own leadership. They also seemed eager to rip up the old playbook in favor of insurgent candidates who were prepared to go scorched earth on Republicans and the so-called establishment.

That gave rise to self-described socialists winning primaries, decimating an old taboo against the s-word. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) officially backed over half a dozen candidates who won.

This included Melat Kiros in Colorado, who took down Rep. Diana DeGette, and Darializa Avila Chevalier, who dispatched Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-NY).

Some of those upsets took place in House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ (D-NY) backyard, where his endorsement appeared to be far less impactful than that of Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The DSA wasn’t the only source of a left-wing revolt. Numerous other hardcore lefties such as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and horny oyster farmer Graham Platner emerged victorious in their primaries as well, though they weren’t formally part of the DSA. Platner ultimately was forced to drop out due to rape accusations he has denied.

Most of the far-left upsets took place in Democratic stronghold districts, but a few, such as El-Sayed and Michigan congressional hopeful William Lawrence, became the standard-bearer in battleground races. Lawrence later dropped his DSA affiliation.

The far-left had long hoped for an uprising, and was emboldened by Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) strong showing in the 2016 presidential primary. But up until this point, the establishment had largely been able to keep them at bay. Now, lefties are hoping this will be their “Tea Party” moment and are feeling momentum.

Meanwhile, Republicans believe the DSA revolt has given them an opening in an election cycle where historical headwinds are against them, and they’ve worked to brand the Dems as communists.

As the saying goes, “it’s the economy, stupid.”

Economic concerns were front and center during primary season as voters still feel the pinch from the post-COVID-19 inflation hangover. Poll after poll showed that affordability is the top issue for voters.

Given that Republicans control the trifecta, it’s Democrats’ turn to pin the blame on the GOP for the so-called “affordability crisis.” They seized on Trump’s dizzying array of tariffs and the war in Iran, which surged prices at the gas pump, to argue that his policies have only worsened the cost of living.

Republicans bragged about the One Big Beautiful Bill Act by focusing on tax breaks on tips, overtime pay and senior citizens.

But the far-left used affordability concerns to make the case for socialism and their goal of expanding government programs.

Other niche issues such as data centers also proved potent, as did concerns about the personal conduct of lawmakers, leading to the downfall of lawmakers such as Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.)

Trump’s status as the GOP kingpin during the midterms was mostly unblemished.

The president had a 96% success rate with his endorsements in primaries, roughly matching his record in 2024, despite intervening in primaries more than ever, according to Ballotpedia.

This got him some key scalps, including libertarian-leaning Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has long been a thorn in the side of GOP leadership, and Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) — the first incumbent senator to lose a primary in nearly a decade. Cassidy had voted to impeach him in 2021.

Much to the chagrin of many GOP operatives, including his former de facto co-campaign manager in 2024, Trump also helped Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

But there were a few notable misses, including in Florida, Michigan, Minnesota, and Tennessee over the past month or so. In Minnesota, for example, MyPillow founder Mike Lindell got trounced in his gubernatorial primary, despite Trump’s backing.

As another example, in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District, Trump-backed Amir Hassan lost to former engineer Thomas Smith, who had suspended his campaign weeks prior.

Looming over the primary season was Trump’s pitched battle over redistricting, designed to wipe out Democrats by redrawing congressional lines in a rare mid-decade push. California responded by gerrymandering more Democratic-leaning districts.

In the end, big gains under new maps approved in Texas and Florida mean the GOP could net about 11 more seats in the House. Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) lost his seat in a redistricting collision course against fellow incumbent Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas), when the two were forced to face off in the primary under the new lines.

Some Dem operatives accused Republicans of carrying out “dummymanders” and spreading out their voters too thin in key states, making them vulnerable. But Republicans argue it will help them defy the historical trend of the party in control of the White House typically losing seats in midterms.

“Even in the most conservative reading, we should stay in the majority as long as we’re doing our work district by district,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told The Post last week.

Beyond redistricting, Emmer touted a Supreme Court decision on the Voting Rights Act that also gave way to southern states redrawing lines to the GOP’s benefit in Louisiana and Alabama.

In the midterms, anti-Israel sentiment was even more potent for Democrats than it had been in the 2024 election cycle. It helped fuel key upsets, including Kiros’ breakthrough victory in Colorado.

American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) was a dirty word in Democratic primaries. Still, some of the most pro-Israel Democrats, such as Reps. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) and Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), managed to survive the backlash.

Anti-Israel sentiment also crept up on the Republican side, with Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) facing a primary from Dan Bilzerian, who spewed shockingly antisemitic rhetoric against the incumbent congressman who bashed Muslims.

Pro-Israel Republicans almost universally survived primary challenges over the Jewish state.

In many ways, the midterm season has been an opportunity for factions within the GOP or Democratic Party to gear up for a much bigger battle in the 2028 presidential contest over the future direction of their respective parties.

Dems are dealing with a moderate vs. far-left dynamic, while Republicans are grappling over whether to move in a more traditionalist or populist direction after Trump.
3200_yo_tomb_discovered_in_luxor:
Another month, another big discovery in Luxor—this time of a tomb with preserved interior frescoes dating back around 3,200 years.

The T-shaped tomb was discovered by a team of Dutch-Egypt archaeologists in the middle of a long-term project to combine proactive conservation strategies with archaeological excavations at the Theban Necropolis.

Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, said that inscriptions inside the tomb identify its owner as a man named Paser. Decorative frescoes lining the walls of the tomb indicate it may have been made and occupied during the 19th Dynasty of the New Kingdom—the Ramesside period, that included who is arguably Ancient Egypt’s greatest-ever ruler, Ramesses II.

Research into the site is ongoing. Its open forecourt leading to an inverted T-shape layout is typical of New Kingdom tombs in the necropolis, and may contain a number of people beyond this mysterious Paser, located in a series of presumed underground burial chambers.

Interior elements include a well-preserved mudbrick bench meant to support stone funerary stelae, though these are missing, if ever they sat atop it.

Frescoes depict the tomb’s owner performing various religious rites in the New Kingdom style, as well as another panel with him seated beside his wife at an offerings table.

The discovery of the tomb was made by Carina van den Hoven, who has directed excavations in the sector since 2018, and was documented while establishing the first comprehensive archaeological survey of Lower Sheikh Abd El-Qurna area, one of the most important burial areas of the Theban Necropolis.

A study being prepared documenting the tomb’s discovery is expected to shed new light on the Lower Sheikh Abd El-Qurna and the relationships between its neighboring tombs, as well as the development of funerary culture there.

The discovery follows up major funerary finds in Luxor, including the tomb of a group of so-described “singing priests,” including 22 priests and priestesses in May, and a trio of official tombs in May of last year.

Four Corners examines the scale of Canberra's revolving door, where former government officials turn to lobbying or accept lucrative jobs representing private interests.

PLAYERS: How are you? How are you?

MARK WILLACY, REPORTER: It's a crisp Canberra morning…and MPs and staffers are gathering at a field in the shadow of parliament house for a friendly hit out. Today's football match has been organised by the Parliament Sports Club.

ORGANISER: hello can I get everyone's attention please?

ORGANISER: anyone this morning that stands out, you could be on the plane to America, so no pressure

MARK WILLACY: To Wallabies rugby union captain turned Senator David Pocock, this morning's match is a welcome antidote to the claustrophobia of the chamber that awaits. But what he doesn't know — at least at this point — is that the privately-owned Parliament Sports Club is about more than sport.

DAVID POCOCK: Turns out, and, you know, myself and many of my colleagues didn't know this, they were essentially being sponsored by a whole bunch of companies, industry groups, including the gambling lobby. And so, the gambling lobby were paying for access to events.

DR MONIQUE RYAN, INDEPENDENT MP: It turned out it was also a way for lobbyists to access politicians when we're off guard in the early morning and basically to cozy up to them.

MARK WILLACY: Watching from the sidelines this morning is the most powerful sports betting lobbyist in the country…the CEO of Responsible Wagering Australia, Kai Cantwell.

REV. TIM COSTELLO, ALLIANCE FOR GAMBLING REFORM: Oh, their access is extraordinary. They're all over every politician. And they never miss a trick.

MARK WILLACY: David Pocock has taken a hard line against one of the gambling industry's most potent weapons — sports betting advertising…he wants it sin-binned from our screens. So, the involvement of Responsible Wagering Australia in the Parliament Sports Club - as well as others like alcohol and fossil fuel companies - meant — to him — that a line had been crossed.

DAVID POCOCK: Because of the way the Parliamentary Sports Club was set up and operating, they had advice that they had to list themselves as a lobbying organisation on the lobbyist register. The prime minister is essentially like the patron of the sports club. And so, you had the prime minister who's essentially the patron of a lobbying firm for all intents and purposes if you go by the lobbying register.

MARK WILLACY: The Parliamentary Sports Club turned out to be a registered lobbying firm?

DAVID POCOCK: It did. And when I raised concerns about this, I was kicked out of the club. Got an angry phone call saying, 'Mate, you're, you know, you're causing trouble. You're out'.

ANDY TURNBULL: Football was the winner, that's time now, all over

MARK WILLACY: The Sports Club CEO Andy Turnbull declined Four Corners' interview request but he told us corporate money was used to hold fixtures and dinners and for running costs and that club members were aware of this corporate support.

MARK WILLACY: You're a former Wallabies captain. Is this the first team you've ever been kicked out of?

DAVID POCOCK: Yeah, I think it probably is, yeah

MARK WILLACY: The Parliament Sports Club removed itself from the lobbyist register just a few days after David Pocock was kicked out

DAVID POCOCK: I think the Parliamentary Sports Club debacle highlights just how normalised it is that for many in there, it's just the status quo. People that are part of industries pay for access. They lobby hard, they get privileged access. And that's just how things work in this place.

MARK WILLACY: Four Corners has examined lobbying registers, ministerial diaries and political donations to investigate who gets access to Australia's decision makers … and how little the public is told about it.

SAFFRON ZOMER, AUSTRALIAN DEMOCRACY NETWORK: Australians do really value our democracy. And we want it to be fair. And broken lobbying system makes our democracy work unfairly in the interest of the powerful few and not in the best interest of everyone else.

MARK WILLACY: Lobbying has been part of the Australian political landscape for decades…but critics say that never before has there been so many lobbyists with so much access to decision-makers and so much influence over policy. Inside the people's house, hundreds of unelected representatives have privileged access to those who make the country's laws.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: You can spot lobbyists in the wild by their orange passes. So you have to have a pass which is sponsored by a member of parliament. Those lobbyists can knock on the door and have free access to parliamentarians, when other people have got very valid concerns or complaints who would like to talk to us are denied that opportunity.

MARK WILLACY: Four of the country's top lobbying firms agreed to talk to Four Corners and to reveal how they operate.

MARK WILLACY: It's been extremely rare for lobbyists to come on television, particularly Four Corners, and explain how it all works. Why did you decide to do that?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE, CHAIRMAN, PYNE & PARTNERS: Well, I don't want people to think that lobbyists are like nocturnal creatures who only come out in the dark and don't want anyone to notice them. There's nothing wrong with advocating on behalf of clients to government.

SIMON BANKS, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER HAWKER BRITTON: There are broadly three types of lobbyists. The first, like me, is a third-party lobbyist. We're effectively contracted in by companies and organisations to assist them with their government relations need and we're required to register under the Commonwealth government's lobbyist register.

EAMONN FITZPATRICK: Well, it's a speed dating event. You know, both sides of all the major parties offer them. Some people get a lot out of it. They get to see policy making, the party coalface, if you like.

MARK WILLACY: This paid-for speed dating isn't restricted to the federal level or to the Labor side of politics.

MARK WILLACY: The Ministerial Diary in Queensland shows that on a single day last year, you met with, sometimes with the client, but you met with nine government ministers in a day, including the premier. That's a pretty busy day.

MATTHEW HARRIS: It was a busy day, and it was a very useful day for the government to hear from my clients and for my clients to put their point of view forward.

MARK WILLACY: Is that just a fact of life to sort of sometimes get that face time that you need, you have to pay for it?

MATTHEW HARRIS: I don't see it as cash for access. The reason we donate is to go to functions so we get to know the MPs and ministers who are there

DAVID POCOCK: I mean, if you asked most Australians should a lobbying firm whose whole business is to lobby to get access, should they be allowed to donate to political parties? I think most people would say no. Uh, that is clearly problematic, before I became a Senator, I really had no idea about the extent of it.

MARK WILLACY: Labor MP Mike Freelander believes there needs to be more visibility around political donations.

DR MIKE FREELANDER: We need to recognize none of these groups are lobbying because of altruistic reasons or very few of them. And I think we should be much more transparent about lobbying from groups that cause social harm.

MARK WILLACY: The Attorney-General's department told Four Corners that since mid-2023, it received 52 reports of alleged breaches of the Lobbying Code of Conduct of those, 12 breaches were substantiated while four investigations are ongoing. But the department refused to tell us the outcome of any of its investigations due to what it called privacy reasons. Four Corners also lodged a freedom of information request but the department again refused to release its investigation reports

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: Why shouldn't the public see? If you put up rules and then even when you get caught, nothing happens, you know, you're going to get a slap on the wrist and then carry on with business. What's the point of the rules in the first place?

MARK WILLACY: Lobbying and its ever-revolving door have been part of the Australian political landscape for decades…and for those in the business, it remains an essential part of the democratic process.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Lobbyists are the sinews that make the arms and legs of government work better. They bring ideas and proposals to ministers and ministers' staff that they wouldn't otherwise necessarily see. And that gives ministers another source of advice, and that's good for the Australian government, and therefore good for the Australian public.

MARK WILLACY: But with more than 350 firms on the federal books — including nearly 70 new players registered this year alone — this is an industry that's growing rapidly, and becoming increasingly sophisticated when it comes to getting what it wants.

SIMON KENNEDY: There are too many lobbyists. I think Australia is governed for vested interests and for the squeaky wheels. And why I came into Parliament is I want to be the lobbyists and advocate for the Australians who can't afford lobbyists. I'm their lobbyists. That's why I was elected.

MARK WILLACY: And the revolving door is spinning faster than ever…with more and more political insiders joining the lobbying ranks

MARK WILLACY: What would happen if that revolving door was slammed firmly shut?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Cutting people like me out of a future career in working with government as a lobbyist is kind of a madness to, to waste all those experiences.

KONRAD BENJAMIN: We paid you between 200 and 500 grand a year. You work it out, mate. You know, I've been a teacher and earning a lot less than that. And I have to work it out when I finish teaching. You'll work it out as well.

MARK WILLACY: The federal regime is almost 20 years old. It still does not reveal the basic facts: who lobbyists meet, when they meet and what they seek. Without that information, Australians cannot properly judge who is trying to shape the decisions made in their name.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: Australians are losing faith in government. They're losing faith in politicians. They think, I think they think we're all a little bit dirty. And with good reason. Because they're seeing us making decisions which are in the best interest of lobbying groups, not in their best interests.

They're unelected, highly paid and represent powerful interests. And there's an army of them. They're lobbyists.

Lobbyists have been a feature of the political landscape for decades, but their numbers have never been greater and, according to some critics, neither has their access and influence.

Next week on Four Corners reporter Mark Willacy investigates the opaque business of political lobbyists — where they go, who they meet and what they want.

In Access All Areas, four of the country's top lobbyists — Simon Banks (Hawker Britton), Christopher Pyne (Pyne & Partners), Eamonn Fitzpatrick (Fitzpatrick & Co Advisory) and Matthew Harris (Barton Deakin) — reveal how they operate and why they believe lobbying makes the process of governing more effective. But advocates for stronger oversight and regulation, including some politicians, say the system that is meant to guard against undue influence is broken and vested interests are winning.

Set against the backdrop of the Albanese government's recent efforts to pass its gambling reforms package, the program interrogates the lack of transparency around lobbying activities, which types of lobbyists are more regulated and scrutinised than others, and the 'revolving door' between politics and private enterprise.

And as Four Corners discovered, blatant pay for access schemes are also alive and well in our political system, with lobbyists using them to get "face time" with ministers. So how much do they pay? Who do they get to lobby? And who are the winners?

As the lobbying industry increases in size and sway and faith in politicians wanes, critics say it's time for an effective and functional lobbying regime.

Four Corners: Access All Areas is reported by Mark Willacy and goes to air Monday, August 24 at 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

The ACT Greens want gambling advertisements banned at Canberra Stadium to limit an industry that "has successfully brainwashed our kids", and have offered to begin fresh negotiations with Labor on reducing gambling harm.

Login or signup to continue reading

Rebecca Vassarotti, the party's gambling harm spokeswoman, said strict restrictions should also be introduced to block online gambling advertisements from being displayed in Canberra during major sports fixtures in the ACT and the territory government should work harder to push for more restrictive national advertising rules.

"By relentlessly inundating 12-to-17-year-olds with constant betting promotions during family-friendly match times, the gambling industry has successfully brainwashed our kids, and as a parent, I know our community has had enough," Ms Vassarotti said.

"Big corporations have conditioned a new generation to believe that you cannot love sport without placing a punt. But sport should be about community, about connection with the outdoors, about teamwork and mateship - not about making a quick buck."

A Legislative Assembly inquiry that examined male suicide rates in June recommended a full gambling advertising ban because "reducing the promotion and accessibility of gambling environments can play an important role in lowering suicide risk among men, particularly in young men".

Gaming Minister Marisa Paterson said many of the Greens' proposals related to areas regulated by the Commonwealth but the ACT was committed to progressing its significant gambling harm reduction agenda.

"We welcome the federal government's proposed legislation to restrict gambling advertising and will continue to work constructively to support its implementation. The proposed reforms include restrictions on gambling advertising at sporting venues," Dr Paterson said.

Dr Paterson said a gambling harm prevention and mitigation fund had been expanded to allow access for research organisations and expert advocacy groups, meaning the government would have stronger advice on practical harm-minimisation measures.

"We also recognise the growing risks associated with online gambling and remain committed to working with the federal government on measures that reduce harm and strengthen protections for vulnerable people," she said.

Ms Vassarotti said the ACT too often suffered from a lack of imagination and belief that it could legislate to tackle big issues.

"But the reality is, we have the levers, we have the power, all we need is a bit of collaboration and old-fashioned political will," she said.

"That's why the Greens are putting forward a decisive list of recommendations for the territory government to prove it's actually serious about gambling reform. The reality is, we are halfway through this Assembly term, and so far, this government has announced exactly zero new reforms to reduce gambling harm."

A May audit found no gambling advertising at ACT government venues during Raiders and Brumbies games, but UniBet was featured on LED perimeter field-of-play and video board graphics at a GWS Giants game.

No direct gambling advertising contracts are in place at ACT government venues but sports teams that hire the venues can have contracts, including on uniforms and screen advertisements.

Ms Vassarotti said federal laws that would delay gambling ads until after 8.30pm did absolutely nothing to protect children or families and would simply safeguard the gambling industry's massive profits.

"Last term, the Greens fought tooth and nail for poker machine reforms to stop Canberrans from being bled dry by the pervasive tactics of clubs," she said.

"But since then, it has become clear the government had a different point of view. But in the urgent interest of our community, the Greens are willing to wipe the slate clean. Today, we are offering to negotiate in good faith with the government on fresh policy reforms that they can actually get behind to protect our community."

Dr Paterson said the government was focused on its significant gambling harm reduction agenda.

"At the 2024 election, we committed to introducing mandatory cashless gaming across all clubs in the ACT. We are also committed to long-term reduction in gaming machines in the ACT and a modernised self-exclusion system," she said.

"Work is underway to deliver these reforms before the end of the current term."

Activists showed up at cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen‘s San Francisco mansion to protest his support of Flock cameras.

A coalition of over 20 immigrant rights groups, climate organizers and others are demonstrating as part of the “National Week of Action Against Automated License Plate Readers.”

They erected dummy yellow cardboard cameras outside Larsen’s Bay Area home with signs inscribed with: “Does this make you feel safer, Chris?”

The protesters on Friday also pasted bright-pink posters with the image of a shocked doll’s face and arrows pointing toward the installed Flock cameras. “There is a Flock camera on this pole. Do something,” read the poster.

“There’s not much evidence that Flock cameras significantly impact crime rates,” Luc Bouchard, an organizer with Sunrise Movement Bay Area, claimed to ABC News.

Bouchard also accused Larsen of investing “more than any tech billionaire in the tech surveillance system in San Francisco.”

“He feels that he’s entitled to watch us; we came to his house to watch him,” Bouchard said.

The series of protests comes on the heels of rising mass surveillance concerns among residents in California and across the nation.

More than 117,000 automated license plate readers from Flock Safety are located across the country, including more than 16,000 in California alone, according to a DeFlock map. Flock’s cameras account for about 83% of the map’s total.

Most of the cameras in the Golden State are in Los Angeles or the Bay Area. San Francisco County ranked third in the nation for cameras per road mile with 1,196 per 1,000 miles, according to the data.

Online tool DeFlock.org had also revealed earlier this month that controversial Flock cameras were installed across six locations in Yosemite National Park despite mass surveillance concerns.

However, park officials claimed that the cameras are not designed to read license plates but to help control traffic.

Amid mounting scrutiny from privacy advocates and politicians, Flock Safety had announced earlier this month that it will reduce the duration of data stored by the license-plate cameras from 30 days to just seven.

The company had also assured that cops would have to justify every search.

CEO Garrett Langley told the California Post the overhaul amounts to the toughest license-plate-reader policy in the country.

About 90% of investigative searches on Flock’s system already occur within seven days, according to Langley.

Mounted on streetlights, these cameras capture images of passing vehicles and log their license plates. Authorized users can reconstruct a vehicle’s route by mapping these photos and locations.

The system automatically converts the imagery into searchable database records by indexing license plates, model, color, unique features and timestamps.

The LAPD has already suspended its contract with the company over privacy and data security fears.

The son of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov has been awarded his second “Hero of Chechnya” award at age 18.

Adam Kadyrov received the title for “comprehensive support” to Russia’s war in Ukraine, Kadyrov senior’s close ally Magomed Daudov wrote on Telegram on Friday.

Daudov noted that the award was also timed in celebration of Russia Day, a national holiday.

Kadyrov received his first “Hero of Chechnya” award at age 15 in 2023 after the high-profile beating in pre-trial detention of a young Russian man accused of burning the Quran.

Since that beating, to which Russian authorities turned a blind eye, Kadyrov has racked up several awards and was appointed to a number of senior positions in his native Chechnya.

In Friday’s announcement, Daudov referred to the young man by his titles of assistant to the head of the republic of Chechnya and secretary of the Chechen security council.

Daudov himself, who fought on the side of rebels during both Chechen wars but later switched sides after then-leader Akhmat Kadyrov promised to pardon separatist fighters, received the Hero of Russia award in 2007.

Kadyrov Sr. promoted Daudov, who has been accused of widespread human rights abuses, to the rank of major-general.

LOS ANGELES — Mia Taylor looked down at her Los Angeles County election ballot a few weeks ago and felt a familiar mix of duty and dread. How could she possibly know the best choices in the dozens of local contests she was asked to vote in? Partly on a lark, she turned to a newly ubiquitous tool: Claude.

Taylor snapped a picture of her ballot and asked: “So, who do I vote for here?”

Claude, an artificial intelligence chatbot developed by Anthropic to analyze data and hold natural conversations, initially declined to answer. Like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, Claude is trained to avoid answering political questions that could expose biases.

So Taylor, a self-described liberal Democrat, sharpened her question, asking it to find links to well-regarded progressive groups and help her come up with strategic voting options.

“Here are some sources you can look at,” it replied, linking to voter guides and describing each race in detail. Taylor was especially torn about her vote for mayor, wondering how she could help stop Spencer Pratt, the Republican who momentarily looked likely to win one of the top two spots in the open primary. Claude’s advice: Vote for the incumbent, Karen Bass, not Nithya Raman, a member of the City Council. (Pratt later lost the race, while Bass and Raman advanced to the general election.)

It was probably only a matter of time before voters began to use artificial intelligence to help guide their choices. The 2026 midterms may be the first U.S. elections in which voters are using AI in meaningful numbers.

Voters are turning to new AI tools to serve as nonpartisan researchers, viewing them as a viable alternative to traditional news coverage, voter guides or social media. They provide an appealing and seemingly efficient way to learn about campaigns and ballot measures, allowing users to bypass the sometimes dizzying array of political literature, advertising and commentary coming their way. But some experts warn that the tools are far from foolproof: The results they produce can be marred by factual errors or shaped by flawed assumptions.

Chris Johnson, a 58-year-old resident of Atlanta, appreciates the allure of relying on AI to choose candidates and the worry about its accuracy.

Johnson, a registered Republican who considers himself a libertarian, has voted in every Georgia election for the past 40 years. When he prepared to vote in the state primary in May, he asked ChatGPT to tell him which of the candidates was the most libertarian. Initially, the system resisted answering directly, so Johnson asked it to rely on the candidates’ voting history. The chatbot suggested Brad Raffensperger, the Georgia secretary of state who was running for governor in the Republican primary and ultimately lost the race.

Johnson felt chagrined by how easy it was. He recalled that for years he read the print edition of the local newspaper to come up with his own sense of which candidates most closely matched his values.

“I felt a bit lazy for not doing more,” he said. “It felt easier, but I am not sure that everything was correct.”

The appeal of artificial intelligence tools, also referred to as large language models, lies in their simplicity: Users often find the information they produce more straightforward and understandable than data from a more traditional internet search. And many welcome the interaction. Researchers and AI companies are already envisioning a time when political campaigns create their own chatbots, enabling voters to question them directly.

“There is a reason these models are persuasive: They come up with facts or factual claims and are just good clear explainers,” said David G. Rand, a professor of information science, marketing and psychology at Cornell University who has done extensive research on the effectiveness of artificial intelligence in political persuasion.

Earlier this year, before voting in a local school board election, Rand turned to artificial intelligence for help. He uploaded an hourlong video of a campaign forum and then asked which of the candidates most closely matched his values. He used this research to make his choices. And when he ran his picks by friends who were more involved in local politics, they endorsed his reasoning.

Still, Rand noted, the output is only as good as the input: AI tends to reaffirm and mirror users’ biases, framing candidates’ views through the voters’ lens, rather than objective facts.

Anthropic, the parent company of Claude, has said users asking about political topics “should get comprehensive, accurate and balanced responses — responses that help them reach their own conclusions rather than steer them toward a particular viewpoint.” In a lengthy statement this year, the company said Claude is trained to “treat different political viewpoints with equal depth, engagement and analytical rigor.”

Jeremiah Hain, a 42-year-old psychotherapist in Los Angeles who has used ChatGPT routinely for other small tasks, recently employed it to help him choose candidates in races for mayor and various other offices.

“I don’t have the time, nor did I want to do the same kind of research I have done in the past,” he said. “This was very intuitive, and I actually respect its intelligence, I guess.”

He was so enamored of the process that he posted a video on TikTok encouraging other voters to do the same. (And because he knows his videos get more engagement when he is shirtless, Hain filmed himself bare-chested. “I wanted to do this as a thirst trap on purpose,” he said.)

But that sense of efficiency may mask the risks of turning over the democratic process to technology, some experts warn. Because most chatbots produce answers that sound confident and authoritative, users may not make the time to check the underlying claims.

Ideally, AI tools for election help would rely on a curated and verified database of political information and policy platforms to help voters, rather than pulling data from across the internet, as the existing tools do, said Yamil Velez, a political science professor at Columbia University who has researched the effectiveness of AI in convincing voters. But he was reluctant to completely dismiss the usefulness of AI in election decisions. “It is important to think about what is the alternative,” he said. After all, he added, most voters are unlikely to spend hours in the county clerk’s office researching their election options.

A year ago, Velez added, he would have said that voters would be better off relying on an internet search, but the AI tools are becoming increasingly accurate.

Nonetheless, he cautioned, the current tools likely benefit candidates who are more vocal in the local press and on social media, making their views easier to find. Campaign strategists are keenly aware that voters are using these tools and have begun looking for ways to get more favorable results by publishing more material online in formats that chatbots prefer, such as using bullet points.

Still, in interviews, people who had used AI to research election choices said it allowed them to vote with more confidence.

Robert Siebelink, a 54-year-old Democrat who lives in Corona, California, turned to Claude after feeling overwhelmed by the prospect of researching the 61 candidates running for governor in his state, not to mention the candidates in less high-profile races. He uploaded his ballot and asked Claude to suggest candidates who most aligned with his values.

Eventually, he had narrowed down his choice for governor to two Democrats, Xavier Becerra and Tom Steyer, and asked Claude how to strategize.

In less than half an hour, he had filled out his ballot and chosen Becerra.

“I just felt so refreshed,” Siebelink said. “That’s the most informed voting that I have ever done.”

“It felt like some political expert that knew all of the research and we just sat down over coffee and chatted, and they took notes,” he said.

Similarly, Rikki Powers, a 31-year-old Democrat who lives in Baltimore, took a photograph of his ballot before the recent Maryland primary and asked Claude to provide bullet points for each candidate. He said he was looking for a broader perspective than what he could get from candidate campaign websites. After checking some of the links for accuracy and to “make sure that I truly like the candidates I am voting for,” he used the summary to fill out his ballot on the spot.

“The last time I voted, I spent probably 20 hours researching,” he said. “This time was an hour.”

Still, Powers said, there are limits: While he had no hesitation uploading a blank ballot, he would never tell AI how he voted.

A pair of pilfering baggage handlers at a New Orleans airport swiped a nearly $80,000 Patek Philippe watch from a passenger’s luggage, police said.

Thaddeus Porter, 42, and Morris Robinson, 18, were busted for allegedly snatching the luxury timepiece from the luggage of a man who had flown from Los Angeles to the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on Sept. 24, NOLA.com reported.

Investigators from the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office said they reviewed security-camera footage and were able to identify Porter and Robinson, who worked handling baggage for the traveler’s airline, as the thieves.

Cops arrested the alleged thieving duo that same day and booked them into the Jefferson Parish Correctional Facility, charging them with felony theft valued over $25,000, court records show.

Records show that a day later, Porter and Robinson posted two separate $25,000 bonds, according to court records.

Porter and Robinson could not be reached for comment.

The value of Melbourne-founded payments company Airwallex has soared to $US11 billion ($16 billion) after it raised hundreds of millions of dollars from investors in new funding, even as it fights a financial-crimes audit at home and mounting pressure in the United States over its links to China.

The $US320 million funding round means Airwallex’s valuation has increased by about $US3 billion in roughly six months, a vote of confidence in one of Australia’s most valuable private companies even as scrutiny of it intensifies on two fronts.

Started in 2015 by chief executive Jack Zhang, president Lucy Liu and three university friends frustrated by the cost of paying overseas suppliers for a Melbourne coffee shop, Airwallex has built a global payments network that sidesteps the ageing bank-to-bank system. It moves more than $1 billion a day and counts Qantas, Canva and Culture Amp among its customers, and is now domiciled in the Cayman Islands, with head offices in Singapore and San Francisco.

The money lands at a fraught moment. In January, the financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC ordered an external audit of Airwallex’s anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing program, at the company’s expense, saying it had “reasonable grounds to suspect” breaches of several sections of the act. The watchdog raised concern that the platform was being used by money mules to move illicit funds; this masthead has reported that authorities feared it was also being used to facilitate payments linked to child exploitation. The auditor’s report will not be made public.

Airwallex has said it is co-operating fully and welcomed the audit as a chance to validate its program. But the scrutiny has clouded a long-expected sharemarket float. Zhang told CNBC in 2024 that the company would be “IPO ready” within two years, then wrote on LinkedIn after the AUSTRAC order that it “never planned to do an IPO this year, or even next year”. Airwallex has since hired crisis public-relations advisers and, through law firm Mark O’Brien Legal, demanded that The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review remove five articles based on leaked internal documents. The articles remain online.

In the United States, the company has become a target for China hawks. On June 17, Republican senator Tom Cotton wrote to Treasury secretary Scott Bessent urging the committee on foreign investment in the United States to review Chinese investment in Airwallex, arguing that its Chinese shareholders could expose sensitive American data to Beijing. Cotton wrote that Tencent and HongShan together held a stake of more than 20 per cent, and had earlier asked the Justice Department to investigate.

Zhang has rejected the claims. In a June 9 blog post responding to “patently false allegations” from a competitor, he said American customer data was stored in the US and that staff in China and Hong Kong could not reach it. The allegations were first aired in December by Keith Rabois, a venture capitalist on the board of rival Ramp.

For all the noise, the business is growing fast. Airwallex reported $US1.3 billion in annualised revenue as of March, up 74 per cent on a year earlier, and an annualised $US287 billion in transaction volume, up more than 120 per cent. The latest round was led by returning backer Addition, the New York firm run by Lee Fixel, with Baillie Gifford, QED Investors, T. Rowe Price, Hedosophia, Haun Ventures and Amex Ventures among those taking part. Australian funds Square Peg Capital, Blackbird Ventures and AirTree Ventures are earlier backers, alongside Tencent.

Alongside the raise, Airwallex unveiled two artificial intelligence products it says will push it from moving money to running finance outright: T:0, a finance “department” in private beta that handles bookkeeping, tax and reporting, and Airi, a consumer wallet built for so-called agentic commerce, in which software makes purchases on a person’s behalf.

Everything we hear about artificial intelligence is conflicting, and hearing about it feels inescapable. AI is terrible. AI is wonderful. It will break the world. It will transform the future. It’s essential to embrace it. It’s a moral imperative to abstain from using it.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Already, AI is projected to generate nearly unfathomable amounts of revenue. In the last quarter of 2025, it represented nearly 60% of the growth in the US economy. Already, pundits and economists wring their hands about what calamity will befall us if and when the AI bubble bursts.

Since ChatGPT, the first of the large language models, was released in late 2022, more than half a million workers in the tech industry alone have lost their jobs. Any mention of AI tends to be accompanied by warnings that deeper jobs cuts across many more industries are coming for us all. Jensen Huang, CEO of chip giant Nvidia, said in 2025: “Every job will be affected, and immediately. It is unquestionable. You’re not going to lose your job to an AI, but you’re going to lose your job to someone who uses AI.” In January, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, predicted: “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.”

Increasingly, people young and old flock to a new gold rush in Silicon Valley to toil away on AI-fueled startups. Many of them are driven less by idealistic enthusiasm and more by the dread of missing a ticket for the last train to wealth – and getting stuck forever in the “permanent underclass” that, with any luck, they themselves will create.

What all these divergently apocalyptic ideas hold in common is their AI absolutism – a way of seeing AI as a godlike force that will either hasten a golden age of productivity and innovation, or will doom humanity. It mirrors the political polarization of our era and even the zealotry found in religious fanaticism. This is by design. Contradictory as they may be, all these arguments and anxieties fit neatly into the overarching message of the people building this technology: AI’s dominance is inevitable. Get on board or you will be left behind. The robber barons of our age stand to profit wildly from not only enthusiasm about their star product, but also, the terror of it.

“If you want to justify this enormous valuation in your IPO, you need to point to the revenue stream that you’re going to generate in the future,” said Suresh Naidu, a professor at Columbia University’s department of economics. “You just need to make it look like you have something that can eat all the work on the planet, so that an investor will think: ‘Oh wow, I don’t want to miss out on this thing.’”

Naidu isn’t refuting claims that AI will cut into jobs or upend certain industries. He called the technology “transformative” and said that he uses it every day in his work as a researcher and academic. It’s just that when he zooms out and puts AI and all its attendant promises and warnings in historical context, he sees a lot of hype.

Anil Dash, the former CEO of the startup Glitch, who’s been writing about tech for decades, is also unconvinced that the AI we’re being sold will do all the things tech CEOs are predicting it will do.

“Any technology that you invest like a trillion dollars into is going to be able to do a lot of things, good or bad. [AI is] a leap forward. I don’t think we’ve ever had a machine learning system that can do as many things as this one does,” he said. But “there’s so much noise that it’s hard to tell what the domains of applicability are.” Coding is an exception, he said. It’s easier to test an AI model’s coding output because it will clearly work, or it won’t. Many other applications for the tech are much more subjective and therefore less prone to immediate job replacement.

That’s why the tech industry has made the deepest job cuts so far – though, amid layoffs at companies such as Amazon, Meta and Block, reports from employees have emerged saying the AI productivity gains their bosses trumpet are overblown.

Even the role AI is playing in those layoffs and reductions to entry-level positions isn’t entirely clear. Martin Beraja, a professor at UC Berkeley Haas School of Business who studies technological innovation and business cycles, said recent studies that have drawn connections between the release of ChatGPT and a decline in entry-level software jobs are “problematic”.

There was “a buildup of jobs in [tech] coming out of the pandemic, and once … consumption patterns moved away from online to the real world again, now we had too many people working in the industry that we didn’t really need”, Beraja said.

Some of the biggest and most loudly pro-AI players in tech have arrived at similar conclusions as AI critics. Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen proclaimed in March that overstaffed companies are using AI as a “silver-bullet excuse” to clean house. In May, OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, retreated on some of his prior claims of massive job replacement by AI, saying: “I thought there would have been more impact on entry-level white-collar jobs being eliminated by now than ​has actually happened.”

And if AI’s worst-case scenario for tech jobs plays out – which would indeed be very bad for many people – that’s still nowhere near the apocalyptic future of labor that many fear. “Is it, in fact, going to destroy all of the jobs?” Naidu asked. “I’m not convinced. Even take software. Software is only about 4 to 6% of GDP. So it’s a lot, but it’s not like the whole economy can be replaced by Claude Code.”

Convincing people that AI will replace human workers in droves is a clever marketing tactic. Not only does it stoke rabid investor speculation, but it distracts from a more realistic application of AI for the global workforce, stretching far beyond the borders of the tech industry: using AI to surveil and micromanage employees to squeeze yet more productivity out of them, all the while pressuring them to feel grateful that they have any kind of work at all. Gig workers, the people who pick you up in Ubers and deliver your food on platforms like DoorDash, have already been the guinea pigs for this kind of algorithmic management, and labor experts predict it will spread.

It can feel like we’re living in an experiment when it comes to the rise of AI. Naidu would like us to update that framing. “An experiment implies a control group of something that’s not affected. There’s no control group here,” he said.

The version of AI that we’re being sold doesn’t have to be the version we buy. Nor does it need to be the story we believe in.

This isn’t an argument for an abstinence-only relationship with AI, something that has too much in common with evangelical Christianity’s unrealistic stance on premarital sex. Anyone with common sense can see how those kinds of ascetic codes play out in reality. It’s happening already with AI. “AI is just another technology Americans don’t like but can’t stop using,” the Washington Post’s Shira Ovide wrote earlier this year, referring to the polarized divide between polling that shows how much they distrust the tech and numbers of rapid user growth in the past year.

Instead, this is an argument for moderation. Beraja, the UC Berkeley professor, said there was too much focus on AI as a job replacement technology. Outside a few industries like tech, he said studies show that the most effective ways for people and companies to use AI is not to replace workers, but to learn more, and learn faster.

“Where I think we have to get to is, there can be alternatives,” said Dash. “What we can imagine is, rather than the ChatGPT killer, a lot of different little AIs from little responsible players.” A few are already quietly cropping up, harkening back to earlier and more optimistic days in the internet’s history, and offering a glimpse of what could be possible if people took AI into their own hands.

And for the industries and jobs that AI is upending, upheaval may open the way for a resurgence in worker power as white-collar workers begin to see the appeal of solidarity, whether with colleagues in their office or workers in the blue-collar world.

After all, the Industrial Revolution, an earlier time of great technological transformation that strangely mirrors our current moment, was a key catalyst for the labor movement – even if its wins took time.
ai_datacenter_heat:
Data centres don’t just use large amounts of water and electricity, they’re heating the environment too, study finds.

Save

Share

Tech giants are racing to build the infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence.

But a growing body of evidence suggests that AI hyperscalers – large-scale cloud service providers like Google, Amazon and Microsoft – are warming the ground around them as well.

A study [PDF] by Cambridge-led researchers found that land surface temperatures around AI data centres rise by an average of 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit), with some areas recording increases as high as 9C (16.2F).

Researchers have called this the “data heat island effect”. Al Jazeera explains what that is, where AI data centres are concentrated and the effects on those living near these facilities.

Every time someone uses ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, the request is handled in a data centre, a vast facility full of specialised computers that run 24 hours a day.

AI data centres use powerful chips that perform thousands of calculations in parallel and running large models continuously makes them much more energy hungry than typical servers used to browse the web.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centres consumed about 415 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of global supply, growing at about 15 percent a year over the last five years. That figure is projected to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030.

Among the most energy-intensive are hyperscale data centres – the largest facilities of their kind, built by major tech companies to support cloud computing and AI at a global scale. According to IBM, they typically house at least 5,000 servers and occupy a minimum of 10,000sq feet (930sq metres).

Hyperscale data centres typically require between 100 and 300 megawatts of electricity to operate (continuously at any given second), enough to power hundreds of thousands of homes.

That energy generates enormous amounts of heat, which must be managed through advanced liquid cooling systems that consume vast quantities of water.

A report by the UK government’s digital sustainability advisory body found that a single 100-megawatt hyperscale data centre can consume about 2.5 billion litres (660 million gallons) of water a year – equivalent to the annual needs of 80,000 people.

The global landscape for AI data centre construction is currently experiencing an unprecedented acceleration, with more than 11,600 data centres active worldwide as of June 2026.

Most data centres are located in the United States, which has more than 4,300 according to Data Center Map, a crowdsourced database that tracks data centre locations worldwide.

Europe is the second-largest hub, led by the United Kingdom with more than 540 facilities, heavily clustered around London, followed by Germany (520+) and France (390+).

Across Asia, China (360+) and India (300+) lead the region, while Southeast Asia is expanding rapidly and is one of the fastest‑growing markets for data‑centre capacity and cloud adoption.

According to Synergy Research Group, the number of hyperscale data centres worldwide has nearly doubled since 2021, from 700 to 1,297.

A study by researchers from Cambridge, Nanyang Technological University and others found that land surface temperature around AI data centres rise by an average of 2C (3.6F) after they open, with effects being felt up to 10km (6 miles) away.

The phenomenon mirrors the urban heat island effect, where concentrated human activity causes cities to run warmer than surrounding rural areas.

Using NASA satellite data, researchers measured land surface temperature globally from 2004 to 2024 and cross-referenced it with more than 11,000 AI data centre locations worldwide.

The study focused on 6,733 centres outside densely populated areas, comparing temperatures in the months after each opened against a five-year baseline at the same location.

Temperature increases ranged from 0.3C (0.54F) to 9.1C (16.38F).

The study found that more than 340 million people living within 10km (6 miles) of a data centre could be affected by the temperature increases – an impact researchers described as having a “remarkable influence on communities and regional welfare” and one that should be part of the global conversation about environmentally sustainable AI.

While most data centres are located in industrial areas away from dense population centres, their waste heat can create a localised “data heat island” with the research suggesting this warming can be detected up to 10km (6 miles) away.

The resulting temperature increases could place additional pressure on nearby communities by affecting health, energy demand and overall wellbeing.

The map below illustrates a 10km (6-mile) radius around four major AI data centres worldwide, showing the areas that could potentially be impacted by this localised warming effect.

Global investment bank, Goldman Sachs, says it expects a combined $5.3 trillion of capital expenditure between 2025 to 2030 for the four largest hyperscalers: Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta.

ai_store_manager_fires_employee:
The AI agent running a San Francisco store has made its first firing decision.

Andon Labs said Thursday that Luna, the AI manager of Andon Market, an experimental retail store run entirely by AI, decided to dismiss a human employee after repeated lateness and other workplace issues. The employee arrived late for 17 of 23 shifts, according to the lab's report.

Luna did not reach the decision entirely unprompted. Conversation logs between the lab and Luna show that the agent had created an attendance policy but later lost track of it, allowing the employee's lateness to continue for months. Andon Labs eventually asked Luna to search her memory for its policies and assess whether the worker was still a good fit.

Luna then recommended "parting ways" with the employee, a decision that the humans in the lab reviewed and carried out.

Andon Labs cofounder Lukas Petersson told Business Insider that the lab would intervene if Luna made an illegal or unethical decision, but he did not believe that was necessary here.

"In this instance, we did not think that that was necessary because the firing was warranted," Petersson said, pointing to the store's policy, which was clearly stated.

"I think obviously the relationship between a manager and an employee is quite delicate, especially depending on the employee's position," Petersson added. "But what we've seen in this experiment is not that the AI would be more ruthless or be worse for the employee in that decision."

According to screenshots and conversation logs posted on Andon Labs' website, Luna gave the employee progressive and repeated warnings, as well as additional training, for months without taking any contractual action.

The firing came after the experimental store officially opened in San Francisco on April 1. Andon Labs, which tests the limits of AI agents, gave Luna a $100,000 budget, internet access, and a corporate credit card, along with instructions to open a store and turn a profit.

Luna, built using Anthropic's Claude models, selected merchandise, hired contractors, posted jobs on Indeed, interviewed applicants, and hired employees for Andon Market, which sells books, candles, prints, games, and branded merchandise. Andon Labs provided support for more difficult tasks, such as permitting, but said the lab tried to be as hands-off as possible.

Based on the experiment guidelines, all store workers hired by Luna are formally employed by the lab, receive guaranteed pay, and have legal protections. The store has generated sales but is not profitable.

Petersson said that the firing also exposed a persistent weakness in AI agents: They often fail to act without a direct prompt.

"We saw that a human boss would probably fire them much sooner," Petersson said. "I think companies will be run completely by AI in the future, and that AIs will become employers of humans."

By ANDREW BROWN

Published:  09:57 AEST, 10 September 2026   |  Updated:  09:59 AEST, 10 September 2026

75

View  comments

Laws being introduced to federal parliament on Thursday will overhaul customs rules to make it easier for illegal 'chop shop' tobacco to be seized.

Under previous customs rules, it had to be proved illicit tobacco was being knowingly imported illegally.

The reforms will mean cigarettes being sold for less than the amount of excise and GST, presented in different packaging or being concealed would be enough for authorities to charge.

Assistant customs minister Julian Hill said the measures would bring customs rules up to date to properly tackle the scourge of illegal tobacco.

'It'll give powerful new tools to border force, but every state and territory police force to go after the crooks,' he told ABC Radio on Thursday.

'This is a major global problem, and Australia's not immune. It's this massive surplus of cheap production of stuff for less than $1 a pack that's been weaponised by serious and organised criminal syndicates flooding national borders.'

The measures follow the coalition pledging to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent in a bid to stop the rise of illegal cigarettes.

The response came after One Nation said it would cut the excise by 75 per cent.

Tackling the illicit tobacco trade has caused ructions among political forces in Canberra

Some have blamed a levy for contributing to a wave of fire bombings on tobacco and vape sellers

About 80 per cent of all tobacco consumed in 2025 was illegal, up from 12 per cent in 2017, according to estimates from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

At the same time, the tobacco excise has more than tripled.

Opponents have said the government increasing the excise by 34 per cent since it came to office in 2022 has contributed to a burgeoning black market and a wave of fire bombings on tobacco and vape sellers.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Wednesday left the door open to cutting the tobacco excise, but also said making legal tobacco and vapes more affordable was not going to help.

'State governments as well have a responsibility to crack down on shops that are selling illegal products,' he said.

Hill said he expected to have support across the parliament for the customs changes.

'They're exactly the powers which our law enforcement officials have been asking for,' he said.

'The way to really hurt these crooks is to go after their cash and their houses and their boats and their cars and their toys and take the profits of their crime off them.'

ANALYSIS: As the US downgrades the nuclear submarines deal to second-hand vessels, Australia’s options to back out have narrowed to one possible shift in domestic politics.

Australia’s future Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines will all be second-hand – it’s about simplicity, according to Defence Minister Richard Marles. Previously, one of the boats was going to come fresh from the American production line but now all will be transferred from United States Navy service. Virginia-class submarines are built in versions or “blocks” so that new technology and design features can be incorporated over time. Australia will now get one block rather than two.

“What we will have here is a simpler pathway,” Marles told reporters at the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore last week. “The Virginias we are acquiring will all be of the same type and I can’t overstate the significance of that.”

Of course, one easily could overstate the significance of this change, as the deputy prime minister went on to demonstrate by acknowledging it won’t make much difference to the price Australia pays for its submarines.

Still, Marles had a point. Before this latest announcement, Australia was effectively proposing to conduct four overlapping submarine projects: the upgrade of the navy’s existing Collins-class boats; introducing two versions of the Virginia-class; and the design and construction of an all-new submarine to be built in the United Kingdom and Adelaide. That’s now back to three, which, given Australia has never managed more than one submarine project at a time, still leaves plenty of room for risk.

Shadow defence minister Senator James Paterson had an uncomfortable question for the government: if getting only second-hand submarines is so clearly the right decision, why wasn’t it taken at the outset? Something else had clearly changed, but what?

The most plausible answer is that the US wants to keep the newest and most advanced version of the Virginia for itself. American shipyards are struggling to raise their productivity enough to fill the US Navy’s own order books, let alone meet the commitment to Australia. So the Pentagon is cutting its cloth, with Marles left to make the best of it.

The announcement reinforced a sense of scepticism about whether the Virginia-class submarines can be delivered at all. Up to this point, questioning of AUKUS has come predominantly from the progressive side of Australian politics. According to a report in The Australian newspaper this week, that now includes Labor Party backbencher Ed Husic and sections of the union movement.

Concerns about AUKUS now appear to be gaining purchase on the right, too. The Liberal Party had hitherto been loath to even consider the possibility of delays, but Senator Paterson gave a speech in April calling for the government to investigate alternative weapon systems that “may help fill any capability gaps that arise”.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities ... We may now have come too far to go back.

Former Abbott government treasurer Joe Hockey was more direct. Hockey is well briefed on this topic, as founding partner of the Washington, DC-based consultancy Bondi Partners, which says on its website: “With the evolution of AUKUS … Bondi Partners footprint continues to grow across the Pacific and the Atlantic.”

Hockey recently told the National Press Club that, for the first time, he was “a little nervous” about the delivery schedule for the Virginia-class submarines.

It raises a question that has seemed implausible until now: could the Albanese government step away from the AUKUS submarines? Is there a realistic pathway towards cancellation?

There are strong reasons to believe the government will maintain its commitment. For one thing, Marles is a powerful figure in the cabinet and appears to sincerely believe in the project.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities. It could have come to office in 2022 announcing an inquiry on the entirely justifiable basis that its endorsement of the project while in opposition was based on very little information released by the Morrison government.

Failing that, the Albanese government could have used the opportunity created by the Pentagon’s decision to review AUKUS, announced in June last year. That would have been the perfect moment to quietly communicate to the Trump administration that, if the review should happen to recommend against proceeding, Australia wouldn’t be too upset. This would have avoided any need for the government to take a “courageous” political stand against AUKUS. The prime minister could have told the nation this was America’s decision and, regretfully, Australia would have to move on from a flawed Morrison government initiative.

We may now have come too far to go back. Governments that invest significant political and financial capital in a major project are typically reluctant to admit a mistake, though it can happen. The last budget saw the cancellation of Inland Rail, which was expected to balloon to $45 billion. And, of course, Australia cancelled the French Attack-class project in 2021 to embark on AUKUS. But Australia had invested a mere $4 billion in the Attack-class before it was terminated; the sum for AUKUS is already more than twice that figure.

You might identify this as a textbook example of the sunk cost fallacy, a cognitive bias that sees people continue to pursue a project simply because they have already invested time, money and effort into it, even though it would be in their interest to stop. It’s not yet clear enough that AUKUS is failing for the government to think in these terms. AUKUS is inordinately risky, but we are still in the foothills of a project that will take 30 years or more, and it can’t be said that project is presently in crisis.

Another argument is that Australia has spent so long dithering over submarines that if we back out of AUKUS now, it will be too late to find submarines elsewhere before the Collins boats are retired. Australia, it is argued, cannot afford a submarine gap.

This elevates submarines to a status they don’t deserve. It is only mildly reductionist to say that a submarine is merely a transportation device, a way to move weapons (torpedoes and missiles) and the sensors that support them (sonars, infrared cameras and more) closer to their targets.

There are other ways to do that. If the mission is to sink enemy ships, you can use aircraft, surface ships and even missile-armed trucks. If the mission is to hit a target on the enemy’s territory, you can use bombers or long-range missiles. Granted, submarines can do things that these other platforms cannot and Australia is better off with submarines than without them – but not at any cost. If we must have a submarine gap, then we can compensate with other capabilities.

The government also has the alliance to consider. It is one thing to upset the French, but the Americans present altogether higher stakes. The entire AUKUS initiative has deep roots in Australia’s traditional fear of great-power abandonment. But we overstate the extent to which the purchase of American equipment will compel them to continue defending us and we exaggerate the damage that will be done by backing out. France, Germany and Türkiye caused far more offence to Washington in 2002-03 when they actively worked against the Bush administration’s plans to invade Iraq. All remain members of NATO to this day.

Should the Liberal Party’s doubts grow stronger, though, it will create “permission” for the government to move in the same direction. The whole reason the Labor government finds itself in this position is that when AUKUS was announced, less than a year before the 2022 federal election, the then opposition spotted a political trap – an unpopular Morrison government was baiting the Labor Party to oppose the initiative so the Liberals could revive their electoral fortunes by engineering a “khaki election”. Labor refused to take the bait, endorsing AUKUS immediately. If doubts on the Liberal side grow stronger and they even begin to see AUKUS as a stick with which to beat the government, the Labor Party’s incentives will change.

This is a slow drip, however. For a circuit breaker, a force that could disrupt AUKUS in a matter of days rather than months or years, it can only be US President Trump. The government recognised Trump’s unpopularity in Australia from the beginning and benefited from it electorally in 2025 when the Dutton opposition flirted with MAGA-ism and paid the price. The 2025 Lowy Institute Poll showed a 20-point drop in Australians’ trust in the US to act responsibly in the world.

We see this anxiety reflected also in Marles’s recent speech to the Lowy Institute, in which he implicitly distanced his government from Trump by arguing that Labor has always been the party committed to Australian independence. Quite how that squares with the embrace of AUKUS and the agreement to station US forces in Western Australia and the Northern Territory was not explained.

Australia has escaped lightly in its dealings with Trump so far. Indeed, last October’s Trump–Albanese White House meeting was a political triumph for the government. But so mercurial is this US administration that the relationship could change in an instant. Canada is the cautionary tale here and it is notable that Prime Minister Mark Carney has responded to Trump’s provocations by insisting that Canada should become less dependent on American weapons “so we are never hostage to the decisions of others when it comes to our security”.

In truth, that’s not a realistic ambition for Canada, which is bound to the US by geography. Australia faces no such physical constraints – only the psychological one of refusing to believe we can face a difficult regional security environment on our own.

AUKUS is inordinately risky, but we are still in the foothills of a project that will take 30 years or more, and it can’t be said that project is presently in crisis.

Another argument is that Australia has spent so long dithering over submarines that if we back out of AUKUS now, it will be too late to find submarines elsewhere before the Collins boats are retired. Australia, it is argued, cannot afford a submarine gap.

This elevates submarines to a status they don’t deserve. It is only mildly reductionist to say that a submarine is merely a transportation device, a way to move weapons (torpedoes and missiles) and the sensors that support them (sonars, infrared cameras and more) closer to their targets.

There are other ways to do that. If the mission is to sink enemy ships, you can use aircraft, surface ships and even missile-armed trucks. If the mission is to hit a target on the enemy’s territory, you can use bombers or long-range missiles. Granted, submarines can do things that these other platforms cannot and Australia is better off with submarines than without them – but not at any cost. If we must have a submarine gap, then we can compensate with other capabilities.

The government also has the alliance to consider. It is one thing to upset the French, but the Americans present altogether higher stakes. The entire AUKUS initiative has deep roots in Australia’s traditional fear of great-power abandonment. But we overstate the extent to which the purchase of American equipment will compel them to continue defending us and we exaggerate the damage that will be done by backing out. France, Germany and Türkiye caused far more offence to Washington in 2002-03 when they actively worked against the Bush administration’s plans to invade Iraq. All remain members of NATO to this day.

Should the Liberal Party’s doubts grow stronger, though, it will create “permission” for the government to move in the same direction. The whole reason the Labor government finds itself in this position is that when AUKUS was announced, less than a year before the 2022 federal election, the then opposition spotted a political trap – an unpopular Morrison government was baiting the Labor Party to oppose the initiative so the Liberals could revive their electoral fortunes by engineering a “khaki election”. Labor refused to take the bait, endorsing AUKUS immediately. If doubts on the Liberal side grow stronger and they even begin to see AUKUS as a stick with which to beat the government, the Labor Party’s incentives will change.

This is a slow drip, however. For a circuit breaker, a force that could disrupt AUKUS in a matter of days rather than months or years, it can only be US President Trump. The government recognised Trump’s unpopularity in Australia from the beginning and benefited from it electorally in 2025 when the Dutton opposition flirted with MAGA-ism and paid the price. The 2025 Lowy Institute Poll showed a 20-point drop in Australians’ trust in the US to act responsibly in the world.

We see this anxiety reflected also in Marles’s recent speech to the Lowy Institute, in which he implicitly distanced his government from Trump by arguing that Labor has always been the party committed to Australian independence. Quite how that squares with the embrace of AUKUS and the agreement to station US forces in Western Australia and the Northern Territory was not explained.

Australia has escaped lightly in its dealings with Trump so far. Indeed, last October’s Trump–Albanese White House meeting was a political triumph for the government. But so mercurial is this US administration that the relationship could change in an instant. Canada is the cautionary tale here and it is notable that Prime Minister Mark Carney has responded to Trump’s provocations by insisting that Canada should become less dependent on American weapons “so we are never hostage to the decisions of others when it comes to our security”.

In truth, that’s not a realistic ambition for Canada, which is bound to the US by geography. Australia faces no such physical constraints – only the psychological one of refusing to believe we can face a difficult regional security environment on our own.
