The likelihood of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese resigning next year would have to be very high if Labor continues to go backward in the polls federally, which they have been doing over the last few months.

Given that the chance of Albanese resigning in 2027 is a real possibility, it’s worth looking at what ramifications it might have for the federal government and the Labor Party.

A recommendation popped up on YouTube today about a Sky News video titled “Albanese tipped to resign as PM next year.”

I rate Murdoch’s Sky News very lowly, but it was worth watching given that Labor leaders in Victoria and Queensland seem to be on the way out because of bad polling, either by resignation or being forced out by state Labor Party MPs. And the same could happen to Albanese.

Roy Morgan polling reported on Tuesday (9/6/26) in an article titled “One Nation surges into first place for primary support – but the ALP is still favoured to win a two-party preferred majority” :

In the last week One Nation primary support increased 2.5% to 29.5% and is now clearly ahead of the ALP, down 1% to 26% and the L-NP Coalition, down 2.5% to 17.5% – Liberals on 14.5% (down 3%) and Nationals 3% (up 0.5%). Support for the Greens was up 2% to 15.5%, and Independents/ Other Parties down 1% to 11.5% according to the Roy Morgan survey conducted from June 1-7, 2026, with a representative Australia-wide cross-section of 1,631 electors.

This is the first time in a Roy Morgan Federal Poll that One Nation has been ahead of both the ALP (by 3.5% points) and the L-NP Coalition (by 12% points).

Since the Federal Budget was delivered by Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Tuesday May 12, 2026, primary support for One Nation is up 5% points to 29.5%, ALP support is down 3.5% points to 26%, L-NP Coalition support is down 6.5% points to 17.5%, and Greens support is up 4% points to 15.5%.

In effect, since the Federal Budget, One Nation has gained support at the expense of the L-NP Coalition, and the Greens have gained support at the expense of the ALP. (Click here to read more)

If the Labor Party stays at 26% of the primary vote, they will be in big trouble come the May 2028 federal election, although the Roy Morgan article says the “ALP is still favoured to win a two-party preferred majority.”

A poll saying “still favoured to win” is not a great position for Labor given they are on 94 seats in the lower house.

But what happens if the federal Labor Party drops to 25% like they have in the Queensland state Labor Party or 23% of the primary vote like they have in the Victorian state Labor Party?

At the May 2025 federal election, the Liberal Party / National Party coalition received 31.82% of the primary vote and is now down to 17.5% in the above Roy Morgan poll.

Labor received 34.56% at the May 2025 federal election and is currently on 26% of the primary vote in the above poll.

But the Liberal Party / National Party coalition have been going down in the polls for almost the entire 12 months since the 2025 federal election and would have to be close to rock bottom at 17.5% of the primary vote.

If Labor ends up with the same drop as the coalition, they will end up at 20%, and if that happens, the backbenchers will start maneuvering to get rid of Albanese.

With Labor currently on 26% of the primary vote in the polls, it would be a huge worry for the federal Labor Party, which they haven’t felt before.

If the Labor Party were to stay at the current 26% of the primary vote, will Albanese stick around? And if they drop to 20%, will Albanese be forced out?

If Labor is low in the polls next year, 12 months out from the May 2028 federal election, it will be very tempting for federal MPs to get rid of Albanese and load him with all the blame for unpopular and/or failed policies like the NACC and AUKUS etc.

One thing in the above polls we haven’t seen before is The Greens have risen to 15.5% of the primary vote, which is possibly the highest they have ever been.

Imagine if The Greens got close to One Nation in the polls, wouldn’t that be a wild time in politics.

As Australia’s political system moves away from the Duopoly / UniParty of the Labor Party / Liberal and National Party coalition, the polls and political landscape will change rapidly, but it needs to be done, as the Duopoly / UniParty can’t be trusted, does not have the answers and is taking Australia backwards.

As for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, he could end with the same fate as coalition leader Angus Taylor and be gone by the end of the year or early next year.

The likely candidates to replace Albanese, while stronger than the coalition candidates to replace Taylor, are not as strong as they have been in the past, and no one is really a huge standout.

Four people have been charged and police have seized multiple flares as the Socceroos end their world cup bid in a heartbreaking penalty shootout.

In a statement, Victoria Police said the arrests were made across two live sites as tens of thousands of fans braved a cold winter morning to cheer on the Socceroos in what would prove to be their final game in the 2026 World Cup.

Around 7500 people gathered at Federation Square, where 11 flares and one smoke emitter were activated during the match.

Six of those flares were lit and thrown immediately after Australia equalised at one-all as fans celebrated an own goal by Egyptian defender Mohammed Hany.

During the incident Victoria Police say one man was arrested for possessing a distress signal and discharging a missile, while three others were arrested for flare possession.

A teenager was also arrested for possessing a flare, but was released pending further inquiries.

In Victoria it is an offence to carry or ignite a flare under the Dangerous Goods (explosives) Act.

In a separate gathering around 6000 fans attended a live site in AAMI park where police say two people were found with weapons by security at the entrance to the venue. They were both issued penalty notices.

Two others were directed to leave the venue after entering the pitch.

All four were released and are expected to be charged on summons.

Despite the arrests, police said they were generally pleased with crowd behaviour and shared their sympathy with the crowd following a disappointing penalty shootout.

The Socceroos World Cup bowed out of the 2206 FIFA World Cup in a dramatic penalty shootout, after extra time was unable to split Australia and Egypt.

Socceroos star Jackson Irvine summed up the mood of many fans as he reflected on the teams cruel exit from the 2026 World Cup.

“We took it all the way to the very end,” he said on SBS.

“Penalties, it’s a cruel way to lose, but anybody who’s got the confidence to step up and take that ball after 120 minutes, however long you’ve played, it takes a big heart.”

‘Week off’ joke

A week off for Australians is off the agenda after the Socceroos’ devastating loss to Egypt in the FIFA World Cup early on Saturday morning.

Anthony Albanese had teased Australians could be granted a week off if we won the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

But that came to an end with a brutal penalty shootout in Dallas on Saturday morning, after the Socceroos and Egypt ended extra time 1-1.

“Heartbreaking way to exit the World Cup after a great tournament – all Australians are proud of our @Socceroos,” the Prime Minister posted on X shortly after pre-dawn loss.

On Friday, after delivering the keynote address at the Airport City Summit, Mr Albanese had playfully joked about giving the country a week off if the Socceroos won the World Cup.

“The truth is that public holidays are completely determined by state governments,” he said.

“But I reckon if we win then we might give everyone a week.”

Thousands of Aussies showed up at live sites and bars and pubs around the country for the knockout round game, which started at 4am AEST.

Millions more were expected to watch from home.

Some betting companies had the Socceroos at a 300-1 chance of winning the World Cup, according to UK based company Squawka.

The event, hosted by the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, explored how the new Western Sydney Airport will support new infrastructure and investment opportunities.

The Prime Minister used his keynote to promote the Socceroos, saying they represent the vision of a multicultural Australia.

“We’re a multicultural nation. It’s who we are, and you know what? We should celebrate. The Socceroos show that, and the pride,” he said.

“We should be proud of it, and we should celebrate it, just as we’ll celebrate every Socceroo, whether their name is Irankunda or Irvine, they’re all just proud to be representing our country, but they’re also proud of who they are.”

TIRANA, Albania (AP) — Police in Albania blocked protesters from reaching parliament on Tuesday as the latest rally against a luxury development linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner turned violent

The march was staged as parliament resumed from a summer recess and after the demonstrations marked their 100th day on Monday. They challenged a police cordon in the center of the capital, Tirana, pelting officers in riot gear with eggs and tomatoes.

Cars transporting lawmakers to the parliament building were confronted by the crowds and were hit with plastic water bottles before police intervened to let them through.

Dubbed the ‘flamingo revolution’ for protesters’ signs depicting the pink bird that could be harmed by the coastal development, the anti-government protests have rocked Albania.

Although Albanian officials have avoided giving details of Kushner’s role in the project, Trump’s daughter, Ivanka, has spoken about her family’s involvement in the venture, describing it as an “incredible project.”

The protests are aimed at stopping the massive project that critics say would cause environmental damage and limit public access to the coast.

The nightly Tirana protests initially only focused on the development but have since grown into a major challenge to the country’s long-ruling Socialist government.

Prime Minister Edi Rama — a target of the demonstrations — strongly supports the investment project, arguing that it would help modernize a country that spent decades in Communist isolation.

“We are here because we want change. Young people are struggling. Life is getting harder, and the government is not listening. We believe Albania can do better,” protester Elidon Mehmetaj said.

“We are not asking for much. We are asking for a better future — for Albanian citizens, for our country, for our future,” he said.

Demonstrators chanted “Arrest Rama!” during the clashes, as police escorted lawmakers to and from the parliament building.

Several protesters were detained, but it was not immediately clear whether any arrests had been made.

Elections Alberta says it has verified that a citizen initiative petition looking to force a vote on the province separating from Canada was able to surpass the number of signatures it required.

But the future of the petition remains on hold, Elections Alberta said in a news release issued Friday afternoon.

The verification process was conducted between July 6 and July 23, and has now been completed, the non-partisan office said.

Gordon McClure, the province's chief electoral officer, determined that while requirements have been met, any further steps in the citizen initiative process are stayed pending direction from the Court of Appeal of Alberta.

Stay Free Alberta, the group behind the petition, previously said almost 302,000 signatures had been collected, far more than the nearly 178,000 needed under provincial legislation.

Elections Alberta said the total number of valid signatures counted was 279,337, and using random statistical sampling, the office said it found 222,597 verified signatures.

Elections Alberta verifies pro-separation petition signatures

Elections Alberta said the most frequent reasons signatures were rejected during the validation phase included incomplete addresses, electors not completing their declarations that they were eligible electors, canvassers signing their witness declarations before electors signed the petition, and electors providing a mailing address instead of the required physical residential address.

Jeff Rath, a lawyer for the group behind the petition, told The Canadian Press he was pleased to hear how many signatures had been verified.

"We knew from the outset that we had to be too big to rig," he said.

The petition was submitted in early May, but just two weeks later, a Court of King's Bench ruling quashed it. The judge ruled McClure made an error in law to approve the second citizen initiative petition and failed to consider an earlier court decision that said separation would violate Indigenous people's treaty rights. Both the Alberta government and Stay Free Alberta have appealed the judge’s ruling.

But last month, Stay Free Alberta earned a partial win in court when another judge ruled the signature verification process could take place while the original ruling is appealed. In that decision, the judge stopped short of allowing those results to be reported to the justice minister and then referred to the lieutenant governor, which could trigger a constitutional referendum.

Premier Danielle Smith has called a referendum for Oct. 19, when Albertans will be asked a number of questions, including if they want to remain in Canada or start the process of having a second, binding vote on separation.

Rath said he believes the numbers released by Elections Alberta should apply more pressure on the Alberta government to put Stay Free Alberta's binding question on the October ballot instead of the current wording to vote for another referendum.

Stay Free Alberta's petition's question is: "Do you agree that the province of Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada to become an independent state?"

Rath said Smith promised that if Stay Free Alberta obtained enough signatures, the group's question would be on the ballot.

"If she doesn't put our question on the ballot, she will have proven herself to be a liar and she has to resign."

A spokesperson for Justice Minister Mickey Amery told The Canadian Press that his government appreciated the confirmation that hundreds of thousands signed petitions regarding the issue of independence.

"That's why our government will continue with the current referendum question," the spokesperson said.

Lori Williams, associate professor of policy studies at Mount Royal University, called the verification an "empiric victory" for the Stay Free Alberta initiative.

While the group can use the verification to call attention to its cause, she said it's unlikely that it would harken any legislative change.

"Their question is not going to be on the [referendum] ballot, and that of course is going to cause continued divisions and criticisms across the board," Williams told CBC News in an interview.

Smith has said interest in the Stay Free Alberta and pro-Confederation Forever Canadian petitions was a factor in her decision to add a question about Alberta's place in Canada to October's referendum ballot.

"The reality still is that the questions that are on the ballot are not the ones that the folks who signed the ... Stay Free Alberta [petition] want or what the Forever Canadian signatories want," Williams said.

"In other words, we've got hundreds of thousands of people in Alberta who don't like or want the question that is on the referendum ballot currently set for October."

Following an unrelated alleged breach of voter data in late April, McClure ordered the verification process for citizen initiative petitions to include an additional step that involves looking for what he calls seeded names.

Elections Alberta said it believes the voter data, which was allegedly leaked by a third-party advertiser, came from an official voter list legitimately obtained by the pro-independence Republican Party of Alberta. The office said each such list is seeded with multiple fictitious names to make the documents easier to trace in the event of a breach, but how the list managed to change hands remains unclear.

In its news release about the Stay Free Alberta petition on Friday, Elections Alberta said it “screened the petition and has confirmed that none of the signatures submitted came from the seeded names on the Republican Party of Alberta’s list of electors.”

The Republican Party of Alberta has told CBC News it is co-operating with Elections Alberta’s investigation into the breach.

In 1913, Antonino Alati left southern Italy to find a better life in a land where many people regarded him as little better than scum.

I’m the beneficiary of birthright citizenship three times over.

Alati wouldn’t let bigotry win. He soon sent for his wife and children, including his infant son Salvatore. Alati turned to Alito, Salvatore became Samuel. A generation later, the family had a Supreme Court justice in Samuel A. Alito Jr. — the second Italian American, after Antonin Scalia, to sit on the highest court in the land.

During his 2005 confirmation hearings, Alito praised his father as an “extraordinary man who came to the United States as a young child and overcame many difficulties” to ensure a better life for him and his sister. By then, Italian Americans were established as an essential part of this country’s fabric, from music to politics to food.

The justice blasts birth tourism, where women from China and other countries travel to the U.S. to have a baby, then return home, benefiting from our generosity and offering nothing in return.

A major power outage hit Almaty and parts of the surrounding region on Friday afternoon after high-voltage transmission lines shut down, triggering automatic protection systems across the electricity network.

The blackout affected Kazakhstan’s largest city, home to about 2.37 million people, and came amid reports of power cuts at around the same time in neighboring Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. According to Alatau Zharyq Company, the disruption began at 2:38 p.m. on August 14 when three 500 kV overhead transmission lines owned by national grid operator KEGOC shut down unexpectedly.

The company identified the lines as L-5400, L-5300, and L-5320. Their shutdown activated special load-shedding and automatic frequency protection systems in Alatau Zharyq’s network, which the company said “led to the disconnection of electricity consumers in the city of Almaty and the Almaty Region.”

The three lines form part of Kazakhstan’s North-South electricity transit system. There was no initial explanation from the company or KEGOC of what caused the three transmission lines to trip.

Residents reported outages in communities across Almaty Region. Electricity failures were accompanied in some areas by disruption to internet and mobile services.

TCA reporters on the ground confirmed outages across large parts of Bishkek. There was no immediate confirmation that the outages in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan had the same root cause.

KEGOC later said preliminary operational data indicated that the disruption was caused by a power surge from the Unified Power System of Central Asia. The company said the disturbance caused southern Kazakhstan and the interconnected Central Asian power system to separate into isolated operation. The underlying cause of the initial surge had not yet been established.

The timing caused an additional complication in Almaty, where one of the city’s largest entertainment events of the year is scheduled for Friday evening. Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, is due to perform at Almaty’s Central Stadium on August 14 as part of his 2026 world tour.

The blackout quickly produced a wave of jokes on social media. One image circulating widely depicted the rapper dressed as an electrician beside a fuse box, with “Yeezy Electrical” on his overalls. Other users joked that the city’s electricity had been diverted to prepare for the concert.

The blackout also struck during a period of intensely hot summer weather, increasing the potential disruption for households and businesses reliant on air conditioning.

This marks the second year in a row the Badger State came out on top in the rankings. Fancy a thorium microreactor capable of delivering up to 30 MWe of juice for up to 30 years?

US startup Ampera has produced what it claims is the first 3D-printed nuclear reactor module. The firm says it is working towards delivering scalable, emission-free power for datacenters, defense applications, and off-grid sites.

Ampera unveiled its first nuclear reactor module during an event at the firm's innovation center in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. More than 100 people attended, including local officials, business leaders and employees.

Founder and CEO Brian Matthews revealed the prototype microreactor, which features a fully 3D-printed silicon carbide reactor core and pressure vessel.

"This next-generation nuclear core and pressure vessel sets the foundation for factory-built, mass-produced nuclear energy," Matthews said. "The advanced technology and additive manufacturing used demonstrate a clear commercial path for new nuclear technology coming to market in an accelerated manner."

His company is developing a subcritical, solid-state, factory-built thorium-based nuclear reactor. Subcritical means the fuel cannot sustain a nuclear chain reaction on its own, which prevents a runaway power excursion.

Ampera uses "solid-state" to describe a design with solid rather than liquid fuel. The proposed fuel uses tristructural isotropic, or TRISO, particles, consisting of a fuel kernel containing thorium, surrounded by multiple ceramic and carbon layers.

Thorium-232 is not fissile. After absorbing a neutron, it ultimately decays through thorium-233 and protactinium-233 into fissile uranium-233. This requires a separate source of neutrons, and Ampera says its design features a proprietary neutron driver to provide a stable external neutron source to start and sustain operation.

In June, Ampera announced it had established an Australian subsidiary to secure thorium supplies, and said it plans to produce the fuel kernels itself.

"Thorium is the future for ultra-safe, clean power production," Matthews said at the time. "By producing TRISO thorium kernels in the United States, we can ensure ample access to the needed fuel supply as we scale up and also minimize price volatility risk."

Ampera also describes the heart of the reactor as as a spherical monolithic gyroid core. A gyroid, as far as we can fathom, is a complex shape that provides a massive surface area relative to its volume, making it well-suited for heat transfer. Its complexity makes it difficult to produce using conventional manufacturing methods, which is where additive manufacturing comes in.

The core is 3D-printed using silicon carbide and designed to operate for up to 30 years without refueling, the firm claims.

Ampera says its planned systems will provide 15 or 30 MWe, depending on the configuration, enough to supply a typical datacenter. Larger configurations are planned.

Matthews said that his company expects to be the first to industrialize factory-built nuclear power with near-term deployment timelines. When The Register asked about availability, their spokesperson said: "We expect the power generation portion of the system to be available as early as 2027, with the nuclear module being available to customers about 2030 based on regulatory approval."

We also asked how neutrons are generated for startup and operation of the reactor module by the Neutron Driver, but Ampera is keeping this under its hat for now.

As well as datacenters, defense customers will be likely takers if Ampera can produce reliable working reactors. Earlier this year, the US Department of the Air Force (DAF) announced it was looking into microreactors for three of its sites, part of a program aimed at improving energy resilience during grid outages. ®

Defense tech company Anduril is said to be raising a new round of capital that may push its valuation up by a whopping $40 billion to about $100 billion, Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.

The company, which raised $5 billion in May at a $61 billion valuation — itself roughly double the $30.5 billion valuation it landed in its June 2025 Series G round — may be structuring the fundraise as a two-stage process, with the second stage bringing in investors at a higher valuation. Both tranches could be closed within the year, Reuters reported.

The news comes as the defense tech industry experiences an unprecedented revival, spurred by demand for drones, autonomous craft, and AI’s role in warfare, as war rages both in the Middle East and Eastern Europe. In the first six months of the year, the sector saw venture funding more than double to over $12 billion, eclipsing the nearly $10 billion that startups in the space raised in all of 2025.

Anduril has benefited from this demand, signing contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense, Air Force, and Army; the Dutch Ministry of Defence; NATO; the U.K. Ministry of Defence; Poland; and more.

The company said in May that it had more than doubled its revenue to $2.2 billion in 2025 compared to a year earlier.

Other startups have cashed in, too: Military aircraft maker Shield AI in March raised $1.5 billion, Mach Industries quadrupled its valuation to $1.8 billion last month, and Europe’s Helsing this month raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation.

A common thread across these deals is a shift toward cheaper, more expendable hardware, often called “attritable” systems, rather than the expensive-to-replace equipment that’s defined defense contracting for decades. Mach CEO Ethan Thornton has said the startup is designing systems for the current era of warfare at significantly lower cost than traditional defense contractors, citing Ukraine’s use of autonomous drones as a model.

Separately, both Mach and Anduril have also moved to secure their own propulsion supply. Mach acquired solid rocket motor maker Exquadrum for $50 million in May, while the Pentagon has funded Anduril’s efforts to expand domestic solid rocket motor manufacturing capacity — moves aimed at a supply bottleneck that predates and cuts across the low-cost-weapons trend.

Anduril’s investors include Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, ICONIQ, Flux Capital, Greycroft, Altimeter, 1789 Capital, and current U.S. Vice President JD Vance, according to PitchBook.

“No decisions have been made about any future financing, and anyone claiming knowledge of its terms, structure, pricing, or timing is speculating or misinformed. As a private company, we regularly evaluate opportunities to fund the growth of the business,” Anduril said in an emailed statement.

Abby Vesoulis9 hours ago

Max Miller, left, and his Democratic challenger, Brian PoindexterMother Jones; Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call/ZUMA; Jeff Swensen/Getty

Max Miller, left, and his Democratic challenger, Brian PoindexterMother Jones; Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call/ZUMA; Jeff Swensen/Getty

Sipping on an iced caramel latte with whipped cream and talking about “squadding up” with his daughters on Fortnite, Brian Poindexter doesn’t necessarily fit the stereotype of a “manly man,” which is how another magazine characterized the congressional candidate in mid-July.

For what it’s worth, it’s his political opponent, Republican Rep. Max Miller, who recently testified about taking testosterone and frequenting half-a-dozen different gyms. Whatever muscles Poindexter has, he confirms, are the result of 19 years spent placing rebar and erecting the steel skeletons of buildings, and before that, working as a cross-country mover for people with too much Ethan Allen furniture.

“I figured out what armoire is French for,” he told me at a coffee shop in late August. “Heavy as heck.”

With a hearty catalogue of dad jokes, Poindexter is running for a seat representing northeastern Ohio as an inversion of Miller, an heir to a real estate fortune whose campaign has been overshadowed by serious domestic disputes in his personal life. So despite being divorced himself, Poindexter is positioning himself as a family man who has paid his dues helping his blue-collar community of Brook Park as a city council member for the past nine years.

He begins our interview by telling me about his kids: His oldest daughter is 25. She works in accounting, and is—he’s excited to share—newly engaged. He has another daughter who is 19, a college sophomore studying nursing. (By the way, did I know the Trump administration tried to remove nursing from the professional degree list? “Kind of upsetting. Nurses are very much professionals,” he said.) Poindexter’s long-term partner (he got divorced in 2022) also has a high-schooler whom Poindexter calls his “bonus daughter.”

“Everyone knows me as a father of two daughters, but I want to make sure I include her because she’s a good kid and I’m proud of her too,” said Poindexter.

I haven’t met them, but I’ve seen them star in an advertisement for their dad. They call him “dorky,” make fun of his dance moves, and thank him for being a present community member and parent. “He always shows up… For family dinner. For games. For help with homework—even when he’s not helpful,” the three girls say, laughing.

Poindexter is running as an inversion of Miller, an heir to a real estate fortune whose campaign has been overshadowed by serious domestic disputes in his personal life.

It is an unsubtle rebuke of Miller, whose ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of throwing boiling water at her, holding a gun against her head, and shoving her against a wall. According to court filings Mother Jones reported on extensively in July, some of these alleged incidents occurred in front of their child. The documents also showed that Moreno was worried that Miller could have caused their two-year-old’s broken collarbone. She told police their daughter was in Miller’s custody when the injury happened. Child abuse investigators said the bruising near the injury resembled a “handprint,” making the injury “suspicious.” Miller had previously been accused of slapping a girlfriend, and pushing a girl down the stairs while in high school. Accusations that would give many parents pause.

Miller has repeatedly denied having ever been violent towards women or his child, and the investigation into possible child abuse was ultimately “unsubstantiated.” But for a moment, over the summer, the series of allegations seemed like they might force him out of the race. His former father-in-law and fellow Ohio Republican, Sen. Bernie Moreno, said Miller “should not serve in the House of Representatives” and that he needed “serious psychological help.”

As evidence of Miller’s alleged depravity, Sen. Moreno accused Miller of withholding a stuffed animal from a toddler. “My granddaughter, she has a little blue bunny that she sleeps with. Max would not hand over the little blue bunny. Literally held it hostage for 48 hours,” Moreno told reporters. “This girl is crying at night because she can’t sleep without her little blue bunny. And his answer is, ‘I’m just not going to give it to you.’” (Miller called Moreno’s characterization “lies,” but Mother Jones obtained texts showing there were multiple incidents in which Miller withheld the stuffed animal.)

When Miller declined to drop out in time for another Republican to replace him on the ballot, Cook Political Report shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “toss-up” in a region that Trump and Miller both won handily in 2024. The odds were suddenly looking much better for Poindexter, who had launched his long-shot campaign out of the garage of his buddy-turned-campaign-manager. Though far from an indication of how people in the district tend to vote, Polymarket shows 89 percent of wagerers think Poindexter will win. A poll from early August showed Poindexter ahead of Miller by 8 points. David Niven, a political science professor at the University of Cincinnati, called the race a “tremendous lesson in the importance of candidate quality.”

“Republicans should be strong, and they have the most loathed incumbent in probably Ohio congressional history running on the Republican banner,” Niven said.

But back in late August, Poindexter was increasingly worried that the Miller controversy could wind up hurting him. What was once a low-profile race between a small town’s city council member and a well-resourced incumbent was now a frequent topic on CNN. The extra attention invited powerful Republicans to come to Miller’s defense—and eventually, dredge up things from Poindexter’s past.

The White House pleaded for House Republicans not to wage a “public pressure campaign” against Miller. President Donald Trump, whom Miller worked for as a campaign and White House aide, called Miller a “good guy.” House Speaker Mike Johnson demurred when asked if he thought the allegations of physical abuse were disqualifying. “People have domestic disputes. It’s part of being flawed humans, as we are,” the Louisiana Republican told Politico.

“I hope he wins reelection. He’s done a good job as a member of Congress,” said Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

Of course, people outside the district weighed in to support Poindexter too. When we spoke, I brought up a new advertisement by the anti-Trump Lincoln Project. The one-minute spot featured an ominous voice flipping through screengrab after screengrab of court documents and headlines that detailed the serious allegations Miller faces, concluding that he’s a “domestic abuser” who “belongs in jail.”

I had sort of expected Poindexter to be pleased by their marketing work; a group founded by Republicans who rebuked Trump was spending $20,000 to batter his Republican opponent. The video cost Poindexter and his campaign $0. Since he didn’t make the advertisement, he didn’t even have to worry about a potential defamation lawsuit from his highly litigious opponent. But Poindexter seemed dejected.

“I did see the ad and I’m not a fan,” the 47-year-old Democrat told me. “What I don’t want to happen is make this a bigger fight. Then they start dumping resources into it.”

By “they,” Poindexter meant moneyed interests. And he was right. The Congressional Leadership Fund and National Republican Congressional Committee quickly got involved, dumping more than $5 million into the district in the final months of the contest.

Those millions were largely spent on media buys painting Poindexter as the dangerous one. At least two ads focused on a police report from the 1990s, which alleged Poindexter tried to “swallow a rock of suspected crack cocaine during a police stop.” One of the ads characterized that incident as part of a “30-year rap sheet for drugs and violence” with charges as recent as this year. Another said Poindexter “wants to go from crack to Congress.” (Poindexter’s campaign notes that he has taken random drug tests for the last 20 years as a union ironworker and never failed one.)

The “crack” allegation stems from a 1998 police report in which Poindexter, then 18, was accused by cops of swallowing what they suspected to be crack cocaine. The officer specified in the police report that past drug-related complaints in the area made them give “special attention” to the block. That’s when they saw Poindexter in his car. They went up to his window, at which point, he allegedly tried to swallow something.

“I tried to recover the objects and the [adult male] struggled to prevent me. We fell to the ground at which time I recovered the above rock of susp. Crack cocaine from the ground near his mouth,” the report says. Though Poindexter was arrested and taken into custody, he wasn’t ultimately charged with a crime. That’s because, he says, “I absolutely did not do that.”

“I did see the ad and I’m not a fan. What I don’t want to happen is make this a bigger fight. Then they start dumping resources into it.”

Former Brook Park mayor Mike Gammella, who worked with Poindexter on the city council, began laughing when I asked him about the police report’s characterization.

“Brian grew up hard. Brian didn’t grow up with a silver spoon in his mouth,” said Gammella, who was elected as an independent the same year Poindexter joined the council. “They mentioned he was in a crack-infested neighborhood. Well, guess what? That’s the neighborhood he grew up in.”

Mother Jones reviewed Poindexter’s legal records dating back three decades. Poindexter faced charges for other violations in the  ’90s and early 2000s: In 1999, when he was 20, he received a citation for carrying an open container in Pinellas County, Florida. In 2000, at age 21, Poindexter received two citations for possession of marijuana (under 100 grams). He pleaded guilty to alcohol-related disorderly conduct in 2002. Although Cuyahoga County has since destroyed the physical files under standard retention rules, archival remnants indicate he spent a brief time in custody. A year later, a 24-year-old Poindexter was charged with “aggravated disorderly conduct.” He was found guilty of a lesser misdemeanor and paid a $250 fine. In 2013, Poindexter was removed from a Major League Baseball game after allegedly slapping a stranger. That man told the Washington Free Beacon that the slap was over a comment the man made about Poindexter’s apparent ability to eat a hot dog in one bite. Poindexter was not convicted; the man he was accused of slapping declined to press charges.

Poindexter’s next brush with the law came a decade later, in 2023, when he pleaded guilty to a charge of setting off fireworks illegally over Fourth of July weekend. Ironically, as a member of the Brook Park City Council, he had previously voted against allowing fireworks in city limits. This year, Poindexter received two traffic violations for failing to leave enough distance from the car in front of him and texting while driving—a first-time offense.

Poindexter chalks many of these indiscretions up to being “young and dumb,” which is how Miller also characterized a series of incidents in his youth: punching a guy in the back of the head and running from the cops (2007), breaking a window at an apartment building (2008), crashing his car into a light pole (2011) with ecstasy and Klonopin in his system. In another, previously unreported police report that I obtained, Miller was said to have been caught smoking weed and then running from the cops while at University of Arizona’s freshman orientation in 2007.

Miller never responded to Mother Jones’ questions about these events. He previously told the Washington Post that, “growing up, everyone makes mistakes.”

For his part, Poindexter eventually fired back at the negative ads with his own aggressive blitz in September and October. One 30-second clip features an Ohio Sheriff saying she would not support Miller because of the serious allegations he faces. “Thirty-four years in law enforcement tells me Max Miller does not belong in power,” Summit County Sheriff Kandy Fatheree said. A later ad from Poindexter’s campaign focused entirely on the blue bunny saga, quoting Sen. Moreno, who called the debacle “the seventh layer of hell.”

But when I followed Poindexter on the trail, he didn’t want to go there. Emulating Sen. Bernie Sanders, who endorsed Poindexter in March, the candidate was focused on the cost of living, which is also what 64 percent of Ohio voters ranked as a top-two issue in a recent poll. It was the only thing he covered in his stump speech.

“Does anybody in here feel like the economy is doing great? How about gas prices?” he asked the 30 to 40 people sitting in a bonus room of the Bedford Branch public library. “How about the grocery store? You guys feel comfortable going to the grocery? I mean, I don’t know about you all, but I have experience putting things back on the shelves.”

Poindexter is doing better than many in his district. His union job as an ironworker and side gig as a Brook Park city councilman are stable—netting him $110,350 in 2025, according to his House financial disclosure form—though his attire doesn’t necessarily reflect a six-figure income. The tops of his gray Nikes have holes and the back pocket on his stained and faded blue jeans is permanently imprinted with the outline of his wallet.

As one of six kids raised on the west side of Cleveland by a bolt-maker and a stay-at-home mom, Poindexter says he’s never been accustomed to fancy things. As Poindexter tells it, vacations growing up were spent camping, and clothes were all hand-me-downs.

“We didn’t have everything, but we had the basics in life: You know, a strong family unit, a roof over our head. We knew we were going to eat every day,” he said.

It’s another way he differs from Miller, who is an heir to a real estate empire that sold to an international conglomerate for $11.4 billion in 2018. Miller now lives in the wealthy enclave of Bay Village, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Erie. Its annual per capita income of $69,148 is nearly double that of the industrial suburb near the airport where Poindexter lives, 12 miles southeast.

Poindexter says he’s running for office because the math—even to replicate his modest childhood—just doesn’t add up in his area anymore.

“I don’t know anybody who has six kids right now, and if they do, they’re not doing it on one income,” he said.

Miller has leaned on Sanders’ endorsement of Poindexter to characterize his opponent as a “socialist” who wants “higher taxes and government-run healthcare.” But Poindexter’s populism is less in-your-face. When asked about his views on implementing Medicare for All at an August event, he was non-committal, promising to look at how any proposed legislation on the issue would affect Ohioans first. “I don’t know if I could support that,” he said.

He told me his initial goal was merely to prevent his neighbors from having to turn to crowdfunding for medical emergencies. “We’re in the richest country on the planet, and we got to pay for medical bills through a GoFundMe. I think that’s way out of touch,” he said.

Far from advocating for a sweeping social safety net, Poindexter said his primary objective for his own daughters is for them to “find a career they love, find something that helps provide for them and brings them security.”

When Poindexter’s two biological daughters were growing up, he said that he and his ex-wife didn’t always have that. On top of his full-time job, he said he worked part-time as a bar-back at a Cleveland night club. His ex-wife worked full time as a chef, mostly during evenings and weekends. The two were like ships in the night. And when they did see each other? “We were arguing over, ‘This bill didn’t get paid, this didn’t get done.’ And it really drove us apart as time went on,” he said.

“That’s what ultimately led to our separation,” he said of his 2022 divorce.

At the time, the split caught Gammella, the former town mayor, by surprise. “When he came in and told me he was in a divorce, I was floored, you know, because I liked his ex-wife. They got along great. I never saw him arguing or fighting or anything like that. I thought he was an excellent father to his children,” Gammella said.

I really wanted to check in with her, but she didn’t respond to my messages. However, as was the case with Miller, there were divorce and child custody legal filings I could look through for clues. The public records were concise. The two shared custody of their younger daughter who was 15 at the time. Their other daughter was, by then, an adult. Poindexter would cover the minor’s health insurance and cell phone bill and contribute to her future college education.

Mutually, they agreed to “treat the child as a unique person with respect to feelings and needs” and “provide the child with an emotional environment in which she is free to continue to love each parent and to spend time with each of them.”

I hadn’t received records from the Cuyahoga County clerk when I spoke to Poindexter in August. But the contents resembled something he said during our interview—about what it means to be “manly” in such a machismo world.

“When my daughters come home with a broken heart or a bumped knee, I don’t have to be super macho. It’s okay to pamper your girls and show them that the world isn’t all brass and crass all the time,” he told me. “I don’t know where we went wrong in society, where we think that being a jerk is showing masculinity. It just tells me you’re an asshole, and I think if you look at any real tough guy, they take care of the people that need taken care of.”

Max Miller, left, and his Democratic challenger, Brian PoindexterMother Jones; Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call/ZUMA; Jeff Swensen/Getty

Sipping on an iced caramel latte with whipped cream and talking about “squadding up” with his daughters on Fortnite, Brian Poindexter doesn’t necessarily fit the stereotype of a “manly man,” which is how another magazine characterized the congressional candidate in mid-July.

For what it’s worth, it’s his political opponent, Republican Rep. Max Miller, who recently testified about taking testosterone and frequenting half-a-dozen different gyms. Whatever muscles Poindexter has, he confirms, are the result of 19 years spent placing rebar and erecting the steel skeletons of buildings, and before that, working as a cross-country mover for people with too much Ethan Allen furniture.

“I figured out what armoire is French for,” he told me at a coffee shop in late August. “Heavy as heck.”

With a hearty catalogue of dad jokes, Poindexter is running for a seat representing northeastern Ohio as an inversion of Miller, an heir to a real estate fortune whose campaign has been overshadowed by serious domestic disputes in his personal life. So despite being divorced himself, Poindexter is positioning himself as a family man who has paid his dues helping his blue-collar community of Brook Park as a city council member for the past nine years.

He begins our interview by telling me about his kids: His oldest daughter is 25. She works in accounting, and is—he’s excited to share—newly engaged. He has another daughter who is 19, a college sophomore studying nursing. (By the way, did I know the Trump administration tried to remove nursing from the professional degree list? “Kind of upsetting. Nurses are very much professionals,” he said.) Poindexter’s long-term partner (he got divorced in 2022) also has a high-schooler whom Poindexter calls his “bonus daughter.”

“Everyone knows me as a father of two daughters, but I want to make sure I include her because she’s a good kid and I’m proud of her too,” said Poindexter.

I haven’t met them, but I’ve seen them star in an advertisement for their dad. They call him “dorky,” make fun of his dance moves, and thank him for being a present community member and parent. “He always shows up… For family dinner. For games. For help with homework—even when he’s not helpful,” the three girls say, laughing.

Poindexter is running as an inversion of Miller, an heir to a real estate fortune whose campaign has been overshadowed by serious domestic disputes in his personal life.

It is an unsubtle rebuke of Miller, whose ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of throwing boiling water at her, holding a gun against her head, and shoving her against a wall. According to court filings Mother Jones reported on extensively in July, some of these alleged incidents occurred in front of their child. The documents also showed that Moreno was worried that Miller could have caused their two-year-old’s broken collarbone. She told police their daughter was in Miller’s custody when the injury happened. Child abuse investigators said the bruising near the injury resembled a “handprint,” making the injury “suspicious.” Miller had previously been accused of slapping a girlfriend, and pushing a girl down the stairs while in high school. Accusations that would give many parents pause.

Miller has repeatedly denied having ever been violent towards women or his child, and the investigation into possible child abuse was ultimately “unsubstantiated.” But for a moment, over the summer, the series of allegations seemed like they might force him out of the race. His former father-in-law and fellow Ohio Republican, Sen. Bernie Moreno, said Miller “should not serve in the House of Representatives” and that he needed “serious psychological help.”

As evidence of Miller’s alleged depravity, Sen. Moreno accused Miller of withholding a stuffed animal from a toddler. “My granddaughter, she has a little blue bunny that she sleeps with. Max would not hand over the little blue bunny. Literally held it hostage for 48 hours,” Moreno told reporters. “This girl is crying at night because she can’t sleep without her little blue bunny. And his answer is, ‘I’m just not going to give it to you.’” (Miller called Moreno’s characterization “lies,” but Mother Jones obtained texts showing there were multiple incidents in which Miller withheld the stuffed animal.)

When Miller declined to drop out in time for another Republican to replace him on the ballot, Cook Political Report shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “toss-up” in a region that Trump and Miller both won handily in 2024. The odds were suddenly looking much better for Poindexter, who had launched his long-shot campaign out of the garage of his buddy-turned-campaign-manager. Though far from an indication of how people in the district tend to vote, Polymarket shows 89 percent of wagerers think Poindexter will win. A poll from early August showed Poindexter ahead of Miller by 8 points. David Niven, a political science professor at the University of Cincinnati, called the race a “tremendous lesson in the importance of candidate quality.”

“Republicans should be strong, and they have the most loathed incumbent in probably Ohio congressional history running on the Republican banner,” Niven said.

But back in late August, Poindexter was increasingly worried that the Miller controversy could wind up hurting him. What was once a low-profile race between a small town’s city council member and a well-resourced incumbent was now a frequent topic on CNN. The extra attention invited powerful Republicans to come to Miller’s defense—and eventually, dredge up things from Poindexter’s past.

The White House pleaded for House Republicans not to wage a “public pressure campaign” against Miller. President Donald Trump, whom Miller worked for as a campaign and White House aide, called Miller a “good guy.” House Speaker Mike Johnson demurred when asked if he thought the allegations of physical abuse were disqualifying. “People have domestic disputes. It’s part of being flawed humans, as we are,” the Louisiana Republican told Politico.

“I hope he wins reelection. He’s done a good job as a member of Congress,” said Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

Of course, people outside the district weighed in to support Poindexter too. When we spoke, I brought up a new advertisement by the anti-Trump Lincoln Project. The one-minute spot featured an ominous voice flipping through screengrab after screengrab of court documents and headlines that detailed the serious allegations Miller faces, concluding that he’s a “domestic abuser” who “belongs in jail.”

I had sort of expected Poindexter to be pleased by their marketing work; a group founded by Republicans who rebuked Trump was spending $20,000 to batter his Republican opponent. The video cost Poindexter and his campaign $0. Since he didn’t make the advertisement, he didn’t even have to worry about a potential defamation lawsuit from his highly litigious opponent. But Poindexter seemed dejected.

“I did see the ad and I’m not a fan,” the 47-year-old Democrat told me. “What I don’t want to happen is make this a bigger fight. Then they start dumping resources into it.”

By “they,” Poindexter meant moneyed interests. And he was right. The Congressional Leadership Fund and National Republican Congressional Committee quickly got involved, dumping more than $5 million into the district in the final months of the contest.

Those millions were largely spent on media buys painting Poindexter as the dangerous one. At least two ads focused on a police report from the 1990s, which alleged Poindexter tried to “swallow a rock of suspected crack cocaine during a police stop.” One of the ads characterized that incident as part of a “30-year rap sheet for drugs and violence” with charges as recent as this year. Another said Poindexter “wants to go from crack to Congress.” (Poindexter’s campaign notes that he has taken random drug tests for the last 20 years as a union ironworker and never failed one.)

The “crack” allegation stems from a 1998 police report in which Poindexter, then 18, was accused by cops of swallowing what they suspected to be crack cocaine. The officer specified in the police report that past drug-related complaints in the area made them give “special attention” to the block. That’s when they saw Poindexter in his car. They went up to his window, at which point, he allegedly tried to swallow something.

“I tried to recover the objects and the [adult male] struggled to prevent me. We fell to the ground at which time I recovered the above rock of susp. Crack cocaine from the ground near his mouth,” the report says. Though Poindexter was arrested and taken into custody, he wasn’t ultimately charged with a crime. That’s because, he says, “I absolutely did not do that.”

“I did see the ad and I’m not a fan. What I don’t want to happen is make this a bigger fight. Then they start dumping resources into it.”

Former Brook Park mayor Mike Gammella, who worked with Poindexter on the city council, began laughing when I asked him about the police report’s characterization.

“Brian grew up hard. Brian didn’t grow up with a silver spoon in his mouth,” said Gammella, who was elected as an independent the same year Poindexter joined the council. “They mentioned he was in a crack-infested neighborhood. Well, guess what? That’s the neighborhood he grew up in.”

Mother Jones reviewed Poindexter’s legal records dating back three decades. Poindexter faced charges for other violations in the  ’90s and early 2000s: In 1999, when he was 20, he received a citation for carrying an open container in Pinellas County, Florida. In 2000, at age 21, Poindexter received two citations for possession of marijuana (under 100 grams). He pleaded guilty to alcohol-related disorderly conduct in 2002. Although Cuyahoga County has since destroyed the physical files under standard retention rules, archival remnants indicate he spent a brief time in custody. A year later, a 24-year-old Poindexter was charged with “aggravated disorderly conduct.” He was found guilty of a lesser misdemeanor and paid a $250 fine. In 2013, Poindexter was removed from a Major League Baseball game after allegedly slapping a stranger. That man told the Washington Free Beacon that the slap was over a comment the man made about Poindexter’s apparent ability to eat a hot dog in one bite. Poindexter was not convicted; the man he was accused of slapping declined to press charges.

Poindexter’s next brush with the law came a decade later, in 2023, when he pleaded guilty to a charge of setting off fireworks illegally over Fourth of July weekend. Ironically, as a member of the Brook Park City Council, he had previously voted against allowing fireworks in city limits. This year, Poindexter received two traffic violations for failing to leave enough distance from the car in front of him and texting while driving—a first-time offense.

Poindexter chalks many of these indiscretions up to being “young and dumb,” which is how Miller also characterized a series of incidents in his youth: punching a guy in the back of the head and running from the cops (2007), breaking a window at an apartment building (2008), crashing his car into a light pole (2011) with ecstasy and Klonopin in his system. In another, previously unreported police report that I obtained, Miller was said to have been caught smoking weed and then running from the cops while at University of Arizona’s freshman orientation in 2007.

Miller never responded to Mother Jones’ questions about these events. He previously told the Washington Post that, “growing up, everyone makes mistakes.”

One 30-second clip features an Ohio Sheriff saying she would not support Miller because of the serious allegations he faces. “Thirty-four years in law enforcement tells me Max Miller does not belong in power,” Summit County Sheriff Kandy Fatheree said. A later ad from Poindexter’s campaign focused entirely on the blue bunny saga, quoting Sen. Moreno, who called the debacle “the seventh layer of hell.”

But when I followed Poindexter on the trail, he didn’t want to go there. Emulating Sen. Bernie Sanders, who endorsed Poindexter in March, the candidate was focused on the cost of living, which is also what 64 percent of Ohio voters ranked as a top-two issue in a recent poll. It was the only thing he covered in his stump speech.

“Does anybody in here feel like the economy is doing great? How about gas prices?” he asked the 30 to 40 people sitting in a bonus room of the Bedford Branch public library. “How about the grocery store? You guys feel comfortable going to the grocery? I mean, I don’t know about you all, but I have experience putting things back on the shelves.”

Poindexter is doing better than many in his district. His union job as an ironworker and side gig as a Brook Park city councilman are stable—netting him $110,350 in 2025, according to his House financial disclosure form—though his attire doesn’t necessarily reflect a six-figure income. The tops of his gray Nikes have holes and the back pocket on his stained and faded blue jeans is permanently imprinted with the outline of his wallet.

As one of six kids raised on the west side of Cleveland by a bolt-maker and a stay-at-home mom, Poindexter says he’s never been accustomed to fancy things. As Poindexter tells it, vacations growing up were spent camping, and clothes were all hand-me-downs.

“We didn’t have everything, but we had the basics in life: You know, a strong family unit, a roof over our head. We knew we were going to eat every day,” he said.

It’s another way he differs from Miller, who is an heir to a real estate empire that sold to an international conglomerate for $11.4 billion in 2018. Miller now lives in the wealthy enclave of Bay Village, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Erie. Its annual per capita income of $69,148 is nearly double that of the industrial suburb near the airport where Poindexter lives, 12 miles southeast.

Poindexter says he’s running for office because the math—even to replicate his modest childhood—just doesn’t add up in his area anymore.

“I don’t know anybody who has six kids right now, and if they do, they’re not doing it on one income,” he said.

Miller has leaned on Sanders’ endorsement of Poindexter to characterize his opponent as a “socialist” who wants “higher taxes and government-run healthcare.” But Poindexter’s populism is less in-your-face. When asked about his views on implementing Medicare for All at an August event, he was non-committal, promising to look at how any proposed legislation on the issue would affect Ohioans first. “I don’t know if I could support that,” he said.

He told me his initial goal was merely to prevent his neighbors from having to turn to crowdfunding for medical emergencies. “We’re in the richest country on the planet, and we got to pay for medical bills through a GoFundMe. I think that’s way out of touch,” he said.

Pennywise lives — in the sewers of Maryland.

A mysterious man living in Baltimore’s sewers has allegedly been taunting and chasing kids down the street, according to an irate mother.

Unique Wiggins initially didn’t believe her children when they told her a creep lurking in the sewers was bothering and harrasing them, WJZ reported.

But after repeated complaints, the mom decided to investigate the subterranean nuisance.

“It was a Friday, and my daughter, who is 21, called and she was panicking. And I asked, ‘What’s wrong?’ And she said, ‘Mom, I’m scared. The man told me I can’t walk right here and to just dip.’ And I’m like, ‘What man?’ And she was like, ‘The man in the sewer,'” Wiggins told the outlet.

“I walk over to the little manhole sewer thing, and I hear somebody singing, and I think, ‘This is unbelievable.’ So I’m like, ‘Yo, yo, you,’ and he’s like, ‘What?’ And I said, ‘Leave my f–king kids alone,” she recalled of a confrontation with the unidentified man.

“And he said, ‘No, tell them to leave me alone’ And I said, ‘They can’t possibly be messing with you, and you are in the sewer,'” Wiggins said.

The sewer skulker even chased her children down the street, prompting Wiggins to call the police.

Cops, however, told her that sewers and culverts are public property, leaving their hands tied for solutions for kicking the man out of his underground home, the mom claimed.

“I don’t feel like I’m protected. I don’t feel like my kids are protected. I’m not saying this gentleman should necessarily go to jail, but he should not live in the sewer. He should not be able to be down there,” Wiggins said.

The concerned mom said officials need to do more to protect her children and the community from the belowground agitator.

“They can put a no trespassing sign there. They can put a no trespassing sign, and they can cover the holes. That’s what I would like to see. I would like Baltimore County to make me feel like I am a member of this community,” she said.

The Baltimore County Police Department told The Post they arrested the man on July 26, but he was released on his own recognizance. A “peace order” unrelated to the July case was obtained earlier this month and served to him on Thursday.

Cops also said they offered the man services but were unsuccessful, and that they installed a no-trespassing sign at a storm drain after complaints. Police added that “no manhole is involved.”

“The County has worked diligently to offer available services to this subject. Additionally, a no-trespassing sign has been put in place. Baltimore County will continue coordinating public safety efforts and outreach,” a department spokesperson said.

“Baltimore County will continue to work with our partners within government and in the community,” they said.

The man is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, police said.

A Florida toddler grabbed his father’s gun and accidentally shot himself fatally in the face while in a Burger King drive-thru Thursday — as his distracted dad tried to pay for dinner, police said.

The dad, who was carrying a pistol in his waistband, put it down in the car after his credit card was declined at the Burger King drive-thru window in Bartow, Fla., causing him to get distracted — and allowing his 3-year-old who was playing in the backseat to pick up the gun and mistakenly pull the trigger, according to FOX 13 Tampa Bay.

“We also know, at least from the initial info, that we can see where there is a bullet hole directly through the roof, and the child shot in the face,” Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd told reporters at a press conference.

The little boy was about to turn 4 on Monday.

The family had recently moved to the Sunshine State from Connecticut just four months earlier, prompting the credit card company to flag the transaction.

While the dad was dealing with the credit card company on his phone, he took his Glock handgun from his waistband and put it down on the seat — and grew preoccuppied while searching for another way to pay, deputies said.

Moments later, the boy grabbed the gun and accidentally discharged it, police said.

“So, subjectively … we think dad took the gun out, laid it down … and while he’s trying to figure out how to pay for dinner on the credit card, the child obviously sees the gun, picks it up, is playing with it, and shoots himself in the face,” Judd said.

A bystander called 911 and first responders rushed the child to a local hospital, but he was pronounced dead at 7:30 p.m.

The father holds a valid concealed carry permit — although that is not required in Florida, according to the sheriff.

If a kid gets ahold of a gun and hurts someone, the parent can be charged with a third-degree felony under state culpable negligence laws, the sheriff said.

While prosecutors with the Florida State Attorney’s Office will ultimately decide whether to file charges against the dad, Judd indicated there is little appetite to press the matter.

Noah LanardOctober 22, 2026

Mother Jones illustration; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty

Mother Jones illustration; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty

In December 2022, a 20-year-old California woman loaned most of her savings to a venture calling itself Lost Basin Holdings. In theory, the $25,000 loan from the young conservative, who asked to remain anonymous, would be used to develop remote land in northwestern Arizona. But when the loan came due in late 2024, she got nothing back.

The company’s founder, Robert McDowell, tried to reassure her. His company, he wrote in a December 2024 text, was “actively looking” for new investors so he could repay her. She asked McDowell, who court records show has been accused of fraud on multiple occasions as part of prior business dealings, about her money roughly a dozen times last year. In March 2025, he informed her, “We have new investors coming on board to raise $20M and buy up all our Notes.”

That is the same amount Arizona Land Reserve, a real estate development venture McDowell co-founded in January 2025, is seeking to raise by telling investors it aims to provide a “constant 20% annual return for the next 20 years.” What makes Arizona Land Reserve unique is its deep ties to David Flippo, a scandal-plagued Republican in an unexpectedly close race for Congress in northern Nevada. The company is Flippo’s largest identifiable asset, according to an unofficial financial disclosure his campaign provided to the Nevada Independent. He values his stake at between $1 million and $5 million.

“If he needs new investor money to repay existing loans, that suggests he lacks sufficient cash to meet his obligations,” Dubinsky said via email. “That dependence on fresh investor capital is a major red flag.”

Flippo’s ties to the company appear to extend beyond those of a typical passive investor. A person pitched on Arizona Land Reserve, who requested anonymity, told me Flippo was present for all of the investment meetings they attended. When the person asked Flippo if he could advise them on the deal, the source said the candidate declined, citing a conflict of interest. A text message I reviewed shows Stephen Tuminello, Arizona Land Reserve’s other co-founder, stating he has a “professional and business relationship with David Flippo.”

Flippo, in turn, has benefited from hundreds of thousands of dollars in political donations from Arizona Land Reserve and people in the company’s orbit. Taken together, it suggests Flippo—a retired Air Force officer and licensed financial adviser—may have used his credentials to help provide an air of legitimacy to a dubious company that spent lavishly on his behalf.

Flippo, McDowell, and Tuminello did not respond to detailed questions and repeated requests for comment for this article and a previous Mother Jones article about Arizona Land Reserve’s connection to Flippo. I initially reached out to Flippo’s campaign about his finances on September 14. The campaign has not responded to those inquiries.

Reached by phone on Wednesday, Rory McShane, Flippo’s main campaign consultant, said he did not have time to discuss my request for comment about Arizona Land Reserve. He asked that I send questions via email. McShane has not responded to those questions, which I initially sent to him and Flippo’s campaign on Friday.

Arizona Land Reserve says it is seeking to build Valle Privado, a “1st class fly-in community catering to the desires of Luxury Home & Ranch Owners in Arizona that prefer to use private aviation.” The raw land is miles from paved roads, according to county maps and land records. Some of the nearest towns are a former mining camp called Chloride, with about 75 residents, and Santa Claus, a Christmas-themed ghost town that was torn down in 2022.

To meet its target of “constant” 20 percent annual returns, Arizona Land Reserve has said it plans to acquire 3,000 apartments in central and midwestern states with $14 million in capital. It claims it will then use the rent money to fund development of the Arizona land it purchased with $4.8 million of debt last year. Mark Stapp, an expert in Arizona real estate development, put the chances of acquiring thousands of apartments for that amount at between “slim and none.” Overall, Stapp said, the project’s “feasibility is zero.”

Arizona Land Reserve is seeking to raise $20 million from investors in exchange for a 20 percent equity stake in the company, which implies a total valuation of $100 million. Stapp, who spoke to me independent of his role as the director of a real estate development program at an Arizona university, called that “insanity.” He added, “You’re not generating $100 million out of that project. You’re just not.” (I have found no evidence of Arizona Land Reserve buying apartments or filing any permits related to developing the main site.)

The contributions from Arizona Land Reserve are notable both because they seemed designed to pave the way for Flippo’s congressional campaign and because the company had no apparent source of funds other than investor capital.

Bruce Dubinsky, a forensic accountant who testified on behalf of the Justice Department in a case against employees of Bernie Madoff, said via email that “20% constant returns are a huge red flag.” He added, “Madoff didn’t even promise constant returns that high.”

Flippo, who first ran for Congress in 2024, has still not filed an official financial disclosure, even though he has been legally required to do so on an annual basis since 2023. Meanwhile, he has reported putting more than $2.5 million of his own money into his campaigns, despite having no apparent source of such wealth. Flippo has also not said whether his major stake in Arizona Land Reserve reflects money he invested or equity received in exchange for services on its behalf.

Bob Seale, who once served as the chairman of the Nevada Republican Party, submitted a complaint to the Federal Election Commission this week about the questions surrounding Flippo’s finances and campaign fundraising. The complaint draws on previous reporting from Mother Jones about Arizona Land Reserve. It also mentions a person listed as a major donor to Flippo’s campaign who told me they did not make the contribution attributed to them. After drawing parallels between Flippo and disgraced former Rep. George Santos, Seale wrote, “Where there is once again smoke, there might well again be fire.”

Flippo has also faced blowback related to false claims that he earned a Bronze Star with valor, when he actually received a standard Bronze Star. Mark Amodei, the retiring Republican congressman Flippo is running to replace, has now said he didn’t vote for his party’s nominee during early voting. When we spoke on Monday, Amodei reiterated his belief that Flippo is a “fraud” in light of the misrepresentations about Flippo’s military record and the questions surrounding the candidate’s personal and campaign finances.

“Where is that [money] from?” Amodei asked about the self-funding Flippo has reported. “Do you have any confidence on the non-answers? Or just plain ignoring the question: Well, who’s paying for this guy’s ‘personal loans’ to his campaign? That’s why I use the word fraud.”

To raise funds, Arizona Land Reserve’s co-founders have courted fellow conservatives, according to David Shapiro, the Las Vegas lender who sold the company its land and holds the debt on the heavily leveraged property. A second person pitched on an investment in Arizona Land Reserve also said Tuminello was targeting people at events in Nevada popular with Republicans. An ad for Patriot View, the name for a separate set of companies McDowell used to promote Lost Basin’s lots, shows the two men pursuing a similar strategy for that venture. In an advertisement in a conservative publication, they marketed the lots as “Prepper Ready.” The tagline of their project was “saving your money from the banks.” A large number of the people they persuaded to invest in that project were women in their seventies or eighties, public records show.

Flippo has known McDowell and Tuminello since at least May 2024, when the two men attended a fundraiser for his first congressional campaign. That month, Tuminello also paid Flippo’s wife on behalf of himself and McDowell in connection with a Las Vegas gala, a public Venmo record shows. Later in 2024, FINRA records show Flippo was fired from his job as a financial adviser for an offense related to “bearer bonds,” a largely obsolete financial product known for its use in money laundering and other illicit activities. (“I wasn’t fined for anything,” Flippo has said. “I didn’t lose any licenses.”)

Less than three weeks after Flippo was fired, a deed of trust filed in Mohave County listed his older brother Stephen Flippo as the lender on a more than $200,000 note to Lost Basin—the same company that owed the young investor. In January 2025, the month Arizona Land Reserve was formed, a second deed of trust named Stephen Flippo as the lender on a $136,000 note. On paper, $340,000 was secured by lots valued by the county at about $30,000 combined. The full picture was even more concerning. Shapiro, whose company also sold Lost Basin its land and loaned it $280,000 to execute the deal, told me earlier this month that he holds the senior lien on Lost Basin’s land, meaning Stephen Flippo’s loans could have been wiped out in the event of financial distress. (Stephen Flippo did not respond to requests for comment.)

That was true for other Lost Basin investors—including the young conservative, who did not know Shapiro was first in line to be paid back until we spoke. As with other investors, the land that theoretically secured her loan is assessed by Mohave County at a fraction of the capital she provided.

Shapiro said that McDowell has not yet paid off the $280,000 loan the Las Vegas lender’s company gave to Lost Basin in 2022. Shapiro added that he increased the interest rate from 6 percent to 12 percent after the original loan was not paid off in time. (He said McDowell remains current on his payments to him.)

McDowell has a record of bad debts and business failures. Two of his earlier ventures filed for bankruptcy in federal court. In one of those cases he was called a “con” by a man who did business with him, according to court records. In an earlier court case, he and his business partners in a gold mining venture called Rock Cabin Mining were accused of operating a “pyramid promotional scheme,” according to Arizona court records. The plaintiff, George Rhoads, said he never received the money awarded to his business after the gold-mining company was found liable for breach of contract. By 2019, after Rock Cabin Mining filed for bankruptcy, court records show that the the value of his claim stood at more than $99,000.

With Lost Basin, Mohave County records show McDowell’s companies paid off prior lenders just as Stephen Flippo’s transactions were recorded—reminiscent of how McDowell told the young conservative investor about using new money to pay off old debts. Found alone and oppressed by scavengers on a remote northern Alaska beach, an orphaned Pacific walrus calf now has a new home at SeaWorld Orlando.

Weighing approximately 220 pounds, the 5-month-old male calf, named Annautaq, is receiving around-the-clock attention from SeaWorld’s dedicated animal care and veterinary team—one of only four US institutions currently capable of housing walruses.

Annautaq’s rescue is quite remarkable. Violet Anniskett, a wildlife research intern and local community member, and US Geological Survey scientist Tony Fischbach discovered the calf on a remote beach in Northern Alaska after a walrus herd departed during heavy surf.

They found the orphaned calf hiding between the older remains of two adult walruses, already being targeted by scavenging birds and unlikely to survive without intervention.

The distance between the beach and human civilization meant that those who could cared for him over several days before he could be flown to the Alaska SeaLife Center in Seward.

The community supported Annautaq’s rehabilitation, knowing he would remain in human care and could help people better understand Pacific walruses. Anniskett named him Annautaq (pronounced “ah-now-tuq”), meaning “axe” in Iñupiaq, in honor of her father’s Iñupiaq name.

SeaWorld sent animal care and veterinary staff experienced with walruses to Alaska to help provide care for Annautaq, and to help the calf prepare for his 4,000-mile journey to Florida, where he would become one of 43,000 orphaned, injured, rejected, or otherwise needy animals since its establishment.

In part, it was because the US Fish and Wildlife Service determined he could not be released back into the wild. Pacific walruses rely solely on their mothers’ milk for nutrition throughout their first year of life and depend on their mother for protection and the development of essential survival and social behaviors.

With his mother out of the picture, his placement at SeaWorld Orlando was guided by long-term care and social needs, including the opportunity to grow up alongside other walruses, 3 others being housed at the center.

“Annautaq’s story shows why having specialized marine mammal rehabilitation capacity in Alaska is so important,” said Jane Belovarac, wildlife response curator at the Alaska SeaLife Center. “Getting Annautaq to this point took an incredible network of people, and we’re proud the ASLC could provide the specialized care that helped carry him from rescue in Alaska to his next chapter.”

RESCUING MARINE LIFE:

At SeaWorld Orlando, Annautaq is receiving up to 6 bottle feedings a day, veterinary care and 24-hour support during a planned 30-day quarantine to help protect the health of the resident animals.

“As he settles in, we’ll make introductions to Garfield, Kaboodle and Uki at his pace,” said Jim Kinsler, curator at SeaWorld Orlando. “Kaboodle’s experience caring for rescued calves and the opportunity to connect with 2-year-old Uki, herself a rescued walrus, make this herd a promising setting for him to learn, build relationships and grow.”

As he acclimates, Annautaq will join Uki in playing an essential role as an ambassador for their species, educating the public on the challenges Pacific walruses face in the wild. His story, like those of many other animals rescued by SeaWorld Orlando, emphasizes the park’s ongoing mission to inspire action toward the protection and preservation of marine life.
